Such faithful retriggering is, in fact, the proper functioning of the brain's emotional learning networks, not a faulty condition of disorder or dysregulation—unless one is prepared to say that it is a dysregulation of evolution itself, not of the individual. Of course, having a non-pathologizing view of emotional schemas does not make their tenacity any less impressive. So it is indeed a big deal that we now have clear, empirical knowledge of the brain's own rules for thoroughly depotentiating emotional learnings through MR. The understanding that a person's unwanted emotions, behaviors, or thoughts may be generated by non-conscious emotional learnings or conditioning has of course figured centrally in many forms of psychotherapy. The approach in this book embodies two major advancements: first, the swift and accurate experiential retrieval of those emotional learnings, bringing them into direct awareness, and second, the non-theoretically based, research-corroborated methodology of memory reconsolidation for prompt unlearning and dissolution of those retrieved learnings at their emotional and neural roots. Viewing symptom production as having a psychological cause in emotional learning is quite at odds with neuroscience research that aims to identify the molecular and cellular processes involved in, for example, anxiety responses, in order to develop drugs that would block or moderate such responses (e.g., Mucha et al., 2023). That reductionistic approach assumes that flawed operation of molecular or cellular processes is causal of unwanted psychological conditions. While such bottom-up, neurobiological causation certainly occurs in some conditions, it is shown to be untrue in all those cases, such as those documented in this book, where the unwanted psychological condition disappears promptly and permanently after a particular emotional schema has been thoroughly unlearned, so that it no longer reactivates or feels subjectively true. In such cases, the true cause of, for example, the person's chronically high anxiety was the schema in implicit memory, and the molecular and cellular processes involved in producing that state of anxiety were functioning properly in service of adaptive emotional learning systems. Therefore, the strategy of preventing that person's experience of anxiety by pharmacologically disabling the bottom-up mechanisms of anxiety generation leaves the distress-laden implicit schema intact and only blocks its affective expression into conscious experience. That is what some individuals do non-pharmacologically by maintaining a state of emotional dissociation, which is well known to psychotherapists to be the principal cause of somatizing, the creation of somatic symptoms due to blocking affective experience of emotional distress (for a vivid example

Maximum Psychotherapeutic Effectiveness 9 of which, see Chapter 12). So, it seems likely that the treatment of psychological symptoms by pharmacological interference of bottom-up processes may be a major cause of somatic symptoms in that manner.

#### The overall framework This book provides a unifying account of:

emotional learning and memory, with emphasis on its adaptive, coherent na-

ture and the specific content and structure of symptom-generating emotional implicit learnings • the unlearning and nullification of emotional implicit knowledge through the sequence of experiences required by the brain for memory reconsolidation to operate • the therapeutic reconsolidation process, which is the entire set of steps needed for consistently putting into practice the required sequence of experiences in psychotherapy sessions We call this unified body of knowledge the Emotional Coherence Framework, and we predict that it will expand your clinical vision and mastery invaluably, as it has ours. The therapeutic reconsolidation process, or TRP, consists of steps that guide you as therapist without cramping your individual style. An unlimited range of techniques can be used to create the set of experiences that fulfills this process, which is largely why your creativity and individual style of working continue to have great scope of expression in this approach. It involves richly experiential work that utilizes your skills of emotional attunement and focuses the use of your empathy so as to cooperate closely with the brain's rules for accessing and dissolving the emotional learnings at the root of your clients' presenting symptoms. Major, longstanding symptoms can cease as soon as their very basis no longer exists, as shown in the many case examples in this book. All of the depth, intimacy, and humanity of talk therapy at its best are preserved in this approach, for these valued qualities of therapy are key ingredients for successfully using the TRP to free clients from entrenched negative reactions, old attachment patterns, unconscious core schemas, traumatic memory, emotional wounds, and compulsive behaviors. New learning can create new neural encoding throughout one's lifetime, but it is only when new learning also revises and replaces the encoding of old learning that transformational change occurs, and this is precisely what the TRP achieves. The process fulfills the brain's requirements for allowing a new learning to rewrite and nullify an old, unwanted learning—and not merely suppress and compete against the old learning or “regulate” it. The result is lasting transformational change, as distinct from incremental change and ongoing symptom management.

10 The Emotional Coherence Framework The emotional learning and memory system converts the past into an expectation of the future, without our awareness, and that is both a blessing and a curse. It is a blessing because we rely daily on emotional implicit memory to navigate through all sorts of situations without having to go through the relatively slow, labor-intensive process of figuring out, conceptually and verbally, what to do; we simply know what to do and we know it quickly. It is easy to take for granted the amazing efficiency and speed with which we access and are guided by a truly vast library of implicit knowings. Yet our emotional implicit memory is also a curse because it makes the worst experiences and emotional learnings in our past persist as felt emotional realities in the present and in our present sense of the future, keeping us “prisoners of childhood.” In the three examples of schemas listed on p. 6, it is apparent that what seems and feels to the person so real about the world is not an external reality at all, but rather a vivid illusion or mirage maintained by emotional memory. It hardly seems an exaggeration to regard the limbic brain's power to create emotional reality as a kind of magic, or maya, that immerses one in a potent spell that feels absolutely real and would last for a lifetime. However, we now know how to induce the emotional brain to use its power to break and dissolve emotional spells that it previously created. The prison of emotional memory, built over the aeons in the course of evolution, comes with a key, and that key has now been found. The limbic life sentence can be commuted. That is what this book spells out. Of course, learning and memory are not at the root of all of the conditions that therapy seekers present. Examples of conditions not based in memory, and therefore not fundamentally dispellable by any type of MR process, include hard-wired neurological situations (such as those causing difficulties with learning or sensory experience) and biological conditions (such as hypothyroidism that causes a mood state of depression). Viewing symptom production as dysregulation may be accurate in such cases, but they are a small minority of those encountered by psychotherapists in general practice.

Book preview The twenty-six case examples of this book show the TRP applied to dispel a very wide range of symptoms and sufferings. If a particular symptom that you want to see addressed by the TRP is not covered here, you may be able to find a published case for it in the online index at https://bit.ly/2tKXdyX. Here is a broad view of the territory ahead in the chapters of Part 1: Chapter 2 explains how memory reconsolidation works by telling the story of the dramatic scientific turnaround caused by its discovery and showing why our knowledge of this phenomenon sets up major advances for psychotherapy. A clear, scientific distinction emerges between transformational change (in which

Maximum Psychotherapeutic Effectiveness 11 problematic emotional learnings are fully depotentiated and symptoms cannot recur) and incremental, partial change (which results from the counteracting of symptoms, requires ongoing effort to maintain, and remains susceptible to relapse). We map out how MR research findings optimally and directly translate into psychotherapeutic application, defining the therapeutic reconsolidation process as a versatile experiential methodology that undergirds psychotherapy for the first time with empirical knowledge of an internal mechanism of change. Chapter 3 presents the case of a man seeking therapy for his daily self- doubting and anxious insecurity at work, in order to demonstrate how psychotherapy can focus on carrying out the steps of the TRP for a given presenting symptom. This chapter also covers the basics of MR, so that the more detailed account of MR in Chapter 2 need not be fully digested in order to understand and begin using this therapeutic framework. It may be surprising to see that in following a potent process of change confirmed by neuroscientists in the laboratory, the richly human and humane qualities of the client–therapist relationship and the depths of personal meaning experienced by the client are not sacrificed at all. If Chapter 2 of this book is its scientific bedrock, Chapter 3 is the heart of its vision for therapy: facilitation of the TRP. The TRP is an integrative and open-access methodology because it is phenomenological and avoids theorybased interpretations, and because it does not impose particular techniques to be used for guiding clients into the necessary sequence of experiences. Thus any case example that illustrates the TRP for instructional purposes shows some particular set of techniques or system of therapy applied for creating those crucial experiences. For that instructional purpose in Part 1 of this book, we use a particular form of therapy—Coherence Therapy—because, as noted earlier, its methodology follows the TRP steps explicitly and recognizably. It is especially easy and transparent, in other words, to see the TRP in case examples of Coherence Therapy. The chapters of Part 2 show the TRP occurring in other systems implicitly, embedded within their methodologies. Chapter 4 puts the key moments of transformational change under still closer scrutiny in three case examples, so that you can see exactly what is involved and how well-defined and guidable the necessary experiences are. The examples— involving obsessive attachment, pervasive underachieving, and stage fright—all show the collaborative journey with each client and the therapist's choicefulness and creativity in finding how to guide each client into the key experiences. The journey metaphor is an apt one, because knowledge of the TRP serves very much as a compass and a map for working effectively in the territory of the client's non-conscious emotional learnings. Coherence Therapy supplies the therapist with a set of versatile techniques designed especially for the steps of the TRP, while always encouraging the therapist to improvise variations, or adapt techniques from other therapies, or invent new techniques as best suits the unfolding process with each client. Once again—because it bears repeating—the process is not defined by any particular techniques (the journey's concrete modes of

12 The Emotional Coherence Framework transportation), including the basic techniques normally taught in Coherence Therapy, though of course the techniques have to be experiential because the core process consists of certain experiences, as distinct from cognitive insights. Chapter 5 focuses on working with insecure attachment using the TRP and the conceptualization of attachment work in the Emotional Coherence Framework. We will see that the fully experiential retrieval of a given symptom's underlying emotional learnings—the shift from implicit knowing to explicit knowing, as required for consistent success with the TRP—makes apparent whether these underlying learnings are attachment-related, not attachment-related, or a combination of the two. This allows a non-speculative, non-theoretical determination of whether a given presenting symptom is or is not a manifestation of insecure attachment—often a matter of considerable controversy among both clinicians and researchers. Such clarity regarding the nature of the underlying learnings in turn sheds light on the optimal role and possible uses of the client–therapist relationship with a given client; there is quite a range of strongly held opinions about this, as well. Here, too, the Emotional Coherence Framework provides an illuminating perspective of a non-theoretical nature, and can help steer us clear of theoretical biases in clarifying some of the more complex and thorny issues in psychotherapy. Chapter 6 expands upon the TRP serving as a unifying framework for the psychotherapy field, thereby setting the stage for Part 2 in which that unification is demonstrated concretely and unambiguously for eight major therapeutic systems. The discussion here includes the challenge that the TRP poses to nonspecific common factors theory and why this may auger a fundamental shift in perspective on common factors theory; and we note supporting findings from psychotherapy process research. Part 2 of the book consists of Chapters 7 to 14, which examine case examples of transformational change from the eight quite different systems of psychotherapy listed above. The original account of each case is fine-grained, allowing the kind of moment-to-moment scrutiny required for detecting whether the component experiences of the therapeutic reconsolidation process occurred. We show that they did, demonstrating the unifying value of the TRP. This framework of unification is also supported by the fact that memory reconsolidation, the existence of which was first established in 2000, remains (as of this writing in 2023) the only type of neuroplasticity known to neuroscience that is capable of fully depotentiating and functionally eliminating a specific emotional learning, as in each of these eight case examples. Part 3, comprising Chapters 15 to 24, consists of case examples contributed by practitioners of Coherence Therapy. We selected these cases because they complement and extend the illustrations of the TRP in Parts 1 and 2 in various ways: different, important types of symptoms dispelled (indicated in the table of contents), child clients from six to fourteen years old, the therapists' diversity

Maximum Psychotherapeutic Effectiveness 13 of styles and choices, larger numbers of sessions in several cases, and candid accounts of how the therapist grappled with challenges and obstacles along the way, including client resistance and the need for technique improvisation. We think you will be fascinated and inspired, as we were, by these true tales of therapeutic adventure and triumph.

The Emotional Coherence Framework and your clinical development In conducting trainings in this approach since 1993, we have seen that most psychotherapists and counselors—ourselves included—seek certain kinds of satisfaction in their practices in order to sustain the inspiration and meaningfulness that originally attracted them to this challenging, difficult work. To conclude this introductory chapter, we list common dilemmas that our therapist colleagues and trainees have described as developing over time in their clinical work, motivating them to seek some revitalizing approach. Along with each dilemma, we preview how this book helps meet these professional challenges. As a therapist I feel I ought to know, in advance, the interventions that will eliminate my client's symptoms, and that burden gives me angst. That assumption and the angst it generates are dispelled by understanding symptom production in terms of coherent, implicit emotional learnings that are unique to each client. For example, each of your panic attack clients has a unique emotional learning history. It is only after finding and revealing a client's specific emotional learnings that a pathway to a liberating change can then be found, without needing to know in advance what the pathway will be. My client's symptoms seem to be maintained by some powerful but elusive force that has a life of its own. Client and therapist can readily find and thoroughly demystify the source of the power driving unwanted states and behaviors. The source consists of implicit emotional learnings that are urgently committed to certain tactics for avoiding suffering and ensuring well-being. You can bring about transformational change through welcoming, valuing, and cooperating with these learnings instead of battling them. Searching for relevant information in a client's past too often feels like looking for a needle in a haystack. Bringing to light the truly relevant elements in your client's emotional memory can become quicker, easier, and more accurate by using simple coherence-guided experiential methods designed for that purpose. I feel that my efforts are too easily rendered ineffectual by clients' resistance. Like other seemingly negative responses, resistance is coherent and full of accessible emotional meaning that can pivotally assist the therapeutic process if it is honored and sensitively “unpacked” and understood.

14 The Emotional Coherence Framework I frequently help clients deeply understand the causes of their symptoms, yet no real shift occurs and their suffering persists. That's because revealing and understanding the underlying emotional learnings is only the first half of the process of transformational change. The rest of the process is well-defined in the TRP, but doesn't just happen by itself, as a rule. I want my sessions to provide me more often with learning experiences for growth of my clinical skill and understanding. The process explained in this book will teach you to make new uses of your existing skills as well as add new skills to your repertoire. Guiding clients to retrieve implicit emotional learnings into awareness involves steady tracking of a client's experience in each session, supplying you with ongoing feedback on your clinical choices, as does eliciting client feedback early in each session on the effects of the previous session and between-session task. At the end of my workday, I seldom feel satisfied that I've facilitated new breakthroughs that end my clients' sufferings. Real breakthroughs can be a frequent occurrence in your day-to-day practice, thanks to the knowledge we now have of the brain's built-in process for profound change of existing, core emotional learnings. For us clinicians, hearing a client report a decisive change in glowing terms is a moment of deep professional fulfillment. Imagine enjoying several such moments every week…

How the Brain Unlearns Memory Reconsolidation Explained Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

A very little key will open a very heavy door.

—Charles Dickens

It may seem too obvious to state that unlearning is a reversal of learning, but when it is the neural encoding of learning and unlearning that we are considering, understanding that reversal is not so obvious. It turns out that a very complex process is being reversed—the process that memory researchers have termed consolidation, which transforms a fragile initial neural encoding, formed immediately after a learning experience and easily undone by various procedures, into a stable, durable neural encoding in long-term memory, elsewhere in the brain (McGaugh, 2000). Before the discovery of memory reconsolidation (MR) in the 1997–2000 period (reviewed by Riccio et al., 2006), nearly a century of extinction studies had achieved only temporary suppression of a consolidated, acquired emotional response, with no evidence of destabilizing the stable state of the neural encoding of that response, nor of fundamentally unlearning the target emotional learning (Bouton, 2004). Extinction studies showed that extinction training forms a separate learning in a physically separate memory system from that of the target learning, and that the extinction learning competes against, but does not replace, the target learning (e.g., Bouton, 2004; Foa & McNally, 1996; Milner et al., 1998; Phelps et al., 2004). Researchers therefore believed consolidation to be a one-time, one-way process producing a permanent, locked state that made an emotional memory “indelible” for a lifetime (LeDoux et al., 1989), in both animals and humans.

The key that unlocks emotional memory: Prediction error The discovery of MR was something of an upheaval for the neuroscience of learning and memory because that discovery consisted of detection of the destabilization, or de-consolidation, of a consolidated emotional learning in rats DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-3

16 The Emotional Coherence Framework (Nader et al., 2000). Through Pavlovian conditioning, those researchers first created the learned, fear-laden expectation of an electric shock occurring after an audio tone, expressed by the rats as freezing in response to the tone. One day later, after that memory had become consolidated, the memory and its behavioral expression could be nullified by first presenting only the tone to reactivate the memory, and then soon administering a chemical agent that prevents a new, notyet- consolidated learning from ever consolidating, but has no effect on consolidated memories. The fact that erasure of the conditioned response resulted from this treatment appeared to mean that in response to reactivation, the consolidated memory's neural encoding became de-consolidated into a “labile,” destabilized condition. If administered at 6 hours after reactivation, the chemical agent had no effect, indicating that by then, memory restabilization or reconsolidation had occurred. Annulment of the memory in this pharmacological manner was possible only during the “reconsolidation window” of about 5 hours. (As can be seen in the last two sentences, the term “reconsolidation” is used by neuroscientists in two different ways—to denote the relocking or restabilization of a neural encoding at the end of the labile period, or to refer to the brain's overall process of destabilizing and then restabilizing the neural encoding of a specific memory. In this book, we have attempted to make each use of the term clear by its context.) Nader et al. (2000), as well as other authors of early MR studies, interpreted their observations to mean that memory reactivation had caused de-consolidation, allowing pharmacological erasure. Their conclusion that every reactivation of a memory induces its destabilization, followed by its reconsolidation, quickly became established, canonical knowledge throughout the neuroscience field, as well as in science journalism. After several years of entrenchment of that model, in 2004 a study by Argentinian neuroscientists showed that destabilization did not occur in response to reactivation alone (Pedreira et al., 2004). Rather, what induced destabilization, launching the MR process, was reactivation of the target learning plus a concurrent, additional experience of a “mismatch” between what the reactivated learning expected and what was actually now perceived. The brain's de- consolidation requirement of that mismatch experience, also known as an experience of prediction error, thereafter has been confirmed by at least 30 other studies (listed online at https://bit.ly/2b8IbJH and by Ecker, 2018). The fundamental role and importance of a prediction error experience for triggering destabilization and launching the MR process is indicated by the publication from 2015 to 2019 of four different review articles focused entirely on the dependence of MR on prediction error (Exton-McGuinness et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2016; K rawczyk et al., 2017; Sinclair & Barense, 2019). In their review of MR research, Silva and Gräff (2023, p. 9) plainly summarize, “PE was found to be paramount for memory reconsolidation in multiple lines of evidence, in both rodents and humans.” It has also been shown that the procedures of the early MR studies, including that of Nader et al. (2000), did indeed contain the necessary mismatch

How the Brain Unlearns 17 experience (Bellfy & Kwapis, 2020; Ecker, 2015a), but evidently it went unnoticed by the study authors. Across those numerous studies confirming the prediction error requirement, concrete procedures for creating the mismatch experience and thereby inducing destabilization have varied greatly, showing clearly that what matters to the brain is the subjective experience of violation of expectation, not the particular procedure used for creating that experience. This distinction between external procedures and internal experiences proves to be crucial for both understanding experimental results and for the translation of MR research findings into therapeutic application (Ecker, 2018, 2021). It means that psychotherapists are not constrained to using any particular techniques for creating the key experiences that recruit the MR process, as is shown abundantly in the rest of this book. However, even as confirmations of the prediction error requirement accumulated steadily after 2004, the erroneous initial inference that each and every reactivation of a memory induces the MR process continued to be believed and promulgated by many neuroscience researchers for well over a decade. This disarray and unawareness of the prediction error requirement has had numerous unfortunate effects, including studies of MR done with no mismatch in the postreactivation procedure, resulting in both failure to induce memory destabilization and misinterpretations of experimental results (e.g., Cammarota et al., 2004; Hernandez & Kelley, 2004; Mileusnic et al., 2005; reviewed by Ecker, 2015a). Researchers view prediction error as a type of “boundary condition” on the MR process, meaning a variable condition or parameter that allows MR to occur only within a certain range of its variation. Many studies have systematically varied the details and degree of prediction error (post-reactivation violation of expectation) in order to reveal the range within which MR occurs, and indeed the observations show that a mismatch implemented in the procedure can be either too weak or too strong to create a prediction error experience that destabilizes the target learning (e.g., Alfei et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021; Díaz-Mataix et al., 2013; Jarome et al., 2012b; Li et al., 2017; López et al., 2016; Merlo et al., 2014; Piñeyro et al., 2014; Schroyens et al., 2017; Sevenster et al., 2013, 2014). In both cases, destabilization and MR do not occur, so the target memory persists unchanged by the procedure. “Too weak” means the mismatch was too subtle to be unambiguous as a mismatch, or even noticed; and “too strong” means the mismatch differed from expectations so much that the experience registered subjectively as not relevant to the target learning's expectations, and therefore was not experienced as an error of expectation (which has been conceptualized as the perception of a different “latent cause” in terms of Bayesian analysis of evolving knowledge; see Courville et al., 2006; Gershman et al., 2013). Analyzing mismatch procedures in that way in human MR studies has been shown by Ecker (2021) to yield a consistent, unified explanation of why twenty studies succeeded and fourteen studies failed to eliminate an acquired emotional reaction.

18 The Emotional Coherence Framework These nuances and complexities of achieving memory destabilization via prediction error in laboratory studies have been viewed by researchers as a problem for therapeutic application (e.g., Beckers & Kindt, 2017; Treanor et al., 2017). However, that problem does not actually exist because, as explained by Ecker (2018, p. 52): the delicacy of mismatch \[i.e., of creating prediction error and memory destabilization\] observed in laboratory studies is a direct effect of the artificially precise structure of the target learnings created by researchers, not an inherent feature of the reconsolidation process that would necessarily carry over into the clinical setting. … \[T\]he detailed structure and content of the target learning determine the post-reactivation experiences that will, or will not, mismatch and destabilize the target learning. Thus the finding that Pavlovian target learnings are mismatched and destabilized by post-reactivation procedures that may vary within only a narrow range of parameters is entirely due to the precisely ordered structure of Pavlovian target learnings designed by researchers. In a similar manner, a careful analysis of important differences between the unnatural conditions in laboratory studies and the conditions in psychotherapy sessions reveals that several other identified potential obstacles to successful clinical use of MR are found not to exist. For extended discussion and analysis of these issues, see Ecker (2018, pp. 51–60). This book is a testament to the absence in psychotherapy of those obstacles anticipated on the basis of assumptions that apply only in laboratory studies.

The MR process of profound unlearning As noted, the full annulment or “erasure” of an emotional learning was first accomplished using a chemical agent to render the destabilized neural encoding of the target memory defunct. Soon, however, came studies showing that without any such pharmacological treatment, the target memory could be permanently altered by relevant new learning during the reconsolidation window (e.g., Galluccio, 2005; Walker et al., 2003), presumably by directly revising or “re-writing” its neural encoding according to the new learning. Then came the first successful use of this MR methodology of behavioral updating to fully unlearn and eliminate a fearful emotional learning, or threat memory, in animals (Monfils et al., 2009) and humans (Schiller et al., 2010). Full, lasting unlearning is precisely what extinction studies had never achieved. Numerous other, subsequent studies then demonstrated the same striking effect—the unlearning and nullification of a fear-generating threat memory response via behavioral updating (reviewed by, for example, Bellfy & Kwapis, 2020; Clem & Schiller, 2016; Ecker, 2021; Elsey & Kindt, 2017; Silva & Gräff, 2023).

How the Brain Unlearns 19 Just as the many studies confirming the prediction error requirement created the same critical experiences through a wide range of different procedures, here too, the same set of experiences was created in all studies that replicated the decisive unlearning effect, though many different concrete procedures were used for doing so (Ecker, 2018; for a detailed review of the first twenty human studies of behavioral updating that reported full unlearning of an emotional memory, see Ecker, 2021). Researchers have also continued to develop the pharmacological approach for therapeutic use (reviewed by, e.g., Pigeon et al., 2022). The potent chemical agents used in animal studies are toxic for humans, so human studies have been limited to the pharmaceutical beta-blocker propranolol, which is the one safe substance known to block neural protein synthesis, as needed for disrupting the reconsolidation process. For both the pharmacological and the behavioral updating approaches to emotional memory annulment in laboratory studies, there have been numerous replication failures, but the large arrays of successes have put the existence of both phenomena on solid empirical ground. This book covers the use of only the behavioral process in psychotherapy because from our point of view, behavioral updating is strongly advantageous for general use in psychotherapy practices, for these reasons:

As stated by two prominent researchers of the pharmacological approach

(Soeter & Kindt, 2011, p. 358), “Obviously, a behavioral procedure will be preferred over pharmacological manipulations provided that similar effects can be obtained.” The wide range of clinical symptoms already observed to be fully dispelled by the behavioral approach is indeed much larger than has been documented using propranolol. (See Table 3.2 on p. 47 for a list of symptoms ended through the behavioral process, and for a list of published cases see https://bit.ly/2tKXdyX, including those documented in detail in peer-reviewed journal articles: Ecker, 2015a, 2018; Ecker & Bridges, 2020; Ecker & Toomey, 2008; Ecker & Vaz, 2022; Vaz & Ecker, 2020.) • The behavioral process has been shown to eliminate threat memory from both the subcortical (amygdala) emotional implicit memory system and also the neocortical declarative memory system (Agren et al., 2012; Björkstrand et al., 2015; Oyarzún et al., 2012; Schiller et al., 2010, 2013), whereas the latter memory system is not cleared of threat memory pharmacologically (Beckers & Kindt, 2017; Soeter & Kindt, 2010). • The behavioral approach is available for use by all psychotherapists, counselors, and coaches, in all categories of licensure, whereas presumably only a small minority of clinicians is eligible to use the pharmacological approach. For those reasons, the focus of this book is the therapeutic application of the behavioral updating process. The implementation of that process allows a wide spectrum of variations in procedure, which can be designed to produce change

20 The Emotional Coherence Framework in the strength and/or content of the target learning in virtually any desired manner. The target learning can be strengthened, weakened, fully nullified, modified in its specific content, or its encoding can be “integrated” (meaning conjoined) with the encoding of the memory of a salient new experience (e.g., Forcato et al., 2010; Haubrich et al., 2015; Lee, 2010).

The unlearning sequence: A critical set of experiences For purposes of psychotherapy, the most potent form of behavioral updating is the one that produces profound unlearning and nullification of a target emotional learning or schema. Profound unlearning results from a set of experiences that is apparent in all human and animal studies that fully eliminated an emotional learning. It begins with the same experiences described in the previous section for triggering destabilization of the target learning, namely, first the experience of the reactivated target learning (a particular, subjective expectation or knowing of how some part of the world will behave) and second, a concurrent experience of anything that noticeably mismatches that expectation or knowing and registers subjectively as a prediction error experience. However, that second step now has this specialization: The prediction error experience consists of a perception or knowing that unmistakeably contradicts what the target learning expects and knows. For example, if the target learning in a laboratory study is the Pavlovian expectation that a particular audio tone ends with an electric shock, for Step 1 a presentation of that audio tone produces reactivation, and then for Step 2 the absence of any shock when the tone ends is a contradiction of the expected behavior of the world (conventionally termed “nonreinforcement” in the procedure-oriented jargon of memory research, but that term does not quite identify the subjective quality of experiencing a contradiction of what was expected). Whereas, if the shock occurs but is felt at a changed, unexpected part of the body, that would be a prediction error experience but not a fundamental contradiction of the target learning. In therapy sessions, there are many ways to find a contradictory knowing that specifically disconfirms the client's unique target schema, as shown in the case examples throughout this book. The possible sources of contradictory knowings include observations and perceptions of the world, personal behavioral experiences, and internal construals of new meaning. The last was shown in a controlled study by Speer et al. (2021) to update a reactivated episodic memory via MR, resulting in a changed emotional response accompanying memory reactivation. As noted, a milder form of prediction error could also do the job of triggering destabilization, but setting up the full-strength contradiction in Step 2 is efficient, because Step 3, the last step of the unlearning sequence, is the repetition several times of that same pairing, or juxtaposition, of Step 1 and Step 2: reactivation and contradiction, reactivation and contradiction, reactivation and

How the Brain Unlearns 21 contradiction. The first such pairing, created by Step 2, has the function of triggering destabilization of the target learning (unlocking its neural encoding and rendering it open to being rewritten by new learning). The repetitions of the juxtaposition in Step 3 function as that new learning, and it is the learning of a disconfirmation of what is known and expected in the target learning. This rewrites the target learning accordingly, cancelling and nullifying the original version. The neural encoding then reconsolidates in its updated form (demonstrated using engram tagging by Khalaf et al., 2018), and the original version no longer exists in emotional memory and therefore can no longer be reactivated (with no dimming of the autobiographical, episodic memory of the original subjective experiences in which the target schema was learned). The fundamental difference between the pharmacological and behavioral methods of nullifying an emotional learning is important to understand. The pharmacological method consists of creating a chemical “blockade” of the protein synthesis necessary for a destabilized neural encoding to reconsolidate. This blockade disrupts the neurophysiological reconsolidation process itself, so the target learning never reconsolidates and becomes nonresponsive after 24 hours, without any unlearning having occurred. In contrast, nullification through behavioral updating consists of an experience of disconfirmation and unlearning that disrupts only the content of the target learning, not the reconsolidation process itself. The revised neural encoding reconsolidates (restabilizes) and continues to function (as shown by Khalaf et al. (2018) using neuron tagging techniques). This difference is particularly significant in the context of psychotherapy, where the unlearning is experienced subjectively as a lucid, meaningful recognition of the falseness of a distressing mental model of the world or oneself, and as a liberating release into a world free of that negative condition. To summarize so far, all laboratory studies that have eliminated an emotional learning through the behavioral updating process of MR did so by creating these three experiences in animal or human subjects, which we term the unlearning sequence1: 1 Reactivation. Retrigger/re-evoke the subjective experience of the expectations and knowings in the target learning by presenting salient cues or contexts, which are components of the original learning. 2 Concurrent contradictory experience. While maintaining reactivation, create an experience that contradicts the target learning's knowings and expectations of how the world is or behaves. This juxtaposition is a prediction error experience that renders the memory's encoding destabilized, or labile, and therefore susceptible to being updated by new learning. 3 Disconfirmation and unlearning. Soon repeat the same juxtaposition several times. This is an experience of new learning that disconfirms the target learning and revises its neural encoding accordingly, eliminating the original learning from emotional memory.

22 The Emotional Coherence Framework The unlearning sequence makes explicit the brain's requirements for profound unlearning and annulment of an emotionally intense mental model or schema. It is a major empirical finding of neuroscience. Importantly, this sequence of experiences is not defined in terms of any particular procedures or techniques, so it can be replicated in psychotherapy sessions using any suitable methods in a therapist's repertoire. This book is a guided tour of a huge array of suitable methods for facilitating this potent process.

Transformational change defined by three markers Following the three-step unlearning sequence, at least one day later researchers also conduct a verification step consisting of behavioral tests of whether the target learning's characteristic behavioral and/or affective, physiological responses can still be evoked by cues that formerly did so. We will refer to this as Step V (for verification). Full unlearning and annulment of an emotional learning produces the following unique, verifiable markers that are crucially important, in both research and psychotherapy, for confirming that unlearning has occurred:

Schema reactivation, in which the knowings and expectations in the target learning feel compellingly real and are accompanied by physiological and emotional arousal, can no longer be triggered by cues and contexts that formerly did so. • Behaviors, emotions, thoughts, and somatic sensations (i.e., “symptoms”) that were expressions of that schema reactivation cease to occur. • Both of those changes persist effortlessly, permanently, and without counteractive or preventive measures of any kind.

We define transformational change as consisting of those three observables, which we refer to hereafter as the markers of transformational change. Observations of those markers verify the complete nullification and elimination of a particular emotional learning (schema, mental model) and all of its expressions in behavior, state of mind, and state of body. According to current neuroscience, only the MR mechanism can produce the markers of transformational change, which are effortless to maintain because the old learning no longer exists in memory. This complete nullification and lasting elimination of an emotional learning cannot be produced by extinction or any other counteractive/competitive/ inhibitory processes (for a survey of which, see Toomey & Ecker, 2009), including most techniques of emotional regulation. Change brought about by all such inhibitory or competitive processes is usually only partial, requires ongoing effort to maintain, and is inherently susceptible to relapse, particularly in new or stressful situations. After successful facilitation of the unlearning sequence in psychotherapy, the markers of transformational change begin to appear next, meaning either later in

How the Brain Unlearns 23 the same session or in the client's daily life before the next session. That strong, unique effect following promptly after a well-defined, distinctive procedure is regarded by researchers as significant evidence of causation, not merely correlation (Ecker & Vaz, 2022; Kazdin, 2007). In animal studies, brain assays conducted after the unlearning sequence have detected unambiguous neurochemical and cellular signatures of the MR process (Bellfy & Kwapis, 2020; Clem & Huganir, 2010; Jarome et al., 2012a; Khalaf et al., 2018; Monfils et al., 2009). Therefore, based on that proof in animal studies, in human studies that carry out the unlearning sequence, neuroscientists regard the markers of transformational change as their best evidence of successfully recruiting the MR mechanism. So whenever the markers of transformational change are observed and established unambiguously in therapeutic work, the unlearning and nullification of an emotional learning via MR is a scientifically valid inference. Likewise, to the extent that any particular system or methodology of psychotherapy is shown to produce those markers regularly and characteristically, it can validly be claimed that that system or methodology utilizes MR to produce transformational change. Parts 1 and 2 of this book show transformational change being achieved in case examples from nine different systems of psychotherapy, and further show that in each case, the markers began to appear promptly after the therapeutic process had created the three experiences in the unlearning sequence listed above. By revealing that shared core process or deep structure—often hidden in plain sight behind salient therapeutic techniques that vary greatly from system to system—MR serves as a unifying framework for the psychotherapy field, which is more fully discussed in Chapter 6.

The many varieties of MR in psychotherapy As noted earlier in this chapter, the unlearning sequence is the particular form of behavioral recruitment of the MR mechanism that produces full unlearning for transformational change, the most liberating and effective result of psychotherapy. The unlearning sequence and its fully nullifying effects are a highly specialized recruitment of MR, not representative of the many other, different ways that the MR mechanism can be recruited for producing many different types and degrees of change in many different types of memory. For example, a different type of procedure uses MR to “integrate”—meaning conjoin or graft— the memory of a new, positive emotional experience with the memory of a traumatic experience, the result of which is the permanent co-reactivation of both, so that the positive memory “interferes” with—partially mutes—the traumatic memory reactivation (e.g., Grella et al., 2022; Högberg & Hällström, 2018; Lane et al., 2015). Advocating this use of MR in psychotherapy, Lane et al. (2015, p. 3) state, “we propose that change occurs by activating old memories and their associated emotions, and introducing new emotional experiences in

24 The Emotional Coherence Framework therapy enabling new emotional elements to be incorporated into that memory trace via reconsolidation.” However, this therapeutic strategy is inherently less effective than transformational change resulting from the unlearning sequence. The overall perspective on MR phenomenology is described in this way by Ecker and Vaz (2022, p. 4): Thus, by itself the term “memory reconsolidation” denotes not a particular type or degree of change, but rather the fundamental mechanism that destabilizes and then restabilizes (deconsolidates and then reconsolidates) the encoding of a target learning. That deconsolidation/reconsolidation process allows a target learning to be re-encoded and updated but does not in itself cause a target learning to be changed. Change is separately driven by current learning experiences during the reconsolidation window. If no learning occurs during that window, the result of undergoing deconsolidation/reconsolidation is only a slight strengthening of the target learning and a slight increase of its precision (e.g., Campos-Arteaga et al., 2020; De Oliveira Alvares et al., 2013; Forcato et al., 2014). The updating (modification) of memory contents by learning during the reconsolidation window is a completely auxiliary and optional process, not an inherent component of the MR process of destabilization/restabilization.

Therapists' most frequent questions about MR The pragmatics of consistently facilitating the unlearning sequence successfully in psychotherapy sessions are mapped out in the section after this one. First, we address in this section several questions that therapists most frequently ask about the unlearning sequence in seeking an adequate scientific understanding of the process:

- • • • • •

How specific and well-focused is the unlearning effect? Does the MR process of unlearning require emotional arousal? Is this old wine (“corrective emotional experiences”) in new bottles (“MR”)? Why doesn't the unlearning sequence induce extinction rather than MR? What really happens to the neural encoding of an unlearned schema? Why are fears and addictions the only therapeutic applications of MR mentioned in research articles by neuroscientists?

(For more extensive discussions of these and other aspects of MR and unlearning, see Ecker, 2015a, 2018, 2021; Ecker & Bridges, 2020; Ecker & Vaz, 2022.)

The specificity of unlearning When an emotional learning is unlearned and annulled via MR, the effect is restricted to precisely the reactivated target learning, without impairing any other

How the Brain Unlearns 25 closely related emotional learnings that have not been directly reactivated in Step 1 of the unlearning sequence. This specificity was shown both in an animal study using chemically induced erasure (Debiec et al., 2006) and in a human study using behavioral updating (Schiller et al., 2010). Furthermore, Kindt et al. (2009) demonstrated in a human study that chemical erasure of a learned fear did not impair explicit autobiographical memory: After the learned fear response had been eliminated, subjects still remembered the experiences in which they had acquired the conditioned fear response, as well as the fact of having had the fear, but the fear was not re-evoked by remembering those experiences. Thus the extent of the learnings and memories nullified via MR is highly defined and controllable, as is necessary for safe clinical application.

Does the MR process of unlearning require emotional arousal? The answer to this question is yes on the operational level in psychotherapy, but also no on the fundamental level of the MR mechanism itself, and it is important to understand both sides of this issue. Step 1 of the unlearning sequence is reactivation of the target learning, so if, and only if, the target memory contains an emotion-generating element—as is nearly always the case in psychotherapy— then emotional arousal is naturally and necessarily part of that experience. This yes answer to the question is due entirely to the reactivation requirement and the fact that the unwanted patterns addressed in psychotherapy do involve emotional learnings, as a rule. With that understanding, it is also important to recognize that the core of an emotional learning, and the target of change in using the unlearning sequence, is a mental model of some portion of the world, not the emotion that arises from that mental model. For example, a man in therapy for social anxiety is found to carry an emotional learning consisting of the mental model of all people as responding to anything they deem erroneous with harsh, angry criticism and shaming (formed as a generalization of experiencing his father reacting to him that way in childhood hundreds of times). That expectation is distinct from, although linked to, the emotion of fear and the feeling of anxious vulnerability that arise when that semantic memory content (memory of a pattern in how the world functions) is reactivated by being among others. So, “It is the model that is being disconfirmed and unlearned, not the emotion. … A transformational change in the model immediately produces profound change in the emotion generated” (Ecker, 2018, p. 80). The fact that a change of emotion occurs due to a change made via MR in the mental model that had been generating that emotion has been demonstrated in a controlled study by Speer et al. (2021). Of course, a therapy client's emotional states during therapy sessions must be facilitated with great care and skill, a task that often necessarily occupies much time and attention in sessions, even though that emotion is not itself the target of change. The process of heading toward and accessing a distressing schema or mental model that is the target of change necessarily first encounters and

26 The Emotional Coherence Framework moves through the emotions produced by that schema. If those emotions cannot yet be tolerated by the client, access to the underlying schema is also blocked. Therefore, making those emotions workable for the client to feel is necessary in order to then access the underlying schema, bring conscious awareness to it, and subject it to disconfirmation and unlearning. Facilitating direct experience of previously blocked emotion tends, in itself, to alleviate certain symptoms, and has been shown to correlate strongly with positive therapeutic outcome (e.g., Elliott et al., 2003; Missirlian et al., 2005), but will not by itself achieve transformational change unless, in addition, the underlying schema undergoes disconfirmation. The no answer to the question comes from a great many laboratory MR studies that have demonstrated de-consolidation and modification or nullification of target memories that have no emotional content, such as a set of syllable pairings in declarative memory (Forcato et al., 2009), object recognition learnings (Rossato et al., 2007), and motor task learnings (Walker et al., 2003). In such cases there is no emotional content in either the reactivated target memory, the experience that mismatches the reactivated memory, or the new learning that then revises the target learning. Thus an extensive body of research has shown that the MR mechanism itself is not defined by any one type of memory and clearly does not inherently require or involve emotional arousal. However, there exist several accounts of the broad therapeutic use of MR that incorrectly assert a fundamental role of emotional arousal in the MR mechanism (Lane et al., 2015; Stevens, 2019; Welling, 2012). These accounts barely reference and do not substantively consider MR research findings, so in them one finds no indication of the prediction error requirement or the unlearning sequence, the two most important findings of MR research. Rather, these accounts adhere to some of the psychotherapy field's longstanding theoretical biases in formulating their own interpretations of therapeutic MR, which diverge significantly from MR research findings. For a detailed critique of these accounts, see Ecker (2021, section 8), and for extended discussion of how emotion figures in therapeutic MR, see Ecker (2015a, pp. 25–29; 2018, section 9.3), Ecker et al. (2015), and Ecker and Bridges (2020, p. 290). Chapter 8 in this book, a case example of Emotion-Focused Therapy, also addresses this issue.

How MR advances the “corrective emotional experiences” framework Here we give a brief, pragmatic distillation of the extended discussions of this question by Ecker (2015a, pp. 30–31; 2018, pp. 60–65), who provides a close examination of how “corrective emotional experience” (CEE) was originally defined by Alexander and French (1946), considered in relation to the unlearning sequence understood as empirical knowledge of the brain's requirements for transformational change to occur.

How the Brain Unlearns 27 Psychotherapists who are guided by the CEE concept understand that the effectiveness of a CEE depends critically on achieving a disconfirmation of an existing emotional learning's negative expectations (Hill et al., 2012). Disconfirmation is usually expected by therapists to result from the client having a new, unexpected experience of a type that was intensely needed but distressingly missing in the course of development. Therapists often find after creating such an experience, however, that it has not produced any lasting shift, even though the experience itself felt richly affective and deeply meaningful and satisfying to the client at the time. Thus a question of much importance regarding CEEs is: Why does such a low percentage of these experiences succeed in inducing lasting, liberating change? The answer to that question is apparent in the unlearning sequence: Actual disconfirmation consists of the new experience occurring concurrently with foreground reactivation of the problematic emotional learning (negative expectation) that has been maintaining the unwanted state of mind or behavior; and the new experience must contradict that negative expectation with high specificity. In other words, actual disconfirmation requires the juxtaposition experience defined in the unlearning sequence, in which both the target emotional learning and the contradictory experience feel real and true. If that juxtaposition isn't actively prompted by the therapist, what tends to happen instead is an internal disengagement from, and suppression of, the negative emotional learning during the positive experience of what was missing, and no juxtaposition occurs. In that case, no disconfirmation occurs, no unlearning occurs, and no transformational change occurs, which puzzles or frustrates the therapist and brings disappointment and perhaps also a sense of personal failure for the client. In short, attempted CEEs often consist of only the desired new experience, without the full juxtaposition. What we learn from the unlearning sequence understood as an empirical research finding is to define CEE = JE (juxtaposition experience). Alexander and French (1946) deserve much credit because one can see the JE requirement implied in their description of the CEE, although their account stops short of stating what the unlearning sequence explicitly states, namely, the operational necessity of prompting the client into explicit foreground awareness of both sides of the juxtaposition, affectively felt. Unawareness of that operational necessity has resulted in therapists believing and expecting that richly creating the needed, missing experience is supposed to automatically generate disconfirmation and lasting change, but in fact it does not reliably do so. “An experience that could effectively serve to create disconfirmation and transformational change fails to do so if the target learning is not concurrently reactivated” (Ecker, 2018, p. 64). Several other ways in which understanding MR induced by the unlearning sequence refines and advances the CEE model are also covered in the articles by Ecker cited above.

28 The Emotional Coherence Framework

How the unlearning sequence differs from extinction Steps 2 and 3 of the unlearning sequence may appear to be indistinguishable from a standard extinction training procedure, which can beg the question of why, in laboratory studies, their effect is destabilization, MR, and true unlearning rather than extinction, competitive counter-learning, and merely temporary suppression of the target learning. The main answer to that question becomes apparent by first recognizing what it means that standard extinction training in laboratory studies—a steady series of presentations of, say, the audio tone without the accompanying shock—is found empirically not to induce destabilization and MR: It can only mean that the subjective experience of that extended series does not create a prediction error experience. That may at first seem counterintuitive, until one remembers that when a procedural mismatch is too large qualitatively, the experience does not register as relevant to the target learning (in Bayesian terms, a different latent cause is perceived) and therefore does not create a prediction error experience. This explanation of why MR is not induced by standard extinction training was first articulated by Gershman et al. (2013). In contrast, a single presentation of the audio tone with no shock does induce destabilization and MR, as shown in many studies (reviewed by Bellfy & Kwapis, 2020; Ecker, 2021), from which we must infer that this degree of procedural mismatch does register as relevant to the target learning and therefore does create a prediction error experience. With the target learning first rendered labile by that single presentation followed by a rest period of typically ten minutes or one hour, then an extended series of unreinforced (such as tone-without-shock) presentations does drive unlearning, re-writing, and nullification of the target learning—in which case, that extended series certainly should not be understood or labeled as “extinction” because it has none of the effects that define standard extinction. Rather, it drives true unlearning, which the standard extinction procedure never does by itself. However, researchers tend to be extremely procedure-oriented, and they nevertheless stuck with familiar procedural terminology and named this the “post-retrieval extinction” or “reactivation-extinction” protocol. These misnomers have resulted in much ongoing misunderstanding of the phenomenology. So it is important to remember that “Reconsolidation cannot be reduced down to facilitated extinction,” which was the conclusion of Duvarci and Nader (2004, p. 9269). Other studies likewise have established that MR and extinction are distinct processes (e.g., Duvarci et al., 2006; Merlo et al., 2014; Pérez-Cuesta & Maldonado, 2009; Su et al., 2021; Suzuki et al., 2004). Thus we see that in laboratory studies, the same counter-learning procedure can have profoundly different effects, depending on whether or not the target memory is already in a destabilized condition. (For detailed analyses of how differences in procedural details of laboratory studies determine whether prediction error or change of latent cause is engendered, see Ecker, 2021, where it is

How the Brain Unlearns 29 shown that replication failures of the post-retrieval extinction protocol can be explained in this way.) Although the above considerations about inducing MR rather than extinction are necessary and important for understanding the results of laboratory studies, they are not relevant for psychotherapists aiming to carry out the unlearning sequence in therapy sessions, because of how the emotional learnings of persons in therapy differ from those created in laboratory studies. In nearly all laboratory studies, the target learning was created by a procedure consisting of a precisely timed series of precisely structured learning experiences, as noted earlier in this chapter. The resulting emotional learning includes, saliently, those strictly defined features—for example, not only the expectation of feeling a wrist shock after a yellow square has been visible on the computer screen for 4 seconds, but also the expectation that after 10 seconds this will happen again, and then again, many times. Those precise timing patterns in the target learning then have a major role in determining the types of post-reactivation mismatch that will, or will not, create a prediction error experience. (For example, a reactivation that includes both the audio tone and then the expected shock, but changes only the expected timing of the shock, is found to cause destabilization (e.g., Díaz-Mataix et al., 2013).) Everything described above regarding the extinction procedure, including the inferred change of latent cause that prevents a prediction error experience from occurring, results from these artificial patterns in the target learning. In contrast, the emotional learnings of persons in therapy rarely if ever contain such precise, repeating structures, so Steps 2 and 3 of the unlearning sequence reliably create not extinction but rather a prediction error experience followed by unlearning, with no need for the delicate fine-tuning of mismatch found necessary in laboratory studies.

What happens to the neural encoding of an unlearned schema? Of great interest to neuroscientists has been the question of whether the observed full annulment of a target emotional learning via MR (by either pharmacological or behavioral means) is due to changes in its stored neural encoding or engram (termed a storage deficit), disruption of neural circuits serving the retrieval of the encoded learning (termed a retrieval deficit), or enhanced suppression by a separate, competing counterlearning (e.g., Hardt et al., 2009; Matzel & Miller, 2009; Silva & Gräff, 2023). Studies using various approaches have consistently indicated a storage effect. First, molecular and neurochemical evidence indicated that the encoding of the target learning is reconstituted by behavioral updating (Clem & Huganir, 2010; Jarome et al., 2012a; Su et al., 2021; for a review of the complex molecular and neurochemical processes that subserve behavioral updating of memory via MR, see Bellfy & Kwapis, 2020). Then Haubrich et al. (2020) reported “strong evidence” of a storage effect based on a

30 The Emotional Coherence Framework review of studies of brain mechanisms of long-term memory. The most conclusive evidence of a storage effect comes from the first study to use the engram tagging technique to visually identify and functionally manipulate the neurons involved in the storage and subsequent reactivations of a long-term fear memory (threat memory) undergoing behavioral unlearning via MR (Khalaf et al., 2018). In concluding their article, these authors also state that their neurophysiological findings imply that effective trauma therapy requires “the engagement, rather than the suppression, of the original trauma” (p. 1241). By confirming that a target learning's neural encoding is revised by the unlearning sequence, those findings support use of the term “erasure” in referring to MR-induced annulment of emotional memory, as numerous neuroscience authors have done (e.g., Agren et al., 2012; Clem & Huganir, 2010; Dennis & Perrotti, 2015; Haubrich et al., 2020; Kindt et al., 2009; Maren, 2011; Sacktor, 2023; Soeter & Kindt, 2010, 2012). It is not yet clear, however, whether erasure is complete or whether some residual traces of a target emotional memory's original encoding can survive behavioral unlearning, though at a level too weak to be cued into expression in any form (Han et al., 2021). Furthermore, among psychotherapists we have found that the term “erasure” often leads to misunderstandings, concerns, or conflicts with existing beliefs, all of which seem to be largely avoided by instead using terms such as the annulment, nullification, depotentiation, or dissolution of core beliefs, schemas, and mental models. Therefore those are the terms usually used throughout this book. Those terms connote only the functional elimination of all expression of a target semantic memory, without addressing or implying anything regarding what such annulment means about the final condition of the underlying engram. Also, as noted above, episodic memory of past events is not erased by the unlearning and annulment of an emotional schema formed in response to those events (Beckers & Kindt, 2017; Kindt et al., 2009).

Why neuroscientists discuss MR only for fears and addictions One of this book's purposes is showing that the unlearning sequence of MR is effective for an extremely wide range of clinical symptoms based in memory. We psychotherapists have a far freer hand in exploring that range of applicability than neuroscientists have. They must restrict their studies to learning and memory phenomena that are unambiguously detectable and measurable by the established, credible techniques of their field. The professional credibility of empirical researchers depends on their acknowledging the existence of only what their limited but proven methods can detect. As a result, nearly all of their MR research has addressed only two types of memory: fear responses generated by threat memory, and addiction behaviors generated by memory of cues and contexts from past episodes of achieving an intensely pleasurable altered state. The existing methods that neuroscientists must use simply do not equip them

How the Brain Unlearns 31 to study MR for anger responses, sexual responses, grief processes, insecure attachment patterns, distress-laden attributed meanings, or myriad other areas of learning and memory that are often central in psychotherapy. Creative controlled studies that have explored such areas, such as that by Speer et al. (2021), are rare. Laboratory researchers therefore have acknowledged, in journal articles reporting their studies, the therapeutic potential of MR only for symptoms of fear (usually PTSD) and addiction. One would never know, from these articles, how broadly effective the MR process of unlearning can be across the full range of memory-based symptoms presented by seekers of psychotherapy, as demonstrated in this book.

From lab to therapy session: The therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP) Now we come to the pragmatics of carrying out the unlearning sequence in therapy sessions. Clearly there are significant differences between the lab, where neuroscientists keep conditions sharply defined, well controlled, and simplified, and the consulting room, where therapists encounter high levels of complexity which, by the very nature of the situation, cannot be well controlled procedurally. What are the main considerations for reliably importing the unlearning sequence from the former domain to the latter? We can find our way by recognizing that therapists face two main differences in the clinical situation relative to the lab: the unknown content of the target learning, and the complexity of the target learning. Carrying out each step of the unlearning sequence requires detailed knowledge of the target emotional learning, but a psychotherapist is completely in the dark in this regard with each new client. Neuroscientists, in contrast, know all details of the target learning from the start because in a lab study of MR they design and create the emotional learning to be unlearned. Instilling that learning in subjects occurs on Day 1 of any given lab study. Then, on Day 2 or later, they make detailed use of their knowledge of the target learning in every step of the three-step process of unlearning—reactivation of the target learning; creation of a single experience that contradicts the reactivated target learning's expectations, generating a prediction error experience to destabilize the target learning; and finally, a series of several more of the same reactivation-and-contradiction experiences, serving as new learning that disconfirms and rewrites (and thereby erases the content of) the target learning. Researchers could not carry out these three essential steps of unlearning if they did not know the specific content of the target learning. In therapy, even the symptoms (the unwanted behavior, state of mind, and/or somatic disturbance) are unknown to the therapist at the start. So, in order to become able to carry out the unlearning sequence reliably and decisively, the therapist must first elicit accurate descriptions of (A) the specific symptom(s) to be

32 The Emotional Coherence Framework dispelled and (B) the specific emotional learnings generating those symptom(s). Those are initial, preparatory steps that must be added in the clinical setting. As a rule, the emotional learnings maintaining therapy clients' symptoms are areas of deep vulnerability that consist of implicit knowledge in implicit memory, so they are not conscious at the start of therapy. Retrieving them into explicit awareness for Step B typically constitutes the greater part of the therapeutic work. Various psychotherapies have developed specialized methods for this focused, in-depth retrieval work, and usually it can be carried out in far fewer sessions than was assumed necessary by most of the clinical field for most of the twentieth century. In all subsequent chapters of this book, readers will encounter examples of how the implicit emotional knowledge underlying and generating a given symptom is brought into explicit awareness in a focused, efficient manner for Step B. Often only a few sessions are needed for this retrieval work, though of course the number of sessions increases commensurate with the complexity and severity of the emerging material. The retrieval work reveals a target emotional learning (a core belief, schema, or mental model) such as the three examples given in Chapter 1 on page 6. These are considerably more complex than the target learnings created in MR lab studies. This turns out to be advantageous because within any one emotional learning, several components may be suitable targets for disconfirmation and unlearning, and succeeding with any one of them is all that is needed. We will map out the structure of human emotional learnings or schemas in Chapters 3 and 4, providing you with a clear guide for working with their complexity. What is relevant to our present discussion is that once a therapy client has accessed and revealed the specific makeup of the underlying learning, making it known to the therapist, the final preparation step, Step C, can then begin: the task of finding a suitable contradictory experience or contradictory knowledge to be used in creating the juxtaposition experience in Steps 2 and 3 of the unlearning sequence. Finding contradictory material means finding living knowledge available to the client from past or present experience that unmistakeably and viscerally contradicts what is known in the target learning about how the world is, or how oneself is. As soon as the contradictory ingredients are identified in Step C, the unlearning sequence can then be carried out immediately. Thus for consistently and efficiently carrying out in psychotherapy sessions the unlearning sequence identified in MR lab research, a preparatory process consisting of the following three steps is needed: A Symptom identification. Actively clarify with the client what to regard as the presenting symptom(s)—the specific behaviors, somatics, emotions, and/ or thoughts that the client wants to eliminate—and when they happen, that is, the percepts and contexts that evoke or intensify them. This information, which in many cases can be obtained within the first session, is needed for

How the Brain Unlearns 33 embarking upon Step B efficiently. It also subsequently helps the therapist to carry out Step 1 of the unlearning sequence, reactivation. B Retrieval of target learning. Retrieve into explicit, direct awareness, as an affective, embodied experience that is verbally articulated while being felt, the emotional learning underlying and driving the presenting symptom(s). Familiarity with this material is what guides the therapist in then carrying out Step C, identification of contradictory knowledge, and also in carrying out a deep, thorough implementation of Step 1 of the unlearning sequence, reactivation. C Identification of contradictory knowledge. Identify a distinct experience or knowing (past or present) available to the client that can serve as living knowledge that is fundamentally incompatible with the model of reality in the target emotional learning retrieved in Step B, such that both cannot possibly be true. The disconfirming material may or may not be appealing to the client as being more “positive” or preferred, and it may or may not be emotional.2 What matters is for it to be experienced by the client as a definite personal truth that is mutually exclusive, ontologically, with the target learning. It may be already part of the client's personal knowledge from past experiences or may be created by a new experience. It will be used to carry out Step 2 of the unlearning sequence (the initial, single juxtaposition and prediction error experience that destabilizes the target learning) and Step 3 (repetitions of the juxtaposition that are the unlearning and annulment of the target learning). We refer to the three preparatory steps, A–B–C, as the accessing sequence required in order to then carry out Steps 1–2–3, the unlearning sequence, knowingly and systematically. Earlier we also defined Step V, the final verification step of observing the markers of transformational change persisting over time. We term the entire series of steps, A–B–C–1–2–3–V, the therapeutic reconsolidation process, or TRP (see Table 2.1). Several sessions are usually needed for the accessing sequence, whereas the subsequent unlearning sequence in itself requires only several minutes. (Schiller et al. (2010) carried out Steps 1–2–3 in 15 minutes to eliminate a purely subcortical, classical conditioning threat memory in humans.) However, complications of various types can arise in the accessing sequence, the unlearning sequence, or both, increasing the number of sessions required. For example, there can be more than one emotional schema maintaining a particular symptom, or a greatly reduced pace of work may be necessary to make it workable to access an intensely distress-laden schema. We discuss these complications in Chapter 3. Neuroscientists follow Steps 1–2–3 with a verification step—Step V— consisting of a test that probes the status of the target learning by presenting a known cue or context that formerly evoked a distinct behavioral and emotional response from the target learning but would elicit no such response if

34 The Emotional Coherence Framework Table 2.1 Methodology for systematic facilitation in psychotherapy sessions of the unlearning sequence identified in laboratory MR studies of behavioral updating of emotional memory Therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP) I. Preparation phase: Accessing sequence

A. Symptom identification B. Retrieval of target learning (symptom-requiring schema) C. Identification of contradictory knowledge

II. Transformation phase: Unlearning sequence

Reactivation of symptom-requiring schema (B) 2. Co-activation of contradictory knowledge (C) (juxtaposition experience) 3. Repetitions of 1 and 2 (juxtaposition experience)

III. Verification phase

Observations of: emotional non-reactivation symptom cessation effortless permanence

full unlearning has occurred. The same is important to do in psychotherapy, both soon after completion of Steps 1–2–3 and at intervals thereafter, if possible, using both imaginal techniques of re-exposure to known cues as well as actual re-exposure in situations in daily life between sessions. Absence of the client's former problematic response gives both therapist and client a clear indication that the sought-for change has been accomplished. Clear-cut verification in Step V is also necessary for documenting single case studies for empirical research purposes. The seven-step therapeutic reconsolidation process summarized in Table 2.1 defines the direct translation of MR research findings to psychotherapy, and it does so in technique-independent and theory-independent terms. The TRP “belongs” to no single system, school, or theory of psychotherapy or personality, though therapy systems differ widely in their native suitability for carrying out this process. The range of experiential methods and styles of working that therapists can use for carrying out the seven steps is open-ended, as shown in all subsequent chapters of this book, and includes verbally guided experiential methods (as in Gestalt-type chair work, parts and ego-state work, Focusing, inner child work, Jungian active imagination, or guided visualization, for example), somatic methods, trauma therapy methods including bilateral (and other dual) stimulation methods, couple and family systems methods, art therapy and sandtray methods, drama therapy methods, and many others. The TRP can be, and often is, fulfilled in many different therapy systems, producing transformational change, by therapists having no familiarity with MR, the TRP, or the unlearning sequence, as is presumably the case for the eight case examples of transformational change presented in Part 2. Furthermore, the unlearning sequence sometimes occurs serendipitously, without Steps A–B–C

How the Brain Unlearns 35 taking place, also producing transformational change. It is even possible for transformational change to result from a therapy client experiencing Steps 1–2–3 without voicing anything of them to the therapist or even without noticing them with metacognitive awareness.
