Therefore, carrying out the entire TRP is not claimed to be necessary for producing transformational change. Rather, the value and importance of the TRP is in giving therapists maximum control over producing transformational change with maximum consistency and efficiency across clients, by making the core process required by the brain explicit in the therapist's mind and explicit in the therapist–client interaction.

The TRP is an evidence-based methodology From the previous section it should be apparent, but is worth emphasizing, that as a psychotherapeutic methodology, the TRP is directly supported by strong empirical evidence of two kinds. First, the unlearning sequence that directly produces transformational change consists of TRP Steps 1, 2, and 3, which are the replication in therapy sessions of exactly the same set of experiences present unambiguously in the each of the first twenty controlled human studies that successfully recruited MR to abolish all reactivation and expression of a subcortical emotional learning (Ecker, 2021). Second, complete abolishing (which we refer to as “profound change” or “transformational change”) has been shown to result promptly from the TRP in many individual cases of psychotherapy, including those in this book, and this in itself constitutes strong evidence of MR recruitment because no other known endogenous mechanism of change can produce such an effect. When therapy clients report in clear, explicit terms in recorded sessions or in writing that a major long-term symptom has completely stopped happening and its non-occurrence continues effortlessly, there is no need for complex questionnaires and statistical analyses to measure the degree of change and to identify the mechanism of change that is thereby indicated. The relevance or ecological validity of laboratory studies of the unlearning sequence for application in psychotherapy sessions is indicated by several human studies with various conditions that were designed to resemble psychotherapy sessions:

In studies by Pine et al. (2014) and Speer et al. (2021), the target memory was

an implicit emotional learning consisting of a complex combination of preferences and meanings, which was fundamentally revised by reactivation plus a disconfirmation consisting of a similarly complex contradictory experience (in contrast to the relatively simple Pavlovian target learning and disconfirmation used in most other MR laboratory studies). • Grégoire and Greening (2019) used Pavlovian conditioning to create on Day 1 the fear-generating expectation of an electric shock upon seeing a particular visual cue, and then, on Day 2, they instructed subjects to form a mental

36 The Emotional Coherence Framework image of that cue appearing without any accompanying shock. This internal mental imagery successfully both reactivated the threat memory and produced a prediction error experience that destabilized the threat memory, allowing it to then be unlearned in the standard manner, i.e., by a series of external, physical presentations of the cue with no shock. Mental imagery techniques are a major category of experiential methods in psychotherapy. • Golkar et al. (2017) reversed that sequence: Physical presentation of the cue without shock was used for reactivation and destabilization, but then unlearning consisted of a vicarious counter-learning experience, namely the viewing of a video of a person calmly viewing a series of presentations of the cue without shock. This vicarious unlearning successfully abolished the acquired threat response to the cue. Vicarious experience is a type of imaginal experience in that it depends on imagining having the same experience oneself. Thus controlled laboratory studies have provided a significant degree of ecological validity in showing that each step of the unlearning sequence is effective when carried out in ways that match real-world conditions in psychotherapy sessions. The TRP applied in psychotherapy can therefore be regarded as an empirically proven causal process of profound unlearning through memory reconsolidation. This is the first time in its history that the psychotherapy field stands upon empirical knowledge of an internal mechanism of change that merits recognition by all involved in this field (Ecker & Vaz, 2022), irrespective of theoretical orientation, giving the field a scientific foundation. As in all scientific disciplines, compatibility with this fundamental empirical knowledge now serves as a validity criterion applicable to all proposed models of lasting therapeutic change. Pragmatically, the observation of transformational change promptly following TRP Steps 1–2–3 in psychotherapy serves crucially as confirmation of successfully replicating the process used in the laboratory studies. In that way, the TRP provides therapists and counselors with an empirically confirmed, atheoretical, transtheoretical, transdiagnostic, comprehensive guiding framework for consistently working at the highest level of therapeutic effectiveness. In addition to the TRP's basis of empirical evidence just summarized, it is important for future empirical studies of psychotherapy sessions to show the causal role of TRP facilitation in producing transformational change. One possible study design for this purpose, described by Ecker and Vaz (2022), uses time-resolved process analysis in many individual cases to test the hypothesis that in any therapy sessions that in fact produced the markers of transformational change, the component experiences of TRP Steps 1, 2, and 3 were created proximally before those markers appeared. That would be a controlled version and quantitative measurement of what is demonstrated in Part 2 of this book qualitatively and anecdotally. As noted earlier, showing that the strong and unique effect of transformational change is consistently preceded immediately by the well-defined, verified occurrence of the unlearning sequence would be

How the Brain Unlearns 37 empirical evidence of causation, not merely correlation (Ecker & Vaz, 2022; Kazdin, 2007). It is important to recognize that the randomized controlled trial (RCT) is unsuitable for this research purpose because it is fundamentally incapable of confirming or disconfirming that the unlearning sequence, TRP Steps 1–2–3, is the direct cause of the full, lasting disappearance of symptoms and schema reactivations. Any RCT's cohort of TRP practitioners would inevitably span a range of TRP facilitation proficiencies, resulting in a measurement of merely that cohort's average rate of successfully carrying out the TRP. Such a measurement would be of no value toward confirming or disconfirming the causal role of the unlearning sequence in producing transformational change. Ecker and Vaz (2022, p. 2) have pointed out the broad relevance and the seriousness of the well-documented issue of a therapist cohort's wide range of proficiencies: The manualization of clinical procedures, intended to deliver consistently better outcomes than nonmanualized treatments, has not done so (Truijens et al., 2019). Rather, researchers have found that some therapists are much more effective than others in carrying out the same treatment and that the difference does not correlate with the therapist's age, gender, or years of experience, or with the type of therapy (e.g., Baldwin & Imel, 2013; Berman & Norton, 1985; Okiishi et al., 2003). In the study by Okiishi et al. (2003), which was not an RCT, data from 1841 clients treated by 91 therapists during a 2.5-year period showed that the most effective therapists in the cohort produced a rate of improvement of symptoms 10 times higher than the cohort's mean rate of improvement, and symptoms actually worsened over time for the least effective therapists, with no correlation between rate of improvement and any therapist variables. RCT results, however, never include individual case effectiveness data, and any occurrences of transformational change in outlier cases remain hidden under the RCT's overall statistical analysis of the data. Transformational change has gone unrecognized by the psychotherapy outcome research field, as noted in Chapter 1, precisely because of that field's heavy reliance and insistence upon the RCT research format. RCTs measure the net efficacy with which cohorts of practitioners implement particular methodologies, with a wide range of proficiencies in each cohort. That is why a remarkably uniform, mild symptom reduction of only 20 to 25 percent has been measured by nearly all RCTs for many decades, also as noted in Chapter 1. Thus RCTs have merely identified features of psychotherapy that correlate with weak change, ungrounded in any empirical knowledge of an internal mechanism of change. That long, inconclusive chapter in the history of psychotherapy outcome research may now come to an end as both the clinical and outcome research fields reorient to our empirical knowledge of memory reconsolidation, the unlearning sequence, and transformational change.

38 The Emotional Coherence Framework

Transformational change versus emotional regulation One of this chapter's main themes has been the contrast between the methodology that produces transformational change and the methodology of counteractive change, in which the client is guided to learn, practice, and build up preferred states of mind and behaviors intended to happen instead of the unwanted states of mind and behaviors. The great complexity of the mind, brain, and personality allows for myriad techniques of counteractive change, but in all of them the preferred new pattern competes with the problem pattern and therefore usually produces only partial reduction of the problem pattern and allows relapse. The possibility of transformational change was virtually unknown to the psychotherapy field for most of the twentieth century. Counteractive change was therefore the nature of the great majority of therapy systems and formed the unquestioned beliefs of most therapists regarding therapeutic process and change. As of this writing, a particular strategy of counteractive change that is widely assumed to be fundamental for psychotherapy is known as emotional regulation. This has many different modes of implementation, such as attentional control (which includes thought stopping as well as various mindfulness practices, as in Attention and Commitment Therapy (ACT)), cognitive reappraisal, positive thinking, the naming of the current mood or emotion, physiological modulation of response, “vagal tone” regulation practices, and use of the client-therapist relationship for stabilizing, secure attachment, sometimes termed reparative attachment. (A spectrum of types of cognitive regulation of emotion is described by Ochsner & Gross, 2005 and reviewed by Toomey & Ecker, 2009.) The widespread adherence of psychotherapists to the concept and methodology of emotional regulation makes this approach an instructive contrast with the TRP, as shown as Table 2.2. Table 2.2 Comparison of the therapeutic effects of the therapeutic reconsolidation process and emotional regulation Transformational change via therapeutic reconsolidation process

Counteractive change via emotional regulation

Eliminates source of problem: Uses new learnings to replace problematic learnings. Symptom cessation is rapid and complete.

Competes against source of problem: Uses new learnings to develop preferred state. Symptom reduction is slow and incremental. Subject to relapse. Preferred state needs effortful ongoing maintenance. Persistent sense of divided self and inner conflict. Symptom production is understood in a pathologizing manner as a dysregulation of brain systems.

Not subject to relapse. Remaining symptom-free is effortless. Increased sense of unified self and wholeness. Symptom production is understood as the normal functioning and expression of emotional implicit memory.

How the Brain Unlearns 39 Extinction training, the prototype of counteractive, regulatory methods, is directly applied in various forms of exposure therapy (e.g., Foa & Kozak, 1986; Foa & McNally, 1996; Tryon, 2005), which has a well-documented problem of relapse (Vervliet et al., 2013). Systems of positive psychology also tend to have a heavily counteractive, regulatory strategy (e.g., Gable & Haidt, 2005). Arden and Linford (2009) regard Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) as emotional regulation and cite brain science to support that view; likewise Brewin (2006, p. 765) reviews memory retrieval research indicating “that CBT does not directly modify negative information in memory, but produces changes in the relative activation of positive and negative representations such that the positive ones are assisted to win the retrieval competition.” In counteractive change, building up a new, preferred response requires great numbers of repetitions of the new response over time, accompanied by mindful attention to choosing the new response each time, in order to establish and strengthen the neural linkages required. The need for many repetitions reflects the principle that “neurons that fire together, wire together,” which is the popular formulation of Hebb's law. In contrast, transformational change through the unlearning sequence does not rely on extensive repetition over time to effect profound change. MR does not occur through the type of synaptic plasticity described by Hebb's law. The swiftness with which deep, decisive, lasting change occurs through the MR mechanism challenges traditional notions of the time required for major therapeutic effects to come about. It seems worth repeating here that effective new learning of any kind creates brain change in the form of new neural connections; but it is only when new learning also nullifies and replaces old learning that transformational change occurs, rather than counteractive change, and this is what the unlearning sequence achieves through MR: learning that drives unlearning. The range of applicability of the therapeutic reconsolidation process is very broad—in principle, covering all unwanted responses arising from emotional learning. Both MR research and clinical experience have shown that the brain is always ready to unlearn and nullify existing learnings through the unlearning sequence in the TRP. However, there are several types of clinical situation in which primary treatment should be not the TRP, but rather counteractive methods that implement harm prevention, crisis intervention, skill-building, resource utilization, or pharmacological measures:

situations of urgent crisis, danger or emergency • conditions known not to consist of underlying emotional learnings (such as

autism spectrum, hypothyroidism-induced depression, and genetically based addiction) • individuals whose stability could be compromised by direct experience of underlying, unresolved emotional vulnerability or distress, or who are unable to attend to and maintain awareness of the content of their own subjective experiencing

40 The Emotional Coherence Framework

severe patterns of personality or character that initially make deeper emotional work and self-awareness impossible for all practical purposes

clients who express a definite choice not to do in-depth work and want to

cultivate preferred states or behaviors without addressing interior, underlying sources of the problem.

For example, with a client who presents PTSD symptoms and extreme characterological avoidance of emotional vulnerability, primary treatment would consist of counteractive methods, such as somatic relaxation techniques, breath awareness practice, and yoga, possibly supplemented gradually by adjunctive use of the therapeutic reconsolidation process in tolerable forms, for example through empowered re-enactment to depotentiate specific traumatic memories (an example of which is included in Chapter 4). In contrast, with a client who presents PTSD, depression, or many other symptoms, but who fits none of the categories of counter-indication listed just above, the therapeutic reconsolidation process can be the primary approach and, in light of the advantages of this approach as indicated in Table 2.2, it may warrant being regarded as best practice in this case.

Use of the TRP for evaluation of therapeutic MR claims The TRP is a map of process, or methodology, that guides psychotherapists as they conduct therapy sessions, in order to reach an outcome of transformational change. Another major use of the TRP is in analyzing and understanding the operation of particular therapeutic frameworks and protocols represented by clinicians and researchers as a recruitment of MR. Many of these are presented using terms that can make it less than readily apparent whether they actually carry out the unlearning sequence. The TRP derives directly from MR research findings and is a general methodology, meta to any specific techniques or protocols, for fulfilling the brain's unlearning requirements according to MR research findings. Any particular therapeutic framework or protocol claimed as utilizing MR must fulfill at least TRP Steps 1–2–3 (the unlearning sequence) in order to be capable of producing transformational change. Closely studying a particular MR framework or protocol and mapping it onto the TRP is a sound method for evaluating its therapeutic capability and understanding its operation and effects. That scrutiny has been carried out by Ecker (2021) for the broad frameworks of therapeutic MR put forward by Lane et al. (2015), Stevens (2019), and Welling (2012), showing, as noted earlier in this chapter, that these accounts include neither the unlearning sequence nor the critical role of prediction error for actuating the MR mechanism, and also misrepresent the role of emotional arousal in relation to MR. Several specially structured therapeutic MR protocols have also been developed for use with a particular clinical population, such as PTSD from a single event (e.g., Gray et al., 2017, 2020; Iyadurai et al., 2018) or a

How the Brain Unlearns 41 particular addiction (e.g., alcohol addiction: Gale et al., 2021; cocaine seeking: Luo et al., 2015; heroin craving: Xue et al., 2012; nicotine addiction: Germeroth et al., 2017; internet gaming addiction: Zhao et al., 2022). As a rule, such special-purpose MR protocols fulfill TRP Step 1, reactivation of the target learning, but not all fulfill Step 2, creation of a prediction error experience, as is necessary for triggering destabilization and launching the MR process, and not all that do create a prediction error experience do so in the form of a decisive contradiction of the expectations in the target memory. A finegrained examination of a particular protocol's steps of implementation reveals which of TRP Steps A–B–C–1–2–3 are actually carried out. That TRP mapping of a protocol produces what Ecker (2018) terms methodology evidence regarding fulfillment of the MR unlearning sequence. Even more decisive is erasure evidence, produced in TRP Step V, the final, verification step, i.e., the degree of change achieved by a particular protocol. The markers of transformational change (complete, lasting, effortless non-occurrence of symptoms and reactivation) are the strongest support for a claim that MR has been recruited, as only MR is known to be capable of that. Lesser degrees of change can result from counteractive learning rather than MR, making MR recruitment by the protocol ambiguous. Even so, partial reduction of symptoms and reactivation can still be validly ascribed to MR if, and only if, those partial reductions persist long-term and effortlessly, that is, without any preventative effort or practice whatsoever. For detailed examples of evaluating specialized MR protocols by using TRP mapping to examine their methodology evidence and erasure evidence, see Ecker (2018, pp. 67–78). Interestingly, one of the analyzed protocols (Högberg et al., 2011) is shown to accomplish significantly more memory processing than the authors claimed, and to be strong in both kinds of evidence—meaning it fully implemented the TRP, which is why it produced transformational change that eliminated the post-traumatic symptomology of suicidal adolescents in a small number of sessions. For another protocol examined by Ecker, quite the opposite evaluation results. Part 2 of this book shows the same evaluations via TRP mapping carried out for eight different protocols that are entire systems of psychotherapy.

Conclusion In this chapter we have seen how memory reconsolidation works and, as demonstrated in a large body of research by neuroscientists, how it unlocks the neural encoding of a targeted emotional learning, allowing that learning to be unlearned and replaced by new learning, producing transformational change. Emotional learnings are extremely tenacious and otherwise normally persist for a lifetime. Based on these findings, we defined the therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP) as a general template of optimal methodology designed to enable psychotherapists to produce transformational change with maximum versatility,

42 The Emotional Coherence Framework consistency, and efficiency, whatever may be their preferred therapeutic systems or techniques. The empirical emergence of MR and its capability to selectively nullify emotional learnings is poised to reverse two major historical trends of the psychotherapy field. First, from its beginnings, the field has been drifting and fragmenting due to having no empirical knowledge of any internal mechanism of the mind or brain for lasting change in existing patterns of behavior and state of mind (Cuijpers et al., 2019; Goldfried, 2019, 2020; Kazdin, 2007). The identification of MR as that internal mechanism is therefore a major turning point for the psychotherapy field, with significant ramifications (Ecker & Vaz, 2022). For example, until now the field has had little engagement in the normal process of scientific development in which confirmed empirical knowledge necessarily imposes constraints on hypothesizing and modeling, and serves to invalidate models that are inconsistent with empirical findings. Suddenly, that healthy process now finally becomes operational for the psychotherapy field (and for an exercise of that kind, see Ecker, 2021). Second, since the 1950s, the predominant beliefs of psychotherapists regarding symptom causation have drifted ever farther away from psychological causation, and have increasingly embraced biochemical, neurobiological, and/or genetic causation of symptoms, often despite weak or faulty evidence for the latter views. (For example, for a review of the invalid evidence surrounding the rise of antidepressant SSRIs and the view that depression is caused by imbalances of neurotransmitters, see Toomey and Ecker (2009).) However, as the unlearning of emotional schemas via MR enters more and more into clinicians' thinking and practices, and as therapists repeatedly witness permanent cessation of major symptoms such as long-term depression, anxiety attacks, and even psychosis (see Chapter 18) as a direct result of a process known to bring about such unlearning, psychological causation will speak for itself compellingly, particularly when this is observed for many different kinds of symptoms. Of course, we must not overshoot in this direction either; as we noted earlier in this chapter, there are important categories of symptoms that we reliably can believe do have genetic and/or neurobiological causes, and are not based on learning and memory, so they cannot be dispelled via MR. And it may be found in the future that, for example, while most cases of depression are due to psychological causes—that is, emotional learnings in implicit memory—some smaller fraction of depression cases may have neurobiological causes that have not been identified as yet. Overall, though, the prevalence of the psychological causation of symptoms can become clearly apparent to therapists as never before as a result of MR research having made a therapeutic reality of emotional semantic memory unlearning. This is a wonderful moment in the ongoing advancement of psychotherapy— the moment when, for the first time in the course of evolution, we recognize, understand, and knowingly utilize our innate capability to free ourselves from

How the Brain Unlearns 43 limiting emotional learnings formed earlier in life. This book is dedicated to spreading that knowledge throughout the field of psychotherapy.

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

The heart has reasons of which reason knows nothing.

—Blaise Pascal

For over a century, the fields of psychotherapy and clinical psychology have been searching for definitive knowledge of how ingrained, negative emotional learnings, which underlie a wide range of clinical symptoms and are extremely tenacious, can be truly unlearned, nullified, and actually replaced by new learning. This is the very knowledge most needed for our clients' well-being and our own professional satisfaction and sustenance. As described in detail in Chapter 2 and summarized briefly below, research by neuroscientists since 2004 has provided the needed knowledge. We now know that the brain has a built-in process of profound unlearning through a type of neuroplasticity called memory reconsolidation, which allows a well-defined, experiential process to nullify a target emotional learning or schema without impairing autobiographical memory of the original experiences in which the learning occurred. The result of this unlearning and deletion is transformational change: the individual is fully freed from the subjective “spell” of the schema or core belief and from the unwanted behavior, state of mind, and somatic disturbance it had been producing. With remarkable synergy, these research findings have confirmed the earlier clinical identification of the same experiential process by two of the authors (Ecker & Hulley, 1996, 2000). This immediate convergence of the applied art and the laboratory science of memory reconsolidation has resulted in extensive clinical experience and know-how for enabling mental health professionals to utilize this innate process of the brain. In this chapter we want to give you a close look at the therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP) being facilitated as a deeply human experience at the core of personal meaning. Below we will be describing and illustrating the TRP in action. The steps of the process define essential experiences the client must have, without specifying methods or techniques for creating those experiences—just as a map does not DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-4

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 45 impose a mode of travel when one is on a journey. This allows each therapist the freedom to choose and use preferred methods to fulfill the sequence of experiences required by the brain for shedding a targeted emotional learning. We show in Chapters 7 to 14 how eight widely used systems of psychotherapy are well suited for this purpose.

Total focus on the TRP: Coherence Therapy In order to illustrate facilitation of the TRP for instructional purposes, its sequence of steps needs to be embodied and applied in some chosen, concrete way. Best suited for this instructional demonstration is a therapy that implements the steps explicitly and recognizably. Across the various psychotherapies that are congenial to this process, there is a wide variation in the degree to which its steps are overtly apparent. In other words, if we were to observe such therapies being carried out successfully (as in Chapters 7 to 14), for most of them, without accompanying commentary we would not easily recognize the steps of the TRP occurring even when the client is, indeed, having the particular sequence of internal experiences that is the true essence of the process required by the brain. To our knowledge, the only form of psychotherapy that has a procedural map or methodology that explicitly calls for and guides every step of the TRP is Coherence Therapy—the approach developed by Ecker and Hulley in discovering the process clinically. For that reason, in this chapter and the next, the non-theoretical, non-pathologizing system of Coherence Therapy will serve to demonstrate the unlocking of the emotional brain and transformational change achieved through the TRP. Table 3.1 maps the steps of the TRP and shows how the phases of Coherence Therapy's methodology are in one-to-one correspondence with those steps. This chapter will give you a basic grounding in understanding those steps of process—the sequence of internal experiences—that unlearn, depotentiate, and eliminate the emotional learnings underlying a given presenting symptom. At first impression, the methodology of Coherence Therapy as mapped out in Table 3.1 may seem rather complex, so we hasten to emphasize that actually the essence of the methodology is so simple that it is captured by a single sentence: Find the emotional learnings generating the client's symptoms, then guide the thorough unlearning of those learnings. How to carry out those two activities efficiently and effectively is the substance of all Coherence Therapy writings, talks, and trainings. Coherence Therapy was initially developed from 1986 to 1993 by Ecker and Hulley (1996, 2000, 2008, 2019) and was first known as Depth Oriented Brief Therapy or DOBT. Clinical training in this methodology began in 1993—more than a decade before reconsolidation researchers arrived at the unlearning sequence in the lab—and it has been in use by psychotherapists since then (e.g., Ecker & Bridges, 2020; Martignetti & Jordan, 2001; Neimeyer & Bridges, 2003;

The steps of methodology of Coherence Therapy listed in Table 3.1 emerged as a result of Ecker and Hulley culling from thousands of their own therapy sessions the outliers that contained the markers of profound, lasting change. Those ultra-effective outlier sessions were closely scrutinized in order to identify the essential steps of process that they shared, across a wide range of symptoms and clients. The very same markers of change later came to be associated distinctively with the successful unlearning of an acquired emotional expectation in lab studies of memory reconsolidation. Neuroscientists relying on those markers identified the same steps of required process in research on MR published since 2004, as reviewed in Chapter 2; for readers who have bypassed that review of research, we note that brief, accessible accounts of MR research and its extension to psychotherapy are available online (e.g., Ecker, 2011; Van Nuys, 2010a; see also the free podcasts and videos listed at https://bit.ly/40kK0uW). Researchers determined that change consisting of those markers corresponds on the neurological level to an unlocking of the target schema's neural encoding,

allowing that encoding to be fundamentally rewritten and replaced by new learning, eliminating the original version from memory. Coherence Therapy is widely regarded as being evidence based because its methodology consists of direct application of a well-defined process—the unlearning sequence, TRP Steps 1–2–3—that was identified in extensive laboratory studies of MR by neuroscientists. A detailed review by Ecker (2021) shows the presence of the unlearning sequence in each of the first twenty human MR studies that successfully nullified an emotional learning. Coherence Therapy equips the therapist with extensive guidance for carrying out the therapeutic reconsolidation process, as well as offering a set of versatile techniques for doing so. It is defined by both the methodology indicated in Table 3.1 and a guiding conceptual map consisting of the research-based knowledge of emotional learning and unlearning in the Emotional Coherence Framework, described in Chapter 1. The limits of applicability of Coherence Therapy are the same as were detailed in Chapter 2 for the TRP. Being entirely a respectful process of guiding clients to attend deeply to their own emotional learnings and attributed meanings, Coherence Therapy, practiced skillfully, is entirely phenomenological and free of interpretation, so it is naturally applicable cross-culturally (see Chapter 19) and across sexual orientations (see Chapter 20) and age groups (see Chapters 22, 23, and 24). It can be conducted with individuals, couples and families, and with children, adolescents, and adults. In describing Coherence Therapy in the following case example, we assume that the therapist–reader already has sound skills of listening, communicating empathetic understanding authentically, attuning accurately, building emotional safety and trust, creating a good working alliance, and repairing ruptures. These

48 The Emotional Coherence Framework relationship skills and qualities, known in the clinical field as “common factors,” certainly are prerequisites for carrying out Coherence Therapy successfully. However, Coherence Therapy is not defined in terms of these common factors, and its specific process of profound change—the therapeutic reconsolidation process—is neither inherent in the common factors nor likely to result regularly from them alone (a point that is further discussed in Chapters 5 and 6).

Case example of anxious low self-esteem The case of “Richard,” a mild-mannered man in his late thirties and the older of two siblings, is relatively straightforward as an introductory walk-through of the therapeutic reconsolidation process in Coherence Therapy. Richard described a chronically disturbing self-doubting and lack of feeling competent and confident during his workday at a company that creates websites for businesses. This self-doubting in turn caused him significant anxiety daily and often blocked him from expressing his knowledge, ideas, and opinions. The mystery deepened as it emerged that in terms of his actual performance and achievements in his work life, he had for many years been consistently successful and even impressive to co-workers and supervisors. Yet at work he regularly fell into paralyzing doubt of his own knowledge and abilities. Regularly regarding one's own knowledge and abilities as invalid or inadequate is a common form of low self-worth. Therapists are well acquainted with the great prevalence as well as the exceptional tenacity of low self-worth in its many forms. It is largely immune to conventional types of therapy, including counteractive or “positive” approaches, in which relapses of low self-worth often occur. As we will see, Coherence Therapy's effectiveness in this area is due to its focus on finding the unique underlying emotional learnings according to which it is adaptively necessary to go into negative thoughts and feelings toward oneself. The direct target for profound change is then those revealed underlying learnings or schemas, not the negative thoughts and feelings toward oneself that they generate. The negative thoughts and feelings cease to arise when the underlying need for them no longer exists, as we will see in Richard's case.

Symptom identification (Step A) In his first session, Richard readily described recent examples of his symptoms of doubting his knowledge and abilities at work. He quoted self-talk such as “Who am I to think I know what's right?” and “This could be wrong” and “Watch out—don't go out on a limb.” Such thoughts arose and stopped him from expressing himself when he had something to say, such as during daily technical meetings. Richard's delineation of what responses constituted the problem and when the problem occurred accomplished symptom identification (the first step of Coherence Therapy and TRP Step A). With some clients, this step is considerably

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 49 more challenging than it was with Richard, and it is critically important to be persistent and diligent in clarifying with the client what experiential elements constitute the problem, even if this step requires multiple sessions. The therapist needs to understand in concrete, experiential terms which specific thoughts, feelings, and/or behaviors to regard as the person's symptoms, in order to be in a position, then, to pursue the discovery of the emotional learnings maintaining those particular symptoms. Clarity and ongoing mindfulness regarding the client's specific symptom(s) are the therapist's rudder in Coherence Therapy, allowing the process to be steered in a definite direction: toward and into the emotional learnings that generate the symptom(s).

Coherence of the symptom The central principle in Coherence Therapy is that as a rule, the problematic patterns or symptoms presented by seekers of psychotherapy are produced by emotional learnings, and that such symptoms exist entirely because they are adaptively and compellingly necessary to have, according to at least one of a person's emotional implicit learnings for how to avoid suffering and have safety, well-being, or justice. That is the principle of symptom coherence, which, as demonstrated below, serves as Coherence Therapy's model of both symptom production and symptom cessation. It is not a theoretical position about the mind or personality, but is based on pragmatic clinical observation as well as a wealth of empirical research on learning and memory (as reviewed by Toomey & Ecker, 2007). A symptom-requiring emotional learning is a schema or mental model that is implicit (outside of awareness, without verbal representation) at the start of therapy, but which proves to be coherent, well defined, experientially findable in a focused manner, and accurately expressible in words. There are three examples of such retrieved and verbalized schemas listed on page 6 in Chapter 1. Such a schema also proves to be disconfirmable and dissolvable by the unlearning sequence, as the work with Richard will show. Symptom coherence means that as soon as all emotional learnings maintaining a symptom have been unlearned and nullified, the symptom fully ceases and its non-recurrence is thereafter effortless, without any ongoing preventive measures. That is transformational change, and it is observed frequently by capable practitioners of Coherence Therapy and of the TRP carried out using other therapy systems, as shown in Part 2. Coherence Therapy is of course by no means original in recognizing that symptomatic behaviors, moods, thoughts, and somatic disturbances may exist as the expression of non-conscious emotional learning and memory. Many different methodologies and theories of psychotherapy incorporate that understanding in varying degrees, explicitly or implicitly. The advance made by Coherence Therapy is in its unprecedented utilization of the principle of coherence to retrieve accurately and efficiently, and then unlock and depotentiate decisively, the non-conscious emotional formations of a lifetime.

50 The Emotional Coherence Framework

Discovery phase (Step B) The therapist's continual mindfulness of the symptom guides the discovery phase of Coherence Therapy, which is TRP Step B. The discovery work needs to be primarily experiential—as distinct from the “talking about” mode—through the creation of discovery experiences. In each discovery experience, the client has a conscious, subjective encounter with the previously outside-of-awareness, implicit emotional meanings and knowings coherently generating the symptom, and in this way becomes aware of this material directly and accurately, not through speculation, interpretation, or theorizing. For pursuing the discovery work, Richard's therapist applied the symptom coherence principle by internally holding the following basic question as his guide: What learned emotional knowledge was making it necessary for Richard to generate self-doubt at work? Or, to put it the other way around: What implicit learning was making it important for Richard not to feel or act competent and confident at work, and important not to recognize viscerally the work history that strongly indicated his competence? These guiding questions were not ones to express to Richard, because doing so would have risked his misunderstanding them and feeling blamed or pathologized for being “self-sabotaging.” Rather, these coherence-based questions served as the therapist's compass, giving clear direction for the discovery work. In order to create a discovery experience that would begin to bring a symptom-requiring emotional learning into awareness, the therapist asked Richard to imagine being present at one of the daily work meetings, making a few brief, useful comments, and feeling confident in his knowledge while doing so. The therapist added, “This is not a rehearsal for actually doing that at work; it's just an exercise to do here with me so we can find out some important things.” This is an example of symptom deprivation, one of several basic techniques often useful for the discovery work. If a client's symptom occurs in a particular situation because it is actually necessary in some unrecognized way, then having the client imagine being in that situation without the symptom is likely to give rise to some specific dilemma or distress, which the client normally avoids, unconsciously, by producing the symptom. The specific dilemma that arises when deprived of the symptom begins to reveal the client's non-conscious knowledge of how, why, and when to produce the symptom in order to avoid suffering that particular distress. Richard closed his eyes and imagined being in the meeting at work, making some useful comments and feeling confident about the knowledge he had shared. This is what ensued: Cl: Now I'm feeling really uncomfortable, but—it's in a different way. Th: OK, let yourself feel it—this different discomfort. \[pause\] See if any words come along with this uncomfortable feeling.

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 51 Cl: \[pause\] Now they hate me. Th: “Now they hate me.” Good. Keep going: See if this really uncomfortable feeling also can tell you why they hate you now. Cl: \[pause\] Hnh. Wow. It's because—now I'm—an arrogant asshole—like my father—a totally self-centered, totally insensitive know-it-all. Th: Do you mean that having a feeling of confidence as you speak turns you into an arrogant asshole, like Dad? Cl: Yeah, exactly. Wow. Th: And how do you feel about being like him in this way? Cl: It's horrible! It's what I've always vowed not to be! Notice that the therapist focused on eliciting attributed meaning as well as the emotional quality of the experience. Construed meanings are key implicit learnings. At this point, an initial discovery experience has occurred. The client has been guided to “bump into,” notice, and reveal to the therapist previously non-conscious constructs, knowings, feelings, and purposes that strongly require his chronic self-doubting and the insecure, unconfident feeling that this self-doubting generates. Thus Richard has begun to retrieve his learned, previously outside-of-awareness schema (Step B) consisting of the knowledge that speaking with any feeling of personal confidence equates to being brutishly insensitive and arrogant like his father and being hated for that by others, so it is intensely important not to let himself ever feel confident. He successfully accomplishes this with frequent thoughts and self-talk that doubt and invalidate his own knowledge, preventing any confident self-expression. Our example is already showing several other things. The particular way in which Coherence Therapy is “experiential” is apparent here: It consists of the client's subjective immersion in the symptom-requiring schema, which is essential in this approach. The therapist guides the client into speaking from and in the present-moment live experience of that material. In that way, the therapist learns accurately from the client the component constructs of the symptom-requiring schema. Those constructs will be the target of change. The therapist watches and listens closely for any and every emerging indication of how the symptom is necessary to have. That selection criterion guides the therapist during the discovery work, and each such indication is what the therapist selects and focuses on next for a further emotional deepening of the discovery work. Closely observing the client's response to each attempted step of the discovery work is the key to an efficient process in this stage. In many cases, the emotional learnings and themes that emerge are outside the range of possibilities familiar to the therapist, so it is important for the therapist to adopt a “not-knowing” stance during discovery and be truly receptive to learning the makeup of the client's world of meaning. The therapist works as an anthropologist does, eliciting and learning the client's reality-defining constructs involved in symptom production just as they are, avoiding interpretive overlay, making as

52 The Emotional Coherence Framework few assumptions as possible, and not at all attempting to change, fix, or correct anything while in the discovery phase. Based on the discovery work described so far, it was apparent to the therapist that Richard's symptom of self-doubting had a function, because it was the very means by which he protected himself from being self-assertive, noxious and hated like his father. The self-doubting of course caused suffering of its own, but within Richard's world of meaning, the suffering it avoided would have been much worse. A fundamental feature of the symptom coherence model of symptom production is the recognition that the suffering due to a functional symptom is actually the lesser of two evils—the other, greater evil being the suffering that is unconsciously expected from not having the symptom. Those are the two sufferings, as they are called in Coherence Therapy. The client's emotional learning and memory systems have full knowledge of them both and compel the production of the symptom in order to avoid the even worse suffering expected from being without the symptom. Richard's learned, implicit knowledge was that being without his symptom of self-doubting would bring the even worse suffering of being hated as a heavy-handed know-it-all, like Dad. Prior to therapy, Richard's neocortical, conscious self was not privy to this trade-off between the two sufferings, so he was mystified and felt afflicted by his insecure self-doubting, which seemed to have an insistent life of its own. However, as the discovery work unfolds in Coherence Therapy and the subcortical or right brain's implicit, visceral knowings and feelings are accessed and shared with the neocortex's conscious awareness and are verbalized, the client experiences lucidly and affectively how the symptom is actually necessary to have—according to the client's own emotional learnings—for the positive purpose of avoiding a worse suffering. As Richard was now beginning to experience, this is the coming-into- awareness and recognition of the client's own urgent purpose for having the symptom, termed the client's pro-symptom position in Coherence Therapy. At the start of therapy, however, clients are in touch with only their anti-symptom position, a stance completely against having the symptom and viewing it as senseless, irrational, valueless, entirely undesirable, and occurring involuntarily with a life of its own, so the client feels powerless over it. In this anti-symptom position, the symptom's existence has negative, pathologizing meanings about self or others (bad, shameful, defective, weak, crazy, stupid, inadequate, uncaring, failure, etc.). In bringing the pro-symptom position into awareness, the client becomes aware of the learned emotional knowledge that is the emotional truth of the symptom—a phrase used almost synonymously with the phrases pro-symptom position, symptom-requiring schema, and symptom-generating emotional learnings. This is not merely cognitive insight, rather it is a felt, experiential, richly subjective knowing, resonant throughout the body. It is new awareness of a

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 53 major formative theme in the client's life, and it makes sense of the symptom in a whole new, de-pathologizing way that disconfirms and dissolves the antisymptom position. Clients often express surprise and strong relief over realizing that the symptom's existence is part of a coherent, sensible response to what they actually experienced in life and does not mean they are defective, irrational, weak, and so forth. That is already a significant therapeutic effect in itself. A functional symptom is itself the very means of avoiding some worse suffering, but not all presented symptoms are functional. The discovery work may reveal the presented symptom to be functionless, though still coherent. A symptom can be recognized as functionless because it is found to exist only as an inevitable result or by-product of a functional (but possibly unpresented) symptom. Examples of such functionless symptoms are loneliness that results from the functional, unpresented symptom of avoiding relationships with people in order to be safe from expected abandonment; or anxiety that results from the functional, unpresented symptom of never asserting boundaries in order to be safe from the expected punitive withdrawal of love. Another type of functionless symptom is the emotional distress felt due to (consciously or unconsciously) perceiving oneself helpless against either dire loss or threat, which generates anxiety/panic states, despair/depression states, or numb/dissociated states. Coherence Therapy's discovery process is a movement into underlying causes, so it always converges to, finds, and focuses on the source of a client's functionless symptom, whether that source is a functional symptom or a dilemma of helplessness. A symptom-requiring schema is a learned but durable mental object having its own definite structure and makeup (which we will examine more closely below). A different practitioner of Coherence Therapy could have used an experiential method other than the symptom deprivation technique for carrying out the discovery process with Richard, but the same material would have emerged. Other discovery techniques are described in case examples throughout this book. (For detailed instructional coverage, see Ecker & Hulley, 2019.) The discovery phase is defined not in terms of techniques or any formulaic protocol, but rather as the use of any experiential methods (including parts work, chair work, Focusing, dream work, bilateral stimulation, inner child work, sentence completion, imaginal interactions and enactments, etc.) to follow the links from the manifest symptom to the underlying personal constructs that necessitate it, drawing that normally implicit material into explicit awareness. As we are seeing with Richard, this discovery process deepens emotionally directly into quite tender territory and areas of vulnerability. In order for the client to open to this process, the therapist must be an emotionally safe presence and communicate genuine, empathetic understanding and full acceptance of the emerging emotional truth of how and why the symptom actually feels necessary to have. A sustained focusing of empathy on that material is a specialized, primary use of empathy in Coherence Therapy; thus it has its own name:

54 The Emotional Coherence Framework coherence empathy. Of course, the more common therapeutic empathy toward the suffering due to having the symptom and toward the client's wish to be rid of the symptom is also communicated in the course of Coherence Therapy. We have found that in general practice, most Coherence Therapy clients have no problem holding the emotional experiences that develop in the course of the work. For some, however, care must be taken to follow a carefully graduated process of small enough steps into the emerging material to limit the intensity of emotional accessing to levels that are not destabilizing or overwhelming. The need for such extra care usually becomes apparent quickly— for example in observing that the client becomes wooden, glassy-eyed, confused, or shifts the focus away from what the therapist was prompting in reaction to early steps of experiential accessing. Such responses indicate that the discovery process is probably heading toward traumatic memory, which is discussed in a section later in this chapter. It is best practice to ask the client after each further segment of experiential work, “How is it for you to be in touch with this?” or, in the latter portion of the session, “How will it be for you to be in touch with this after you leave my office today, and you don't have me accompanying you in it?” in order to learn each client's emotional tolerances, detect any incipient destabilization or problematic reactions, and take measures to ensure workability, safety, and stability. A client's emotional experience during a session may feel tolerable due to feeling sensitively accompanied by the therapist, but being alone with the experience after the session may feel daunting and prove not to be workable. When a client indicates that such a between-session difficulty looms, or even seems unsure about that, the therapist stabilizes the situation by saying, “I understand, and what I want to suggest is for you to forget all about these things between sessions, and only when we are together during sessions will we revisit them. How would that be, for you?” With such permission to re-suppress what was retrieved in the session, all clients to whom we have ever offered that option have been fully successful at utilizing it. In many cases, a significant contribution to the client's suffering is an objective, intense hardship of some kind. Obviously, an existential condition of hardship cannot be dispelled through the TRP, but also present nearly always is some schema (perhaps invoking certain meanings, expectations, limiting assumptions, or limiting behaviors) that is generating suffering in addition to the suffering of the hardship itself. Any such schema is fully susceptible to being unlearned and eliminated through the TRP, which can significantly reduce the client's net suffering in the situation, improving energy, mood, and other invaluable factors. An example is a person struggling with an objective hardship who also has a schema in which requesting help is a shameful sign of weakness, keeping this person unnecessarily overburdened and exhausted, as well as unnecessarily alone in this ordeal, both of which are potent amplifiers of misery. That schema can be unlearned and dissolved by the TRP.

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 55

Integration phase (Step B continues) Richard's new, direct awareness of why he avoids speaking with confidence occurred in an altered state—that is, while accessing an area of emotional experience not normally connected to conscious awareness, as is typically the case with any newly conscious emotional truth—so it was likely to disappear from awareness again if no further steps were taken to help integrate it into routine, ongoing, stable awareness. The therapist therefore pursued integration, Coherence Therapy's next phase, through the creation of integration experiences, which are simply repeated experiences of the discovered material both during and between sessions. Stable integration into everyday awareness completes the retrieval of a symptom-requiring schema from implicit memory into explicit awareness (TRP Step B). The first integration experience that the therapist created for Richard consisted of inviting him to make a simple overt statement of what had emerged: Th: So, let's see if it feels true to you to say this sentence: “Feeling any confidence means I'm arrogant, self-centered, and totally insensitive like Dad, and people will hate me for it, so I've got to never feel confident, ever.” Cl: Feeling any confidence means I'm arrogant, self-centered, and totally insensitive like Dad, and everyone will hate me for it, so I've got to never ever feel confident. Th: Does that fit or feel true for you, in your body? Cl: My body is buzzing with how true it feels. Th: Mm-hm. A few minutes ago you seemed surprised by getting in touch with this—with realizing you have this powerful purpose for not getting anywhere near feelings of confidence. Cl: Yeah. \[pause\] But it's kind of a relief, too. I mean, I feel so screwed-up at work and I thought that's just how I am. Th: I see. And now you're in touch with the deep sense it really makes in your life to keep yourself feeling the opposite of confident. Cl: Yes, I am. Fullest emotional deepening occurs in the integration work. In that segment, notice that the therapist, in expressing coherence empathy, made comments reflecting Richard's own purpose and agency in producing his symptom of selfdoubting. The therapist was simply making explicit the key elements that had already emerged in the prior discovery experience, not imposing an interpretation or getting ahead of Richard's own recognition of emotional truth. The explicit, experiential recognition of one's own purpose and agency behind a symptom is a key milestone of retrieval in the integration phase and key marker of integration. In Richard's response, “But it's kind of a relief, too. I mean, I feel so screwed-up at work and I thought that's just how I am” we can

56 The Emotional Coherence Framework see that his new awareness of the underlying coherence of his self-doubting was quickly dispelling his previous pathologizing way of making sense of that symptom. For Richard, making the overt statement above was an integration experience because it was a repeated, explicit, subjective experience of his own symptomrequiring emotional schema or pro-symptom position. The essence of an integration experience lies in having the client again speak from and within the felt emotional reality of the pro-symptom position, expressing it overtly as personal emotional truth. What matters is for the client repeatedly to have a bodily experience of the emotional realness of the discovered material—not necessarily a cathartic, dramatic, or intense experience, but an unmistakably embodied, authentic one. For that purpose of guiding truly experiential work, there is a style of phrasing that is particularly effective for verbalizing the retrieved emotional truth of the symptom—the style used in the overt statement offered to Richard above: “Feeling any confidence means I'm arrogant, self-centered, and totally insensitive like Dad, and people will hate me for it, so I've got to never feel confident, ever.” That style of vivid, present tense, first-person, emotionally candid, highly specific phrasing for naming one's living knowledge of what is at stake, what one's vulnerabilities are, and what measures are therefore urgently necessary, is called limbic language in Coherence Therapy, referring to the brain's limbic system, the major seat of emotional implicit learning and memory. Crafting this style of phrasing requires empathic attunement to the texture of subjective reality in the emotional brain. Such phrasing is important because it brings both the specific content and the native quality of the emotional material most fully and faithfully into direct experience. In contrast, everyday colloquial and social phrasing tends to intellectualize, minimize, depersonalize, and avoid facing or contacting the full-strength, living emotional vulnerabilities involved. For example, Richard's everyday phrasing for the same material, had he not been guided to use limbic language, would probably have been something like, “people won't like you if you're confident in what you say to them, so it's good to be careful.” That phrasing would have yielded a quite weak accessing of his actual emotional knowings, possibly too weak for the subsequent transformation phase to succeed. Emotionally deep experiential work requires, in addition to limbic language, comfort on the therapist's part in being in the presence of the client's emotional experiencing, as well as use of softer voice tones, slower pacing, and silences to facilitate emotional deepening in areas of vulnerability. If the therapist were to continue speaking in an ordinary voice during experiential work, emotional deepening would be limited or even discouraged, because an ordinary voice implicitly signals that the speaker is not attuning sensitively and empathetically to the delicacy of the listener's experience. These elements are of course not apparent in transcripts.

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 57 Perhaps most importantly, the deep retrieval work in Coherence Therapy requires the therapist to refrain from following any counteractive reflex—the urge to apply immediately all possible influence against the newly found prosymptom schema to correct it, refute it, fix it, override it, avoid it, disconnect from it, or manage it, believing that this could yield lasting change. Such wellintentioned counteracting fails to produce profound change, as a rule, because counteracting quickly re-suppresses the material that has been brought to light, pushing it back into a dissociated, implicit state where it remains unavailable for transformational change. Instead, the coherence-focused approach follows a completely non-counteractive process of integration: The therapist guides the client simply to stay in touch with, and keep having experiences of, the symptom-requiring emotional truth, embracing and integrating the schema into conscious awareness just as it is. The integration motto in this approach is, “Once you have arrived at the symptom's emotional truth, stay there. Pitch a tent. Set up camp right there” (Ecker & Hulley, 2019, p. 36).1 The end of the session with Richard was now approaching, so the therapist created a simple between-session task that would “stay right there” and continue to create integration experiences. On a pocket-sized index card, the therapist wrote the same sentence that Richard had spoken as an overt statement: “Feeling any confidence means I'm arrogant, self-centered, and totally insensitive like Dad, and everyone will hate me for it, so I've got to never ever feel confident.” Handing this card to Richard, the therapist suggested, “Read this once a day for a minute or two, and also whenever you're noticing any self-doubting, and just let it bring you back in touch with how true this feels for you, just the way you're feeling it right now. Don't try to analyze or overcome any part of it. Just use the card to stay in touch with all of this on a feeling level.” For sessions done remotely, the “card” can be given to the client as a text message or email. In whatever form, use of a card to guide a between-session task that maintains or even forwards the work is standard practice at the end of every session. For Richard, each reading of this card would be another integration experience as well as a practice of mindfulness of the retrieved material. The integration work is mindfulness training focused on the specific area of a newly conscious pro-symptom schema. At the start of the second session one week later, the therapist needed to assess whether the card task had successfully achieved further integration of the emotional truth written on it, and therefore asked Richard simply, “Were you able to stay focused on what we put on that card?” The absence of specifics in that question was deliberate, so that it would be apparent from Richard's reply whether he could now readily refer to the specifics of his pro-symptom position. Richard reported that he had read the card every day at first and then less often. He said it was something of a surprise to recognize “what a big deal it is for me to not be anything close to how heavy-handed and dominating Dad was—and he still is.” He said it was also a surprise to find how “black and white” it was

58 The Emotional Coherence Framework for him, meaning that “any degree of confidence or real assertiveness on my part does mean that, to me—which hasn't changed now that I know it.” Richard's specific references to the key elements on the card were markers confirming that integration of this material had occurred. Now that awareness had been extended “down” into the underlying emotional theme and purpose requiring the symptom of self-doubting at work, it was time for the return trip back “up” into experiencing the concrete, manifested symptom with this new awareness of its emotional necessity. This return trip, which largely completes the integration phase, took only a few minutes: The therapist invited Richard to return, in his imagination, to the moments of a recent occurrence of his self-doubting, self-invalidating self-talk at work, and simply to add onto that self-talk an overt statement (explicit verbalization) of his now-conscious need and purpose for it. The self-talk in this instance was, “How could I know what's right here? Who do I think I am?” In this replay the therapist now guided Richard to add, “And I'm telling myself that so that I'll keep quiet and won't confidently say what I know and be hated as a domineering know-it-all, like Dad.” This lucid linkage of purpose and symptom was full integration and ownership of his pro-symptom position. The therapist then asked, “How does it feel to really stand behind your own deep purpose for doubting yourself?” Richard replied, “I feel somehow more solid, but at the same time I'm surprised, again, to see how big this is to me,” which confirmed the experiential quality of this further step of integration. Near the end of this session, the therapist engaged Richard in collaboratively writing the card for his next between-session task: If I say anything with confidence, I'll be just like Dad—a know-it-all lording it over everyone. And then people will hate me for that, just the way I hate him for it. So I'd better keep myself quiet by thinking, “What do I know?” even though that makes me feel so insecure that I don't express what I do know. This phrasing felt resonantly true to Richard, and the therapist recommended reading the card immediately whenever he noticed self-doubting thoughts appearing. This mindfulness practice would continue to firm up Richard's integration of the pro-symptom emotional learning he had now largely retrieved (completing Step B of the therapeutic reconsolidation process). The client's integration work in Coherence Therapy is a guided, persistent practice of mindfulness of the specific emotional learnings that have been brought into the foreground of awareness from the implicit background. The therapist works to build up the client's mindfulness as well as an unreserved acceptance of his or her own symptom-requiring emotional knowledge. This embracing of the very material causing all the trouble is exactly what it seems,

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 59 a straightforward process of integration, not a paradoxical intervention. In order to sustain the integration work for relatively complete retrieval of a prosymptom schema, as illustrated here with Richard, clearly the therapist has to be able to refrain completely from the urge to counteract or oppose the symptomnecessitating theme—and that is a discipline that can require some cultivation for therapists steeped in using counteractive methods.

The anatomy of a symptom-requiring schema The retrieval work with Richard had at this point revealed and put him directly in touch—emotionally, bodily, and cognitively—with enough of his symptomrequiring schema, or emotional learning, to fulfill TRP Step B. In order for the therapist to know when a schema has been thoroughly retrieved, an understanding of the basic structure or anatomy of emotional implicit schemas is valuable. Our decades of closely studying our clients' retrieved schemas has led to a simple but universal map of schema structure. A symptom-generating schema consists of two main parts: knowledge of a problem, which is a suffering that is urgent to avoid; and knowledge of a solution, which is the tactics urgently necessary for avoiding that problem or suffering. The various components of Richard's pro-symptom schema illustrate this schema map of problem and solution as follows:

The problem: knowledge of a vulnerability to a specific suffering. Confident

assertiveness in any degree inflicts crushing oppression on others and is hated by them. If I assert my own knowledge or opinions confidently, I would be horrible like Dad and hated by others, as he is. • The solution: knowledge of an urgent strategy and concrete tactic(s) for avoiding that suffering. Never feel or express any confident assertiveness, to avoid being horrible and hated (general strategy), by vigilantly noticing any definite knowledge or opinions forming in myself and blocking them from forming by generating potently self-doubting, self-invalidating thoughts (concrete tactic and manifested symptom). While pursuing the discovery work in Coherence Therapy, internally referring to that simple map of schema structure greatly helps orient the therapist in (a) readily recognizing and understanding the coherence of the client's emerging material by sorting all items for whether they are part of a problem or part of a solution, and (b) focusing the ongoing discovery work to elicit all needed parts of the schema. The discovery work aims to reveal both what was suffered and, even more importantly, what was learned from what was suffered. Those are two different things. What was suffered is known from memory of personal events and experiences, which is episodic memory. What was learned from what was suffered is knowledge of a pattern or quality of the world, held as a schema in

60 The Emotional Coherence Framework semantic memory—a schema in which the symptom is necessary to have. Identifying what was suffered (in episodic memory) does not reliably also identify what was learned from what was suffered (in semantic or schema memory), so the discovery work must actively elicit and reveal the latter. That discovery process of finding and revealing the symptom-generating schema(s) can certainly be aided by any available episodic memory of the emotional learning history, but does not fundamentally require or depend on knowing that history from episodic memory. The schema exists in the present in implicit semantic memory and is “in the room,” available to be elicited into direct experience and explicit awareness and verbalization through any suitable experiential methods, even if the original learning history is completely unknown. Both parts or sections of the schema, the problem and the solution, are the client's mental models of how the world works, formed and learned in response to life experiences. Schemas and mental models are acquired knowledge of a pattern in how the world is. They are what the client has construed for making sense of experience. What we construe is what we learn, but we are not aware of construing and learning, rather we believe that we are seeing how things objectively are, so our resulting mental model then seems to be the truth of the world itself.2 Mental models are recognized and studied by a number of overlapping disciplines (see, e.g., Held et al., 2006) and have become an important element of case conceptualization in psychotherapy (see, for example, Brown & Elliott, 2016; Teyber & Teyber, 2016). The mental models underlying clinical symptoms operate as automatic, imperative instructions to the self for proactively avoiding the suffering or maintaining the reward experienced in the original learning experiences. The presenting symptom is among the behaviors, thoughts, and/or emotions that such models generate with fully adaptive intent, that is, to avoid suffering and arrange for safety, well-being, or justice. Because the mental model is the core material that necessitates and drives production of the symptom, it is the therapist's target for profound unlearning and nullification through the therapeutic reconsolidation process. As is characteristic of the modular, schematic, and hierarchical manner in which the brain organizes and retrieves knowledge (Eichenbaum, 2004; Rumelhart & McClelland, 1986; Toomey & Ecker, 2007), the client's schema operates as a multi-component whole. Integration of a pro-symptom schema or position is not complete, as a rule, until all of its components have been experienced emotionally and, while being experienced, verbalized accurately by the client, and then incorporated into everyday awareness. Richard had been guided to feel, recognize and verbalize all of his schema's initially nonverbal, linked elements in an experiential (rather than intellectual) manner. It was now lucidly clear to him that what he had viewed as the problem—his self-doubting thoughts and the resulting insecure, unconfident feeling at work—were actually his solution to

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 61 the previously unrecognized and implicit but now explicit problem of expecting to resemble his father and be hated for any degree of confident self-assertion. Our mapping of symptom-generating mental models in terms of problemand solution-defining sections is a phenomenological finding that is strongly consistent with many previous writings and findings in the field of phenomenology (e.g., Husserl, 2010) as applied to psychotherapy (e.g., Gendlin, 1996; Laing, 1995), such as this one by McLeod (2001, p. 40): there are points in therapy where most therapists will encourage their clients to bracket off their assumptions about their problems, describe their experiences in detail, express their sense of their experience in fresh language, and in general “overthrow and build anew” their understanding of self and relationships… in seeking to bring to light the experiential data that constitute the “problem” and its “solution,” and in finding ways to uncover the “essence” of the problem, the therapist can be seen as teaching, guiding or coaching the client in the self-application of phenomenological principles which were first identified by Husserl. We have been describing a synthesis that combines well-established phenomenological principles with advanced knowledge of the subjective and neurobiological processes of emotional learning and unlearning. This synthesis is a defining feature of the Emotional Coherence Framework, which is the guiding conceptual framework for Coherence Therapy.

Transformation phase begins: Finding contradictory knowledge (Step C) The depotentiation and nullification of an emotional learning or schema occurs only when these constructs encounter such a direct, decisive, specific disconfirmation that the emotional brain itself recognizes and accepts the disconfirmation of its own constructs. In those moments of disconfirmation, what had seemed to be the reality of the world is finally recognized as being only one's own fallible constructs. Only upon their unmistakable experiential disconfirmation are the constructs that make up emotional learnings recognized by the individual as constructs, rather than reality. That is how true unlearning operates. The result is a fundamental change in one's experience and perception of the world. Something that seemed self-evidently true about the world no longer seems true at all. We will see next how this remarkable shift unfolded for Richard. This constructivist understanding of learning, meaning-making and change is extremely valuable for working with mental models in psychotherapy, and is another defining element of the Emotional Coherence Framework. (Recommended readings on psychological constructivism include Guidano, 1995; Neimeyer &

62 The Emotional Coherence Framework Bridges, 2003; Neimeyer & Raskin, 2000; and for a review of neuroscience research supporting this perspective, see Toomey & Ecker, 2007.) When the client's formerly implicit pro-symptom schema has become conscious and explicit, revealing its specific constructs of both problem and solution to therapist and client, and the client has daily, integrated, metacognitive awareness of the schema as a subjective emotional truth, TRP Step B is complete and the work moves next into Step C: finding or creating the client's own living knowledge that sharply and very specifically contradicts the pro-symptom mental model. Only by first identifying the targets for disconfirmation—namely, the specific constructs within the pro-symptom schema—can the reliable identification of specifically contradictory knowledge be undertaken, launching Coherence Therapy's transformation phase. In Richard's third session two weeks later, he reported that on numerous occasions he had carried out the integration task: He had noticed his specific thoughts of self-doubt, then read the card and acutely recognized and felt his purpose for having such thoughts. Each of those instances was another integration experience, and the net result was that Richard now routinely had experiential, metacognitive awareness of his pro-symptom position or schema.3 The therapist therefore now began TRP Step C, the search for contradictory knowledge that could then be used in the unlearning sequence, Steps 1–2–3. There are many pathways available to the therapist for finding the needed contradictory knowledge, as we will see in Chapters 4 and 5. Here we cover only the pathway that developed with Richard, the one we call an opposite current experience. It often happens that experiences in daily life provide living knowledge that is contradictory of a person's pro-symptom mental model, but because this model is normally unconscious, compartmentalized, and sealed off from contact with other knowings, the contradictory knowledge is not recognized as contradicting anything, use is not made of it, and the fleeting opportunity passes. However, when such an opportunity develops at the point in Coherence Therapy where the client's pro-symptom schema is well retrieved and unsealed, as it was for Richard at this juncture, the client feels and notices the significance of the contradictory experience and the therapist can make highly effective use of it, as follows. After reporting that he had carried out his last task of reading his card and recognizing his own purpose for not speaking up many times, Richard wanted to describe an incident that had struck him. He said, “I was in a technical meeting at work and I thought of a good solution to a problem being discussed. But I went into “What do I know?” and kept quiet. A moment later, somebody else spoke up and suggested the same solution, and he said it pretty confidently. That jolted me, and immediately I looked around the room—and then I saw that everybody seemed glad to get this useful solution from this other guy. It was weird, how differently it went from how I expected it to go if I had said it confidently like he did.”

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 63 Because Richard was now aware of his pro-symptom schema and its expectation of how people will respond to confident self-expression, this experience at work had struck a disconfirming chord quite noticeably. What he himself had seen and heard registered as a violation of expectation. The therapist recognized that vivid contradictory knowledge was now at hand, which accomplished Step C and allowed the therapist to proceed directly to guide Richard through Steps 1–2–3, the unlearning sequence.
