Schema unlearning via juxtaposition experiences (Steps 1–2–3) To begin that sequence, the therapist asked, “Would you be willing to conjure up that scene at work in your mind's eye and sort of be back in the meeting for a few minutes, with me guiding you to try a few things?” Richard readily agreed, so the therapist, in a somewhat softened voice, began guiding an imaginal series of experiences: “The moment to revisit is that point during the meeting when you've squelched your own good idea to keep from being hated like Dad, because expressing any confidence would make you resemble him. Just be back in touch with that, in your body, in that scene, to whatever degree you can.” This was Step 1, the reactivation of the target emotional learning. It was fully deliberate on the therapist's part to re-evoke explicitly the key target construct, “expressing any confidence makes you resemble Dad.” The therapist continued, “Do you have that? Good. And now the action continues: the other guy confidently comes out with the same solution that you've doubted away, and you're looking around the room and it feels really surprising and weird that folks are fine with hearing him put forward that same good idea with such confidence. \[Brief pause\] Can you feel that moment, to some degree?” This was the concurrent experience or juxtaposition of contradictory knowledge needed in Step 2. As shown in neuroscientists' lab studies of MR, it is this step in the unlearning sequence that unlocks the neural encoding of the target learning. Richard had closed his eyes while listening to these instructions, and he now answered, “Mm-hm,” in a much lower and slower voice, indicating that he was immersed in subjective experiencing, as needed. “Good,” replied the therapist, who then proceeded to guide him into repetitions of the same juxtaposition experience for Step 3: Th: Stay with that. Stay with being surprised at what you're seeing—surprised because in your life, you've had such a definite knowing that saying something confidently to people will always come across like Dad, like an obnoxious know-it-all, and people will hate you for that. That's what you know, yet at the same time, here you're seeing that saying something confidently isn't always like Dad, and then people are fine with it. And it's quite a surprise to know that. \[That was an explicit prompting of another

64 The Emotional Coherence Framework

#### Cl: Th: Cl: Th:

side-by-side experiencing of the two incompatible knowings, with the therapist expressing empathy for both, with no indication of any favoring of one knowing over the other. The therapist paused for several seconds, then asked:\] Does it feel true to describe it like that? Your old knowing right alongside this other new knowing that's so different? \[Quietly, seeming absorbed in the experience\] Yeah. \[Softly\] All along, it seemed to you that saying something confidently could be done only in Dad's dominating way of doing it, and now suddenly you're seeing that saying something confidently can be done very differently, and it feels fine to people. \[This was another deliberate repetition of the same juxtaposition experience.\] Yeah. Mm-hm. \[Silence for about 20 seconds\] So, how is it for you to be in touch with both of these knowings, the old one telling you that anything said with confidence means being like Dad, and the new one that knows you can be confident in a way that feels okay to people? \[Asking this question repeated the juxtaposition experience yet again, and, in addition, the “how is it” portion of the question prompted Richard to view the experience with mindful or metacognitive awareness, while remaining in the experience.\] It's sort of weird. It's like there's this part of the world that I didn't notice before, even though it's been right there. I'm intrigued by how you put that. Sounds like a significant shift for you. Yeah, it is. Huh. You're seeing both now, the old part of the world and this other part of the world that's new, even though it was right there all along. \[That cued the juxtaposition experience for a fourth time, followed by silence for about 30 seconds.\] So, keep seeing both, the old part and the new part, when you open your eyes in a few seconds and come back into the room with me. \[Richard soon opens his eyes and blinks a few times.\] Can you keep seeing both? Yeah. What's it like to see both and feel both now? \[With the unlearning sequence complete, this question begins the next step, the step of verification— Step V—because it probes for whether the target learning still exists as a real-feeling emotional experience.\] \[Pause, then sudden, gleeful laughter\] It's kind of funny! Like: What? How could I think that? \[This is an initial marker indicating that the prosymptom schema may have been successfully disconfirmed, depotentiated, and dissolved by the unlearning sequence.\] Do you mean, how could you think that simply saying what you know, or mentioning some good idea that you've had, would make you seem arrogant, insensitive, and dominating like Dad and be hated for it? \[Laughing again\] Yeah!

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 65 In an empathic and natural manner, the therapist has guided four repetitions of the juxtaposition experience for Step 3 of the unlearning sequence. Those juxtaposition experiences are the actual moments in which profound change occurs—the radical unlearning and clearing away of troubled emotional learning by contradictory knowledge. Each juxtaposition experience consists of metacognitively experiencing the pro-symptom schema side by side with the sharply contradictory knowledge, with both knowings feeling vividly real, yet both cannot possibly be true. For the client, holding two utterly contradictory but equally real-feeling personal truths simultaneously is a peculiar experience, yet it is the experience required in order for new learning to nullify and replace old learning. This edgy experiential dissonance can be viewed as an enriched extension of the phenomenon of cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957). Memory reconsolidation research tells us that in these repeated juxtaposition experiences, the contradictory knowledge serves as new learning that rewrites and replaces the pro-symptom schema. Notice that the therapist gave recognition and empathy equally to both knowings— the knowledge that speaking confidently would make him noxious like Dad, and the knowledge that it would not have that effect. In fact, it was by empathizing explicitly with both of those knowings that the therapist again and again prompted Richard to bring both of them into his field of awareness together, as needed. For facilitating a successful juxtaposition experience, the client must be guided into feeling open to attending to both of the mutually incompatible knowings, and the therapist's welcoming attitude toward both is crucial for this. In contrast, any attempt by the therapist to use the contradictory knowledge counteractively, as proving the incorrectness of the pro-symptom knowledge, would be unwelcoming and suppressive of the pro-symptom schema. That could prevent genuine juxtaposition and unlearning from occurring, because disconfirmation occurs only if both knowings are experienced as true and the dissonant impossibility of that is keenly felt. For the therapist to take sides is to short-circuit the client's own process of encountering the juxtaposition and determining what to regard as true. In setting up a juxtaposition experience, the therapist is simply fulfilling the condition that the client's brain and mind require for revising existing emotional schemas. The therapist's stance is one of cooperating with and trusting the client's inherent capability of revising emotional learnings. A few repetitions of a juxtaposition experience, as defined in Coherence Therapy, fully implement the unlearning sequence identified in memory reconsolidation research. After a successful set of juxtaposition experiences lasting only a few minutes, the client finds that the pro-symptom emotional reality or schema no longer has its former emotional realness or grip. Though it had shaped and constrained life for decades, its strangle-hold is suddenly gone and the symptoms it maintained simply cease (unless there is more than one schema requiring the same symptom, in which case each such schema must be unlearned in order to arrive at symptom cessation).

66 The Emotional Coherence Framework Juxtaposition experiences in Coherence Therapy differ fundamentally from the techniques of cognitive restructuring (a major component of Second-Wave Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy; see, e.g., Frojan-Parga et al., 2009) and cognitive defusion (the major strategy of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy or ACT, widely regarded as third-wave CBT; see, e.g., Deacon et al., 2011). Both techniques are forms of counteracting. In cognitive restructuring, the therapist challenges and disputes the client's symptom-producing beliefs as being “irrational,” “maladaptive,” or “pathogenic” and sets up tests of those beliefs aimed at convincing the client of that, thereby motivating the client to then resist and choose not to obey them. In cognitive defusion, similarly to certain mindfulness meditation practices, the client learns to notice negative thoughts, emotions, and urges from an observing position, regarding them as normal, transient mental events and therefore allowing them rather than opposing them, while recognizing that they simply need not be heeded as truth or necessity. That can significantly reduce their influence, but it cannot fundamentally unlearn, nullify, and eliminate them, for transformational change. For that, the brain requires the MR unlearning sequence, TRP Steps 1–2–3, a series of several juxtaposition experiences.

Verification of schema nullification (Step V) After Step 3, the therapist's question “What's it like to see both and feel both now?” was the beginning of Step V, the first probe to verify whether or not nullification of the symptom-requiring schema has occurred. If the schema has indeed been dissolved, its familiar emotional grip is strikingly absent in the scene where it has always been present, and the client's response reveals this absence as well as the client's feeling about this surprising absence—which can range from a silent blinking of eyes, to an amused observation that now it seems “silly,” “funny,” or even “absurd” to imagine “feeling that way,” to gleeful laughter expressing true joy over suddenly feeling liberation and well-being, to a shout of amazed recognition of new meaning, to feelings of compassion for self or others; or, in some cases, to feelings of grief over a loss entailed in the change. The end of the session was approaching and the therapist asked, “How about if we write some of this new perspective on a card for you, so you can stay in touch with the felt sense of it?” The joint effort produced this card: All along it's been so clear that if I confidently say what I know, I will always come across as arrogant, insensitive, and dominating like Dad, and be hated for it. And it's so weird, looking around the room and seeing that it doesn't come across like that. Richard was to read that card before he left for work each day and also once during any meeting over the course of the day. This practice would continue to

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 67 create repetitions of the juxtaposition experience. This was desirable because, while only a few repetitions are often enough to yield lasting depotentiation, some pro-symptom schemas have a large contextual range, so they exist in memory in a distributed manner involving several different memory systems corresponding to different contexts of experience. Therefore it is prudent to extend Step 3, the repetitions of the juxtaposition experience, as long as possible and into as many contexts as possible through use of a between-session task. The therapist emphasized, “The aim is only to stay in touch with what's on this card while you're at work, not to try to say anything confidently or do anything differently.” At his fourth session one week later, Richard reported, “Something has really changed. I feel really different at work, but it's not how I always thought I'd feel if I could stop feeling so shaky. I always thought I would feel super-confident, like some kind of genius, but I don't. The change is just that I don't feel uncertain anymore, or insecure. That's a big relief, but there are no bells and whistles. It's kind of ordinary, actually. When I have something to say or contribute, I just say it, and it's no big deal.” The therapist replied, “Mm-hm. That's quite a change. I'm really glad to hear it.” Dropping his voice to a quieter tone, the therapist added, “But tell me, when you have something to say and just say it, what about the danger of coming across as a know-it-all, like Dad, and being hated for that? What about your fear of that and how urgent it is to protect yourself from that?” The therapist deliberately implemented verification Step V again, applying cues that previously had been effective for evoking Richard's pro-symptom position into direct emotional experience, in order to probe for any remaining life in that schema. Unlearning is reasonably well established only when a pro-symptom position is consistently no longer activated by cues and contexts that formerly did activate it prior to juxtaposition. This experiential way of verifying unlearning by confirming the markers of transformational change is an important final step in Coherence Therapy's methodology. Richard took in the question, gazed at the therapist in silence for a few seconds, and then replied, “Well, I don't know what to tell you. All I can say is, that doesn't trouble me anymore. And hearing you say it, it seems a little strange that it ever did—like, what was my problem?” This reply once again had the characteristic quality indicating that the pro-symptom schema has thoroughly lost its former emotional realness. The withered lifelessness of the pro-symptom schema and the effortlessness of remaining free of the symptom are the hallmarks of the therapeutic reconsolidation process and the main signs of successful Coherence Therapy. The nature of the liberating shift was captured well by a different male client who had presented social anxiety and then described his new comfort in social settings by saying, “Something's shifted that's allowing that. I'm not doing something volitional and I'm not being brave. I'm not overcoming my fear; the fear just isn't there.”

68 The Emotional Coherence Framework

Transformational versus counteractive change Think of the start of the first session with Richard: A man whose knowledge, skills and contributions are already respected by his co-workers wants to stop doubting himself and feeling insecure at work. There is no awareness and no sign whatsoever that his wobbly lack of confidence is urgently important for never replicating his father's noxious, hated behavior. In counteractive therapies, that imperative emotional necessity would typically remain unrecognized and intact as the therapist works to build up Richard's trust in his proven knowledge and skills at work, aiming to override and correct his “incorrect” and “irrational” self-doubts. How likely is that to bring about a lasting shift, given that the underlying, passionate, urgent need for self-doubt remains in force from outside of awareness? Counteractive overlays may take effect temporarily, but then they usually prove to be no match for the compelling intensity of the client's implicit pro-symptom position, and relapse occurs, which the client construes and feels as a personal failure. Furthermore, counteracting exacerbates the “divided self”—the inner conflict between the conscious personality's anti-symptom position and the pro-symptom position held in non-conscious emotional learning and memory systems. Richard came for two more sessions over the next six weeks. The therapist asked him to consider additional sessions to address any other, lingering aspects, such as a process of grieving the close, warm father–son relationship he never had. Richard thought about it and said he felt no need to extend the work beyond the change for which he had come. This case vignette has shown the TRP being carried out in Coherence Therapy in a straightforward manner, which is often the case and which makes the example of Richard useful as an introduction to this methodology. There are, however, complications that arise with some clients, namely symptoms arising from traumatic memory, and resistance, which are addressed following the next section's summary of the process.

The process in summary The case example of Richard provides a basic familiarity with the steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process, labeled A–B–C–1–2–3–V in Table 3.1 for easy reference. In review of what we have seen above: The steps of the process are well defined, internal experiences to be created, not particular external techniques to be followed by the therapist. Thus the steps must be carried out uniquely with each client, requiring clinical skill as well as comfort with emotional processes. The process begins with the identification of the client's presenting problems or symptoms described in concrete, experiential specifics (Step A). The next step consists of drawing into explicit awareness the implicit emotional learning

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 69 underlying and maintaining the symptoms (Step B). The schema or mental model at the core of this emotional learning is the target for unlearning and nullification. (Sometimes the same symptom is necessary according to two or more different schemas, so that symptom will cease only after each of its underlying schemas has been eliminated by the TRP.) Understanding the specific makeup of a schema revealed in Step B then allows for finding contradictory knowledge that feels unquestionably real to the client (Step C; numerous methods for this step are described in Chapters 4 and 5). Steps A, B, and C—the preparatory, accessing sequence—gather the ingredients needed in order for the therapist to carry out the next phase, Steps 1, 2 and 3—the unlearning sequence—that depotentiates the target learning and eliminates it from emotional memory (without impairing autobiographical memory of life experiences). In the unlearning sequence, first the symptom-generating learning or knowledge is re-evoked and reactivated (Step 1). Then, concurrently, the contradictory knowledge is activated (Step 2) for a juxtaposition of two knowings, side by side, both of which cannot possibly be true. It is this step that unlocks the neural encoding of the target learning, opening a time window—the “reconsolidation window” of about five hours—during which the target learning is susceptible to being fundamentally unlearned by new experiences that disconfirm it. A few repetitions of this both-at-once juxtaposition experience, as it is termed in Coherence Therapy, function as the new learning that rewrites and nullifies the target learning (Step 3), completing the unlearning sequence. The final, verification step of the TRP, Step V, consists of observing the distinct markers of transformational change, which we repeat here from Chapter 2, p. 22:

Schema non-reactivation. The reactivation of a particular, distress-laden

mental model or emotional state no longer occurs in response to cues and triggers that formerly evoked it. • Symptom cessation. Unwanted patterns of behavior, emotion, somatics, or thought that were expressions of that mental model and emotional state also disappear permanently. • Effortless permanence. Non-recurrence of symptoms and schema reactivation continues effortlessly and without counteractive or preventive measures of any kind. The importance of these markers lies, of course, in their declaration of a therapeutic breakthrough. That is not all, however. Their importance also lies in the fact that, according to current neuroscience, these markers can result only from successful elimination of emotional learnings from memory, which can occur only from memory reconsolidation. Therefore, these markers serve as clear feedback to the therapist that the therapeutic reconsolidation process has been carried out successfully. If these markers do not appear, this is an equally clear

70 The Emotional Coherence Framework signal to investigate how and why the process was incomplete or blocked. Thus the markers foster the therapist's effectiveness and learning.4 Some schemas operate across a range of different contexts, as noted earlier, and the client might report markers of transformational change in one context but not others. Compare, for example, one woman's retrieved schema containing the (verbalized) construct, “Expressing any anger makes me unlovable” with another woman's schema containing the construct, “All women are viciously competitive with each other and dangerous.” The second schema comes into play in a far wider range of contexts than does the first, namely in every context in which women are present—at the workplace, with relatives, at social events, visiting with friends, shopping in stores, attending classes, etc. A schema that is strongly relevant in many different contexts becomes part of each separate neural memory network corresponding to each context. If a juxtaposition experience that fulfills the TRP's unlearning sequence engages the target schema in only one of its multiple contexts, the schema will probably be unlearned and depotentiated in only that context and remain in effect for the others. Eliminating the schema across all of its contexts may require separately carrying out the unlearning sequence in each context, in order to nullify the schema in each memory network that has incorporated it.5 Life between sessions serves up useful instances in the various contexts very helpfully, but waiting for life to cover all relevant contexts is not actually necessary because the therapist proactively can guide either an experiential revisiting of past experiences or an imaginal new experience in each relevant context. The fact that TRP Steps A–B–C–1–2–3–V are defined as subjective experiences, without reference to concrete techniques for inducing those experiences, is a great strength, because it means that the therapeutic reconsolidation process can be facilitated through all manner of experiential methods, limited only by our ingenuity and stylistic leanings. Therefore, although the process itself is well delineated, clinicians can exercise great freedom and creativity in using their preferred methods to fulfill it. Any case example of the TRP is necessarily an example of a choice of particular techniques for creating the experiences defined by the TRP steps. Here we have used Coherence Therapy to embody and demonstrate the steps because the phases of Coherence Therapy's methodology correspond directly to all steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process. Quite different methods that fulfill these same steps in other psychotherapy systems less obviously are the topic of Part 2.

The TRP applied for traumatic memory and PTSD Dispelling traumatic memory and post-traumatic symptoms is the explicit focus and purpose of several different systems of psychotherapy, two of which (EMDR and Somatic Experiencing®) are explored in Part 2 of this book. However, some systems that do not categorize themselves as “trauma therapy” can also be

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 71 effective for that. We know from decades of experience that the TRP as facilitated in Coherence Therapy can be highly effective for ending post- traumatic symptoms (PTSD) by depotentiating the various types of traumatic memory (Ecker & Bridges, 2024). The latter range from memory created by single-incident trauma to memory created by multiple co-occurring forms of traumatization by abusive parents in daily life throughout childhood (the condition usually termed complex attachment trauma or developmental trauma).

Defining trauma and traumatic memory How to define trauma and traumatic memory, as distinct from sufferings that are intense but not “traumatic,” is a matter of long and ongoing debate among psychotherapists. For example, one often encounters a distinction between “big-T Trauma” and “little-t trauma,” but there is a wide range of opinions about how these categories are best defined. Our pragmatic point of view in conducting psychotherapy is to understand that traumatic memory is involved if the person seeking therapy describes three or more of the symptoms that are well known to be post-traumatic effects:

- • • • • • • • • • • • • • •

Anxiety or panic attacks Anxious hypervigilance Emotional flatness Dissociation, numbness Sensory flashbacks Avoidance behaviors Interpersonal invisibility Intrusive images or scenes Sitting still, without doing, is intolerable Surges of wretched somatic sensations Large gap in autobiographical memory Narrative reference to extreme ordeal Lack of coherent autobiographical narrative Situational triggering into intense emotional or altered state Ongoing nightmares or persistently repeating dream

Some of our therapy clients don't have three or more of those symptoms, yet earlier in life they did suffer intensely in certain ways that produced emotional learnings (schemas) that have remained outside of awareness, generating symptoms. The fact that we do not categorize their earlier sufferings as “trauma” does not diminish our recognition of how intensely they suffered and how strongly that suffering has shaped their lives. So, as we see it, not all therapy is trauma therapy, and the TRP is applicable and effective for producing transformational change whether or not traumatic

72 The Emotional Coherence Framework memory is involved. As noted previously, a therapist always has to choose suitable techniques and styles of interacting for facilitating the TRP with a particular client, and this custom tailoring is nowhere more critical than in working with traumatic memory, for the obvious reason: Due to its unbearable and therefore terrifying intensity, the memory of a truly traumatizing experience is always largely if not entirely suppressed out of awareness self-protectively, yet its therapeutic depotentiation requires accessing consciously both what was suffered and, critically, what was learned from what was suffered in TRP Step B, as noted earlier in this chapter. The experiential accessing of the memory of a traumatic experience must be done in what Coherence Therapy terms small enough steps that feel tolerable and workable to the client at every point, avoiding an excessive degree of subjective immersion that would be retraumatizing and destabilizing. This is what the trauma therapy field recognizes as the necessity of keeping the therapeutic process inside the client's window of tolerance so that the client's state allows fruitful participation in the therapeutic process. By very carefully co-maintaining a suitably gradual, workable pace of accessing through continual, transparent checking with the client, while persisting in progressively prompting the client to attend further to the traumatic memory, always in small enough steps, therapy clients finally find that they have fully de-suppressed and are processing traumatic memory that initially seemed impossible and unsurvivable to de-suppress. That very experience creates a powerful disconfirmation of the client's initial (usually non-conscious) expectation that de-suppression would cause permanent engulfment in agony and therefore must never be allowed. The disconfirmation of that expectation, noted by the therapist and acknowledged explicitly by the client, proves to be a major, liberating therapeutic breakthrough in itself, and in some cases even produces a complete depotentiation of a severe traumatic memory. Several post-traumatic symptoms in the list above (such as emotional flatness, dissociation, avoidance behaviors, and lack of coherent narrative) exist because they are necessary as the client's very means of maintaining memory suppression, and these symptoms can disappear as soon as memory suppression is no longer self-protectively necessary.

Two main types of traumatic memory The traumatic memory of the ordeal-event itself—memory of the sensory, somatic, and emotional experience, or episodic memory—is only one of the two major forms of traumatic memory, though it is the form that therapists usually have in mind when “traumatic memory” is under discussion, we have often observed. The other, less recognized form of traumatic memory consists of the schemas or mental models formed in response to the traumatic experience— what was learned from what was suffered. This is post-traumatic memory of specific, learned patterns of danger and suffering and of one's vulnerability to

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 73 that suffering (the problem), and of the tactics that are urgently necessary for avoiding that suffering (the solution). This is semantic memory. Such posttraumatic schemas are not fundamentally different from that of Richard in the case example earlier in this chapter or those listed on page 6 in Chapter 1, though the urgency, hypervigilance, anxiety, and somatic tension generated by post-traumatic schemas are more intense and continuous. PTSD symptoms are generated by post-traumatic schemas and mental models at least as much as by post-traumatic suppression of episodic memory, in our clinical experience.

Complex attachment trauma Complex attachment trauma, sometimes termed CPTSD, is one of the more challenging types of symptomology for therapists because it is indeed complex, in more than one way: the client has numerous different symptoms of behavior, state of mind, and somatic disturbances; the many traumatic experiences and memories are of numerous different types; they occurred across many or all developmental stages; and they are inherent features of the child's primary attachment relationships. As conceptualized in the Emotional Coherence Framework and in Coherence Therapy, for each distinct form of suffering repeatedly experienced as part of family life, the child's adaptive emotional learning creates a separate schema, consisting of the child's knowledge of how that suffering occurs and feels (the problem) and the urgently necessary tactics for preventing or avoiding it (the solution). For example, different schemas are formed in response to being unexpectedly blasted with rage and shaming from Dad for making a simple mistake, being disallowed dinner and confined to one's bedroom by Mom for coming home with soiled pants, and being sexually molested each time a certain uncle visits. As kaleidoscopic as the client's array of symptoms may seem initially, every symptom proves to be the coherent expression of at least one underlying schema. Therefore, Coherence Therapy can dispel complex attachment trauma through persistent implementation of its usual methodology: The client's manifested symptoms are the points of departure for accessing and revealing each of the underlying schemas, which are then subjected to the MR process of unlearning and nullification. Because there are many schemas—over twenty in the more severe cases—many sessions are required for thorough dispelling of complex attachment trauma. It is sometimes possible to keep sessions focused on a single schema until it is fully depotentiated and the symptom it was producing has ceased, but often two or more schemas are in different stages of the process and the work on them advances nonlinearly. Keeping track of the process for each schema requires the therapist to maintain session notes with adequate specificity and detail. Schemas formed in complex attachment trauma are subjected to the TRP in Chapters 4 (the case of Ted), 5 (the case of Regina), 7, 8, 10, 12, and 21. The

74 The Emotional Coherence Framework effectiveness of the TRP for unlearning and depotentiating a schema formed in an acute traumatic incident is shown in Chapter 4 (stage fright due to suppressed memory of childhood traumatic incident), Chapter 9 (PTSD symptoms following a tornado catastrophe), and Chapter 14 (physical assault and attempted rape).

The TRP applied for dispelling resistance Resistance—that is, some form of conscious or non-conscious non-cooperation with the therapist's current step of therapeutic process—can develop at any step of the TRP. In Coherence Therapy, the therapist welcomes resistance by working with it as described in the Coherence Therapy Practice Manual and Training Guide (Ecker & Hulley, 2019, p. 54): The therapist responds to resistance by applying the usual Coherence Therapy methodology to it: Temporarily the therapist regards the resistance as the “symptom” and accords it the same empathy, acceptance, and respectful assumption of cogency \[coherence\] that all symptoms receive in Coherence Therapy. Therapist then works to discover the emotional truth of the resistance—how and why, for the client, the resistance is necessary to have at this moment. That emotional truth consists of expecting that cooperating with the therapist's current promptings would result in suffering a specific, unavoidable negative effect. Fully eliciting and verbalizing that expectation reveals a particular schema or mental model of the negative effect and how it would result from cooperating, which completes TRP Step B. The therapist then carries out Step C, finding contradictory knowledge, which consists of identifying a reliable way to prevent the expected negative effect from happening by using internal and/or external resources already available to the client. The client's schema is disconfirmed by the recognition that the expected negative result is not unavoidable. In some cases, the client recognizes that the negative expectation is based entirely on memory of childhood conditions and is now no longer possible in adulthood. Either way, then the unlearning sequence, Steps 1–2–3, is easy to facilitate or, more often, occurs spontaneously in seconds. The client then expresses relief and comfort with cooperating with what had been resisted. (For an instructional survey of techniques for working with resistance in Coherence Therapy, see Ecker & Hulley, 2019.) A unique type of resistance can arise in response to TRP Steps 2 and 3 in the unlearning sequence—the creation of a juxtaposition experience repeated a few times. This is resistance to allowing the target schema to be disconfirmed and rendered unreal and depotentiated, or resistance to transformation (as distinct from resistance to discovery and resistance to integration that may occur at the earlier stages of Coherence Therapy).

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 75 Despite well-designed, well-guided juxtaposition experiences, the target schema can remain in force, as shown in the case of the underachieving Ted in Chapter 4. This indicates that the process of schema disconfirmation and nullification is being blocked for self-protection from some intense disorientation, loss, pain, fear, or hardship that the client expects, non-consciously, to result from the longstanding symptom-requiring model of reality no longer being true. Loss of an important part of familiar personal reality can involve significant, difficult emotional adjustments, even though it was a very problematic, distressladen part of seeming reality. Perhaps the most frequently encountered instance of this occurs with a target schema in which the cold, harsh treatment regularly received from one or both parents throughout childhood is construed as being one's own fault and deserved for being fundamentally unworthy, disgusting, incapable, or unlovable. A person with such a schema can allow a decisive disconfirmation of that model of the cause of the harsh treatment only by tolerating knowing that it was not deserved at all—a knowing that inherently brings with it the deeply distressing recognition of suffering parental abuse. Construing the mistreatment as deserved had been self-protectively blinding the individual from recognizing that it was abuse, but if that painful recognition is not tolerable initially, the schema will be immune to disconfirmation at that point in time, no matter how skillfully the therapist sets up a juxtaposition experience. Such resistance to transformation then has to be rendered unnecessary through the process described above: The therapist regards the resistance as a new “symptom” that is coherent in itself, and guides discovery of the underlying need for it by bringing into awareness the specific sufferings expected if the target schema were to no longer feel at all true. When, as a result of this work, those expectations have been transformed and the ramifications of schema nullification now feel tolerable in all areas, the previously ineffective juxtaposition experience is repeated and now unlearning and nullification of the schema readily occur. Thus the unlearning and nullification of emotional learnings is “gated” by a top-down process, that is, it is allowed to proceed, or not, depending on whether the emotional results expected by the client's emotional memory systems feel tolerable in all areas, both consciously and unconsciously; the nature of the process is not simply mechanistic or neurological. Using active, focused, experiential methods, usually this work on resistance to transformation of a single schema is accomplished in a small number of sessions.

The TRP applied for the neurodiverse population Skillful facilitation of the TRP has been effective for neurodiverse individuals, only some of whom already view themselves as being neurodiverse at the start of therapy. As a rule, these individuals—each unique—share a lifelong, troubled sense of being different and often socially marginal, and feel intensely alone as a

76 The Emotional Coherence Framework result. Usually, but not always, there are sensory, social, or cognitive challenges that may affect autonomy or emotion regulation. In therapy, these clients often prove to be not only deeply insightful but also deeply feelingful even when they have a detached or flat-affect presentation style. Here, we very briefly sketch the contours of how the TRP applies with this population.6 One main focus of the therapeutic work tends to be the core belief of being fundamentally defective and inferior. There are three main avenues for creating disconfirmations that effectively unlearn that model of self:

One avenue is the same approach that is effective for most cases involving

significant low self-worth and self-devaluing: immersive revisiting of key scenes of mistreatment that was suffered, with experiential reversal of the attributed meaning from “I deserve this because there is something wrong with me” to “this is mistreatment and a failure to be kind and caring, and I don't deserve it.” • When the therapist truly sees and experiences the client as an inherently valid, full member of the human family, and authentically conveys that quality of regard, the client's experience of being seen by the therapist in that way can be an effective disconfirmation, which enables these clients to dare to cease any cover-up behaviors that have been masking their true inner experience and their actual ways of functioning, at first only during sessions and soon elsewhere also. • Disconfirmation can also be created by psychoeducationally developing the client's understanding of neurodiversity, including radical self-acceptance for having a “different kind of mind” that has its own particular capabilities and great strengths, and has had its own types of success where there was a rightness of fit. Thoroughly discovering and recognizing those experiences of rightness of fit is a crucial part of the work. The client understands that people thrive only under conditions suitable to their constitution, and the fact that they do thrive when there is rightness of fit means that there is no fundamental defectiveness. As the mental model of defectiveness and inferiority is more and more fully drained of its seeming realness as a result of those three processes of disconfirmation, the shame that had been generated by that mental model correspondingly ceases to be felt. Another important focus of the therapeutic work tends to be fearful expectations about venturing outside the very small, familiar social and sensory bubble that many neurodiverse individuals dearly wish to escape in order to have satisfying relationships and jobs. Progress with dispelling shame and identifying right fits, as noted just above, proves to be a major factor in dialing down the fearfulness of venturing out and in developing capacity for more independent, connected, satisfying engagement in the world.

The Transformational Psychotherapy of Emotional Unlearning 77

Conclusion Our aim in this chapter has been to show the therapeutic reconsolidation process in action, illustrating its abundant value to therapy clients and psychotherapists both. This process fully dispels symptoms as a result of profound unlearning of a distress-laden mental model, or schema, formed earlier in life; and that unlearning is also the thorough resolution of that particular distress through an advance in one's living knowledge of the world and oneself. As noted, any case example of the TRP is an example of a choice of particular techniques used for facilitating the process. Here it is some of Coherence Therapy's methods that have been used, showing how the explicit revealing of symptom coherence depathologizes both symptoms and clients' sense of self, instilling a sense of the fundamental validity and coherence of self. The client not only becomes free of the symptoms, but also deeply recognizes that having the symptoms was never due to being bad, sick, stupid, defective, or crazy, and knows that the therapist knows this also. Such liberating change is the therapeutic ideal. In the TRP as carried out in Coherence Therapy, the therapist's stance is one of facilitating clients' own innate capabilities and processes for further evolving the world of meaning and the mental models that they previously had construed and learned, in that way freeing themselves from the limiting and unwanted negative effects of those earlier construals. The therapist's expertise consists of knowing how the innate capabilities and processes of unlearning and revising function—namely, as mapped by the TRP—and of having the interpersonal skills needed for facilitating them effectively. Therefore, the therapist leads in process but not in content, always learning from the client what emotional learnings are present and what is occurring at each point in the process of their transformation. Now that we understand such fundamental, lasting change both experientially and neurologically—through both the top-down and bottom-up lenses—it has become possible for this level of therapeutic breakthrough, which we call transformational change, to be a regular occurrence in the daily practices of psychotherapists and counselors, rather than an occasional, unpredictable victory that depends too much on luck or guesswork to happen regularly. The next chapter focuses closely on creating the all-important juxtaposition experience that fulfills the unlearning sequence and nullifies troubling emotional learnings.

Notes 1 The important exception to this practice is when the client indicates distress or even just some concern over staying in touch with newly emergent material between sessions, as described in the previous subsection. Only after that initial intensity has diminished and the material feels workable should a between-session focus on it be maintained.

78 The Emotional Coherence Framework 2 For a more fine-grained map of schema structure, see Ecker and Hulley (2000, 2019).

Memory of patterns in the world is termed semantic memory by researchers, as distinct from episodic memory of the personal experiences and events in which a pattern was learned.

Reactivation of a schema memory does not also reactivate memory of the original learning experience, as a rule, and an implicit emotional schema can be brought into awareness without remembering the original learning experiences, though accessing the latter memory is helpful when available.

For discussion of the roles of semantic and episodic memory in symptom production, see Ecker (2018).

3 This state of mindful, metacognitive awareness of the contents or processes of one's own mind has also been termed the observing self, the observing ego, and witness consciousness.

In this state, the individual's consciousness is not merged with any particular mental, emotional, or somatic experiencing and therefore has some separation from all such contents and can observe, consider, and even choicefully interact with them.

The active use of this state is apparent in Coherence Therapy's integration and transformation phases.

How other therapy systems utilize meta-awareness is illustrated in Chapters 7 (AEDP) and 10 (IFS).

4 As noted earlier, the client initially expresses an anti-symptom position and wants the presenting symptom to stop.

However, the meaning of having the symptom is changed completely by bringing into awareness the underlying, adaptive purpose that actually produces the symptom.

With awareness of how and why the symptom is emotionally necessary to have, the client in some cases no longer wants it to cease and instead wants to retain it.

This is termed reverse resolution in Coherence Therapy.

The client no longer views the symptom as an unwanted, involuntary behavior or state of mind, but rather as an adaptive response of great personal value.

An illustration of reverse resolution, provided by Ecker and Hulley (1996), is the case of the graduate student troubled about warnings of expulsion from his program due to his extreme, pervasive inaction on all fronts, which he called “procrastination.” In therapy he became aware of his underlying emotional truth that what he had been calling procrastination was actually his refusal to follow an unwanted path in life.

His parents had chosen his graduate program and forced him into it.

He now recognized the true meaning of his inaction as being a desirable strength of selfdetermination that he wanted to retain, and he soon withdrew from the program.

5 Corroborating this understanding of how schemas are held in memory in a contextspecific manner, on 24 March 2023 one of the authors (RT) received the following personal communication from clinical psychologist Peter Barach, PhD, Clinical Senior Instructor in Psychiatry, Case Western Reserve School of Medicine and past President of the International Society for the Study of Trauma & Dissociation.

It is reproduced here with his kind permission: “I have had some surprising good results using MR in my practice.

Most of my caseload is people living with dissociative identity disorder (DID).

I find that the MR process has to be adapted for this population's multiplicity of identity states.

First, it's sometimes the case that several alters (dissociated self-states) hold different memories that support the old emotional learning, yet the alters are amnestic for each other's histories and experiences.

Therefore, unless there is a way to effect temporary blending of these self-states, the MR procedure, in whatever form, has to be done with each of them.

Similarly, various disconfirming experiences are sometimes available to the memories of some alters but not others—the more alters can be co-conscious during the therapy work with MR, the greater the likelihood that the old learning will be erased and replaced.” 6 For this section, the authors consulted with Narrative Therapist Gail Noppe-Brandon, LCSW, a Certified Advanced Practitioner of Coherence Therapy in New York City who generously shared her extensive experience in working with the neurodiverse population.

She also contributed the cases in Chapters 20 and 22.
