#### Th: Cl: Th:

doesn't change because of imperfections. Can you just look at him, knowing and feeling that? Mm-hm. Yeah. Good. And now keep him in view and keep knowing that, as you widen the picture and also see, maybe over on the other side of the room, your mom. Can you do that? Yeah. And what you know about her love is so different, because her love quickly disappears and turns into disgust and rejection when any imperfections show up, yes? \[Client nods yes.\] So, just see how it is for you to be in touch, like this, with both kinds of love at once, and each is so clear, but they're so different: On one side, there's Mom with love that's so fragile and so quickly flips into rejection over any imperfections that displease her; and you could easily expect that's how it would be with anyone. \[That is a deliberate, explicit re-evoking of the target construct.\] And on the other side, there's Uncle Theo with love that is so steady and reliable and unaffected by imperfections, and he just sees and feels how lovable you are and nothing changes that. And both kinds of love feel so real, but they're so different. Can you feel both at once? \[Client nods yes.\] Good. \[Therapist now prompts a repeat of the juxtaposition experience:\] How is that for you—seeing so clearly that both kinds of love exist, and that you're actually experiencing both kinds? \[silence for many seconds\] I never thought of it like this before. \[pause\] Yes, it's very new to see it this way—that you actually already experience both kinds of love. \[pause\] And as you look back and forth at Mom and Uncle Theo, what happens? \[Prompting her to look back and forth at them is another repetition of the juxtaposition experience.\] \[silence for about 15 seconds\] It's strange, but my Mom looks smaller. \[This is a first marker of a transformational shift in her mental model of Mom.\] And it's like—what's wrong is in her, not in me. \[pause\] It's over there in her, not over here in me. \[This is a marker of a transformational shift in the meanings she has attributed to her mother's harsh, rejecting behaviors.\] Mm-hm. And as you are knowing that, what are you feeling? It feels scary—because, you know, then I can't have any control over it. If it's in me, I have a chance of controlling it. \[That is new awareness of her own purpose and agency for believing Mom's blame and denigrations, as her solution to the problem of terrifying powerlessness over the abuse.\] Control it by hiding everything imperfect? Right; and being really, really good. But if the reason she blows up at me is that she's messed up, then I can't possibly control it, and that's scary. \[silence while gazing into her lap\] But I'm also feeling relief, too. Relief because—?

130 The Emotional Coherence Framework Cl: —because if she's the problem, then maybe there's nothing seriously wrong with me after all; and maybe I won't be rejected forever by anyone who gets to know me. Th: Does Uncle Theo know you pretty well? Cl: \[grinning happily\] He does, yeah. Th: So, look at him again and this time, try out saying to him, “You love me with my imperfections, and that means the world to me.” Cl: \[silence as she says that to him\] Yeah. Th: It fits and feels true? Cl: Yeah, it does. And he smiles at me; he's happy that I understand. The therapist and Regina then worked on writing some simple limbic-language sentences to put on an index card to help her stay in touch between sessions with key elements of this work. The card read: Mom's kind of love, and Uncle Theo's kind of love: With Uncle Theo, I don't have to be perfect to be lovable and loved. Mom's love is so fragile because of trouble inside her, not because of me. That means I don't have control over getting her to stop rejecting me, the way I thought I had, and that feels scary and sad. Read daily, those sentences would prompt repeated experiences of the juxtaposition and of the knowings that emerged from it. The therapist also asked Regina to read the card just before phoning her mother and to keep the card in front of her during the conversation. Regina's juxtaposition experience had begun to dissolve her implicit mental model that love operates only in her mother's manner and that the cause of her mother's eruptions of hostility was her own defectiveness. Those models were replaced by a new, expanded model that included her mother's type of love but also recognized the existence of her uncle's type of love, as well as the view that the cause of her mother's eruptions was something “messed up” in her mother, not in herself. She was therefore now beginning to inhabit a world in which steady, secure love was possible and available to her, and she was worthy of it. In the next session, the therapist invited and guided her to identify who else, among her relatives, friends, teachers, and work colleagues, would similarly feel hurt by learning that Regina sincerely believed that their fondness of her was only a superficial enjoyment of how perfectly she pleased them. She was surprised by how many people were in this group. This exercise, understood in terms of the therapeutic reconsolidation process, was an accessing of the same contradictory knowledge in many different contexts so that the target constructs would undergo a disconfirming juxtaposition experience in each context, which, as noted previously, tends to be needed for thorough unlearning when a target

Is It Always About Attachment? 131 schema operates in different contexts that have different memory networks. This work continued nonlinearly across about 10 sessions, alongside and alternating with other lines of coherence work that had developed. Imaginal work, such as was done with Regina, is of enormous value for creating strong experiences of both target schemas and contradictory knowledge, as needed for successful schema-dissolving juxtaposition experiences. Creative use of imaginal process gives therapists virtually unlimited avenues for facilitating such experiences beyond the limitations of relying solely on the client's experiences of the therapist for reparative attachment work. At the start of her fifth session, Regina described a particularly strong panic attack that had occurred on the previous day as soon as she left a lunch meeting with several co-workers and returned alone to her car; one day later, she was still feeling quite shaky from it. At lunch there had been more than enough snide comments made and ambiguous social signals sent to trigger Regina's expectation of disastrous rejection several times over. In fact, in re-telling the incident to the therapist, she became retriggered into a significant level of anxiety, and said so. The therapist saw this incident as an opportunity to use another type of experiential process that has several important therapeutic effects in working with traumatic memory and its reactivations in Coherence Therapy. We refer to this process as the I'm in memory practice. Its immediate and most obvious effect is to make a reactivated traumatic memory promptly begin to subside rather than persist gruelingly for many hours or days. Its other, less obvious effects go far beyond symptom relief, subjecting the traumatic memory to both integration experiences and juxtaposition experiences, as will become apparent. The therapist then said, “Okay, I'll guide you to try something that could help with this, and I'll explain it first. In our previous sessions, we've learned a lot about what it really means when your anxiety or panic ignites: It means somebody's behavior has at least looked like a possibly negative response toward you, and we know why that perception is so charged and scary for you: It's all those hundreds of times when you first saw a negative response starting in your mom, and then whammo! Really painful, humiliating, scary things would happen—a grueling ordeal that could keep going for days. Your emotional brain learned that the first moment of displeasure toward you means that now a horrible ordeal is coming. All of that emotional learning and suffering went into your emotional memory, and emotional memory just doesn't fade out over time— that's how the brain evolved. Someone seeming to become displeased with you in the present closely enough resembles that terrible moment of your mom becoming displeased with you that it retriggers all of that emotional memory, and to your emotional brain this means that the ordeal is about to happen again right now! The emotional brain mixes up the past and the present. It uses the past to make sense of what's happening in the present, and expecting the same ordeal

132 The Emotional Coherence Framework to happen again now triggers an anxiety or panic attack. So here is what I want you to try doing right now: “Put one of your palms on your heart, the way you might do if you were comforting a child who's terrified. Good. Next, softly but out loud say this sentence to yourself about that lunch meeting: 'This situation is reminding me of what I suffered back then, when Mom would start to get displeased with me.' \[Regina said the words.\] Good. Now say, 'This raw fear I'm feeling is my living memory of what I felt and suffered back then.' \[Regina said the words.\] Good. Now, as you say this next sentence, gently pat your heart area with your hand: 'It was so awful; it was so horrible for me—and this situation is reminding me of it.' \[She did this.\] Good. Then say all of it one more time; I'll lead you again…” After saying those self-compassionate sentences a second time, Regina said with surprise that her anxiety had already diminished greatly—on a scale of 0 to 10, it was down to 2 from 8—and she added, “It has never faded out so fast once it's triggered!” She also commented—and this was particularly indicative that the technique was working as intended—that “saying those words made something shift in my whole perspective—it was such a relief to realize that something awful isn't really happening now, and also that this crazy feeling is actually coming from something and I'm not crazy.” The therapist then assigned the I'm in memory practice to Regina as a between-session task by giving her an index card with these instructions written on it: Whenever you notice that either the fear or the pain has been retriggered, put the palm of one or both hands over your heart and say to yourself: This situation is reminding me of what I suffered back then, with Mom suddenly turning against me. I'm feeling my living memory of what I felt back then. \[With patting:\] It was so awful for me; it was so horrible; and this situation is reminding me of that experience. \[Then say it one more time.\] In each session, Regina reported the latest incidents of retriggering and how she used the I'm in memory practice in response. Each time, the therapist asked her to say a bit more about the living memory that had been evoked, and in that way, Regina continued the process of revisiting and integrating what she originally suffered. Across several sessions she became able to enter deeply and unhurriedly into strong emotional recall of childhood experiences that initially had been too raw to re-contact even lightly for more than a few seconds. Feeling closely accompanied empathetically by the therapist in these deepening immersive recalls was a crucially important condition that made this work possible.

Is It Always About Attachment? 133 Regina's increasingly clear, direct awareness of what she endured in childhood had powerful, natural effects. Her retrieved knowledge directly turned into new, coherent narratives for major areas of life experience that previously had been baffling, unrepresented, or covered over with rationalizations. For example, she said, “My feelings get hurt so deeply so easily, all my life, and I could never tell anybody why or even tell myself why I'm so, you know, delicate or something. It never crossed my mind that that's the intense hurt I always felt when my mom would tell me I'm so bad even though I didn't do anything wrong and was trying so hard to be so good. But now I remember feeling that same hurt \[indicating her heart area\] as a little girl, alone in my room for so many hours until I'd be allowed out again.” Another area of new, coherent narrative was expressed by Regina in terms of new awareness of “so much that I didn't get,” meaning warmth, cherishing, understanding, and feeling taken care of and secure. This in turn opened a process of self-compassionate grieving that was the indispensable de-suppression and emotional processing of so much deprivation that she endured. Development of coherent autobiographical narrative is widely regarded as an important goal of psychotherapy (e.g., Schore, 2003). The viewpoint within the Emotional Coherence Framework is that the most authentic and therapeutic narrative is formed through retrieving and verbalizing what the client's emotional brain already coherently knows in implicit memory regarding what was suffered. Nothing is invented in that process, only discovered. The I'm in memory practice is a specialized form of mindfulness and metacognition applied for bringing implicit memory into explicit awareness. It is often highly useful for facilitating the integration and transformation of emotional implicit memory containing traumatic levels of severe distress, including complex trauma within attachment relationships as well as trauma in other areas. The technique has been shaped into the particular experiential form described above for use in Coherence Therapy, but the essence of the practice—maintaining mindful recognition of being in a triggered state of reactivated emotional memory—has its origins in the human potential movement of the 1960s and early 70s. The most salient effect of this practice, as Regina demonstrated, is to spare oneself the experience of unknowingly projecting the reactivated memory of suffering onto the present external situation and suffering the present situation as if the original raw ordeal were dangerously happening again, which is the view of the subcortical emotional system. That would be immersion in a flashback (retriggered traumatic memory) without awareness of it as a flashback. Instead, the I'm in memory practice utilizes each such episode of reactivation for further, mindful recognition and integration of the retriggered emotional memory, which in turn allows retrieval of meanings, constructs, and models formed and learned in the original sufferings. These then become targets for disconfirmation and unlearning in juxtaposition experiences, completing the therapeutic reconsolidation process.

134 The Emotional Coherence Framework Table 5.1 Juxtaposition experiences created by the I'm in memory practice carried out when traumatic memory has been retriggered Symptom-generating construct (existing, old implicit knowing)

Contradictory knowledge (new knowing created by I'm in memory practice)

Something extremely harmful and terrifying \[or hopeless, devastating, etc.\] is happening to me right now.

What I'm feeling is my living memory of what I suffered back then. The present situation is only reminding me of that. It isn't happening to me again now. These extreme feelings and thoughts are parts of my living memory of what I actually suffered back then. I am not engulfed or destabilized by letting the memory come into awareness. I am larger than the memory and capable of knowing and feeling the truth of what I have experienced. It is safe for me to fully inhabit my body, my feelings, and my knowledge.

These extreme feelings and thoughts mean I'm crazy \[or defective, dysfunctional, irrational, etc.\]. I would be undone by facing, knowing and feeling what I suffered and still carry inside me! The memory is much bigger than I am and would engulf me in agony forever. I need to live disconnected from knowing or feeling what I have experienced.

In addition to the integration of traumatic memory that is gently but steadily achieved through the I'm in memory practice, this deceptively simple exercise also creates three different juxtaposition experiences, spelled out in Table 5.1. The rapid reduction of emotional distress observed to result from this practice can readily be understood as a direct effect of these juxtaposition experiences disconfirming (a) the view and feeling that something truly terrible is happening right now, (b) the view that the extreme feelings and thoughts I'm having mean there is something terribly wrong with me, and (c) the presupposition (implicit knowledge) that living my life in an emotionally suppressed, dissociated, disintegrated state is my only viable option. Being freed of those three states of mind is a very big relief. Naturally, this calming, comforting effect is what makes the I'm in memory practice so appealing to clients, but from the more technical viewpoint of therapeutic methodology—specifically, in relation to the therapeutic reconsolidation process—it is the integrative effect plus the three juxtaposition experiences that make this practice so valuable. It shifts the perceived source of presently felt distress from the present to the past, but notice how this shift comes about: It results from the prior, deep work of emotionally revisiting original sufferings, giving the client direct, experiential awareness that the actual source of the present distress is living memory of past sufferings. If, without that prior work, the therapist instead merely explains reassuringly to the client that his or her ordeals are safely in the past and are not happening or possible now in the present, this cognitive-insight form of the past/present

Is It Always About Attachment? 135 distinction typically proves to have little therapeutic potency or holding power, because it is counteractive. Returning to the work with Regina: In response to perceived negative responses from others, her self-blame and her anxiety or panic decreased fairly steadily after her fifth session, as did her perfectionism, because it was a solution to a problem that had less and less realness for her. She was largely free of symptoms by her 16th session, felt well equipped to continue working on her own with the occasional situation that still “tweaked” her, and saw no need for therapy after her 18th session. Regina's therapy shows that in cases where the client's problematic attachment learnings could, in principle, be transformed by utilizing the client– therapist relationship reparatively to create contradictory knowledge, other sources of disconfirming, contradictory knowledge exist and can be equally or more effective. Another example of this type is the use of empowered re- enactment in Chapter 4 with client Brenda, who suffered stage fright based on traumatic memory. The attachment rules governing her emotional and behavioral world conceivably could have been disconfirmed in reparative attachment work but were dissolved instead by working imaginally with her interactions with her parents. Similarly, in the case of Richard in Chapter 3, reparative work in the client–therapist relationship could have been used to disconfirm his expectation that if he were to express his knowledge or views with any confidence, he would be hated for being a dominating know-it-all, as his father was—but the therapist recognized the disconfirmation opportunity provided by a group interaction at Richard's workplace. Many of the case examples in Parts 2 and 3 of this book also show core, attachment-based learnings and symptoms dispelled by being juxtaposed with disconfirming living knowledge sourced outside of the client–therapist relationship. We emphasize that point not to diminish the value or importance of reparative attachment work, but to expand the range of effective options available for attachment work so that more therapists can be more effective more of the time in more settings. Of course, the client–therapist relationship was a crucially important catalytic, facilitative ingredient in the work with Regina and Brenda, even without serving a disconfirming, reparative attachment function.

When disconfirmation via therapeutic dyad is not possible Positive experiences of a therapist cannot possibly disconfirm and dissolve some attachment-based, symptom-generating schemas. That assertion is not theoretical in nature, rather it expresses the phenomenological observation of the specific, revealed contents of clients' schemas, and two case examples follow below. In such cases, reparative attachment work would necessarily fail to create transformational change of the schema. Methods of schema

136 The Emotional Coherence Framework disconfirmation other than reparative attachment are then necessary, not optional. The case in Chapter 4 of Ted, who had, with unconscious purposefulness, made his life a shambles in an attempt to rebuke and elicit repair from his father, provides our first example of this kind. His presenting symptom of pervasive underachieving was maintained, it was found, by an emotional implicit schema that became verbalized in this way: The most important thing to me is to get Dad to see that he failed at being a father to me. I hate to admit it, but that's so important to me that I'm willing to keep my own life a mess, and get nowhere, to get him to see how badly he screwed up by tearing me down all the time. That the content of this schema consists thoroughly of attachment learnings and memory of attachment experiences is clear. However, this particular schema does not consist of terms of attachment—specific rules and requirements defining how to be acceptable to Dad—so Ted's experience of the therapist's empathic attunement and acceptance could not possibly disconfirm this material. To see in detail why this is so, one considers each way in which the client could have an experience of the therapist that might possibly be relevant either to disconfirming the schema's component constructs or fulfilling needs or solutions specified in the schema.

If Ted deeply recognized and felt that he was utterly safe from being torn

down by the therapist as he was by his father, and even that the therapist strongly wanted to protect Ted from being torn down by anyone, would this knowledge either disconfirm his need for accountability and justice from his father or somehow end that need by satisfying it? No, it would not. • If Ted experienced the therapist's (instead of Dad's) genuine, empathetic understanding that he had been horribly hurt and harmed by his father and that his father was therefore a complete failure as a father, would this experience either disconfirm his need for accountability and justice from his father or somehow end that need by satisfying it? No, it would not. With reparative attachment ruled out for this schema, the therapist used a different method for guiding Ted into experiencing the needed contradictory knowledge. A second example is the brief but deep work conducted by psychologist Sara K. Bridges to address the marital sexual aversion of a mid-thirties woman called Carol, the mother of an 11-year-old daughter, Dana (Neimeyer & Bridges, 2003, pp. 291–292). Carol had no idea why she always felt so avoidant of sex with her husband despite their emotional closeness, other than to say that she “just didn't like to have sex very much.” Using Coherence Therapy, Carol's

Is It Always About Attachment? 137 symptom-necessitating schema was soon retrieved and found to have formed on the basis of much suffering in childhood due to her parents' flagrantly erotic behavior. In a quiet tone, with her legs crossed and her head in her hands, Carol then recalled a time when she was about 15 years old when her mother walked into the bathroom and found her masturbating. Far from being angry, her mother was so pleased that she not only told Carol's father but also called several friends and told them about this “beautiful good news.” Carol identified her decision to shut out sexual feelings from that very point. Discussing this series of memories and associated feelings, she also realized that enjoying sex with her husband subjectively meant being like her mother, and closer to risking mortifying her own daughter, Dana, in the same way. At the end of that session, Carol left carrying an index card with the following sentences expressing the emotional truth of her newly conscious compelling purpose for avoiding sexuality. Reading these words would create integration experiences each time. I hate to admit it, but experiencing sexual pleasure with my husband makes me more like my mother. So, even though it is hurting my marriage, I will continue to avoid sexual contact, because it is better to sacrifice pleasure and intimacy than to risk doing to Dana what my mother did to me. Before that therapy session, Carol (non-consciously) expected that for her to engage in any marital sexuality would cause her own daughter the same sorts of harm and suffering as were inflicted on her by her parents' eroticism, making it urgent for her to avoid feeling or being sexual with her husband. Was Carol's sex-avoiding schema amenable to reparative attachment work? That is, could it be disconfirmed by her experience of receiving the therapist's attunement, empathy, and acceptance? To answer that question, we use the reparative attachment decision process defined above. Clearly her schema was forged in the crucible of her attachment relationships with her parents, but are the constructs in this schema terms of attachment, i.e., primary rather than secondary (other attachment-related) learnings? In our view the answer is yes, they are primary, which is apparent as follows. Her mother's terms of attachment, as learned by Carol, could be verbalized approximately as, “Be erotic like me, out in the open where I and my friends can delight in it. This is what most strongly gets my attention and fondness and connects you to me. There must be no boundaries hiding your sexual behavior from me.” The essence of these terms of attachment is: Sexuality must have no boundaries of privacy between us. That implicit construct defined Carol's emotional learning of how sexuality

138 The Emotional Coherence Framework operates in a family. Inhabiting that problem-defining construct, Carol was implicitly expecting her sexuality to violate her daughter's boundaries. The last question in the decision process is this: Is it conceivable that Carol's experience of her therapist's empathy, sensitivity, validation, safety, and so on could disconfirm those terms of attachment? Only if the answer were a clear yes could reparative attachment be a suitable approach for transforming this schema. There is no reliable form of such disconfirmation that we can envision, though there is the following possibility that is an uncertain maybe: Carol's female therapist, upon learning the makeup of Carol's symptom-necessitating schema and recognizing in it the terms of attachment described above, could have begun to express sensitive, overt recognition and respect for the fundamental privacy of Carol's sex life in relation to herself, the therapist. This overt, emphatic honoring of Carol's sexual privacy would have been in sharp contrast to her experience of her mother. For example, the therapist might have said, “Naturally, you're here to address a sexual problem so you are telling me about your sex life, but I just want to say—in case there is any part of you that might be wondering, from a certain angle, about our interaction—that I'm feeling no need of my own to hear about your sex life, and I deeply regard your sex life as your private domain. And only with your permission and wish for me to hear about it will we talk about it, because otherwise I feel it is your private domain.” That would be followed at some later point by asking, “How is it for you to see and understand that I'm so different from your mom in this way?” Whether work along those lines would have served as a disconfirmation of the authority of her mother's requirement is too uncertain to predict; and even if it had done so, it is also uncertain whether that shift would have disconfirmed the construct that was directly maintaining Carol's aversion to marital sex—her expectation that any experience or expression of her own sexuality would harm her daughter, as she was harmed by her mother's sexuality. Thus, we do not see any clear, reliable disconfirmation of that master, target construct developing within the client–therapist interaction, so the result of the decision process in this case is, for us, a ruling-out of reparative attachment work. The contradictory knowledge that would successfully disconfirm Carol's expectations would have to be found outside of the client's experiences of the therapist. How the schema was dissolved was described by Neimeyer and Bridges (2003, p. 292) in this way: In the next session, Carol reported that the statement \[on her index card\] began to seem almost silly to her during the week, and although she knew it would take time and practice, finding a new way to understand her sexuality as her own and not her mother's was a freeing experience for her and also for her relationship with her husband. Once held as a conscious rather than unconscious position, the previously prevailing view soon lost much of its power, permitting the client to relinquish it as her governing emotional reality.

Is It Always About Attachment? 139 In that account are two markers of transformational change. One is her reporting that “to understand her sexuality as her own and not her mother's was a freeing experience.” That is a description of contradictory knowledge—my sexuality is not the same as my mother's—that came into Carol's awareness in response to her overt statement on the index card, which maintained her awareness of her retrieved presupposition that her sexuality functions the same as Mom's. (Emergence of contradictory knowledge in that manner is the fruit of the brain's mismatch detection activity, as described in Chapter 4.) The other marker is the report that emotional truths on the card that had felt deadly serious and compelling to Carol when first retrieved into direct awareness a week earlier now felt “almost silly” to her. That is a direct indication of the loss of subjective realness of a schema successfully disconfirmed by a juxtaposition experience. The termsof-attachment construct of identical sexualities and the associated expectation that her sexuality would harm her daughter simply no longer felt true, eliminating the need to protectively refrain from sexuality with her husband. The examples of Ted and Carol illustrate the class of psychotherapy cases in which a retrieved schema is not disconfirmable through reparative attachment work, so utilizing other sources of disconfirmation is necessary. Another type of situation in which reparative attachment work is infeasible warrants mentioning here. It occurs with adult clients who seem to be good candidates for reparative attachment therapy—in that they have a full-blown history of insecure attachment, feel the emotional woundedness that that entails, and in their sessions have opened up without resistance to experiencing deep areas of emotional distress and vulnerability (indicating the presence of adequate emotional safety, trust, and empathy in the client–therapist relationship)—but they find the prospect of having their need for secure attachment met through interactions with a therapist to be utterly unsuitable, unreal, non-credible and impossible. As one such client, “Tomás,” a man of 45, honestly put it to his older male therapist, “Look, you're a professional practitioner who offers expert services that I'm paying you for. We might do 5 or 50 more sessions, but then you won't be in my life any more. So, when you ask me how it is to be feeling so understood and seen and validated by you after never getting any of that from my mother or father, no, it doesn't fill those empty slots that should have been filled by them doing it right. That's just not how this could work for me. Maybe it could work with someone who's in my life for real.” Of course, it is possible that responses such as Tomás's might be a rationalized expression of unconscious resistance to the emotional vulnerability involved in allowing a therapist to “fill those empty slots.” However, we have observed this response from clients with whom such resistance was not a very plausible explanation, given their demonstrated tolerance of the vulnerability of doing deep, painful emotional work in their sessions. Rather, it seems more likely to us that these are individuals who have a welldeveloped and authentic adult identity, and that reparative attachment can take place in therapy most readily for adults who lack a firm state of adult identity

140 The Emotional Coherence Framework and are based largely in a child identity or ego state, which allows the therapist to be a plausible attachment figure. The example of Tomás drives home to us that the fully adequate presence of the non-specific common factors in the client–therapist relationship (trust, empathy, alliance, shared therapeutic goals, etc.) and the full, emotional engagement of the client in the work do not mean that the client necessarily experiences the therapist as an attachment figure or is having an experience of secure attachment. A therapy client can experience secure attachment with the therapist only if he or she experiences the therapist as an attachment figure. However, trusting a health care professional enough to cooperate with the therapeutic process, including putting oneself in a vulnerable position, is not, in itself, an attachment relationship. Thus, the common factors may be fully present without an attachment relationship or secure attachment experience being present. In other words, the common factors are a necessary but not sufficient condition for an attachment relationship and secure attachment to occur, because for that, conditions in addition to the common factors are required. Further, as we have discussed in this chapter, if an attachment relationship and secure attachment are present, this does not necessarily mean that reparative attachment work is taking place, because reparative attachment requires, in addition to secure attachment, the disconfirmation of the client's specific insecure attachment expectations, which requires juxtaposition experiences, fulfilling the therapeutic reconsolidation process. In this way, the therapeutic reconsolidation process helps us to clarify the relationship between the presence of the non-specific common factors, the occurrence of secure attachment experiences, and the occurrence of a reparative attachment process in therapy.

Conclusion: A coherent resolution Our examples of Raoul's anger, Ted's underachieving, Carol's aversion to marital sex, and Tomas's “can't work for me” show that reparative attachment therapy is not universally applicable and, as such, does not provide a sufficiently inclusive framework for unifying the field of psychotherapy. Attachment dynamics and relationships are vitally important to virtually all emotionally functional human beings, but people in their complexity also have other dimensions and other domains of learning that can generate clinical symptoms and require psychotherapy. The Emotional Coherence Framework enables therapists to distinguish between symptoms that are generated by attachment learnings and those that are not, and to utilize reparative attachment work as one important option among many different methods for guiding therapy clients into the contradictory living knowledge that unlocks the emotional brain, drives profound unlearning, and breaks the spell of ingrained emotional learnings. A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy Introduction to Part 2 Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

Truth is ever to be found in the simplicity, and not in the multiplicity and confusion of things.

—Isaac Newton

In previous chapters we examined a variety of therapy cases showing that carrying out the therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP) fulfills the brain's requirements for unlearning and nullifying a specific emotional schema, producing transformational change. Through ongoing, close study and use of the TRP, therapists become increasingly proficient at applying it successfully in their sessions, for a significant and very satisfying enhancement of therapeutic effectiveness. In this chapter we shift and widen our scope to examine how the TRP additionally empowers therapists by unifying the panoply of psychotherapeutic systems. It does so by inducing a transformational change in how therapists view those diverse systems, which cease being perceived as dissonantly dissimilar, competing, and mutually incompatible, and instead are recognized as forming a rather wondrous and vast array of alternative options at the therapist's disposal for facilitating the TRP. The steps of the TRP are often facilitated successfully in many different systems, and yet are usually indiscernible behind salient therapeutic techniques that vary so greatly from system to system. However, when a therapist's guiding mental map consists of the TRP rather than any particular techniques for fulfilling it, the technique level of any particular therapy system becomes transparent and no longer hides the TRP being carried out by those techniques. Then the differing techniques and methodologies of diverse systems no longer seem to belong to different worlds. Rather, the utility of each technique or methodology for facilitating the TRP (perhaps in a particular type of clinical situation) is now apparent. It even becomes workable and comfortable to switch, during a therapy session, from one system's methods to another system's methods without causing any confusion or disruption to either the client or the process. Imagine that! DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-7

144 The Emotional Coherence Framework (For an in-the-trenches view of switching from one system's methods to another's in mid-session in response to the client's emerging material, showing how the TRP unification positions the therapist to make deft use of the great plethora of therapies, see Ecker, 2015c.) The steps of the TRP are defined in Table 3.1 on page 46; in addition, here is a simplified listing for ease of reference when the steps are mentioned in the rest of this chapter and in the case examples in Part 2:

Step A: Symptom identification • Step B: Retrieval of symptom-necessitating emotional schema • Step C: Identification of contradictory knowledge • Step 1: Reactivation of symptom-necessitating emotional schema • Step 2: Juxtaposed, lucid experience of contradictory knowledge • Step 3: Several repetitions of the juxtaposition of Steps 1 and 2 • Step V: Verification of unlearning by observing markers of transformational change

The core process shared by therapies of transformational change TRP Steps 1–2–3 are the set of experiences that the brain requires for fundamental unlearning and dissolution of existing, problematic implicit knowledge. Completing Steps A–B–C is how therapists can most consistently and efficiently arrive at carrying out Steps 1–2–3. The TRP's capability for playing a unifying role in the psychotherapy field is based in its inherent qualities:

Directly grounded in empirical research in neuroscience • Non-theoretical, transtheoretical, and technique-independent • Applies to emotional implicit learnings of all types, whether formed in at-

tachment, existential, social, traumatic, sexual, or other areas of emotional learning • Provides an intuitively appealing understanding of how subjective experiencing and neurological processes operate together, intricately and coherently, to revise learning and memory In other words, “transformational therapeutic change can be recognized as a process that is both deeply subjective and scientifically well defined” (Ecker & Vaz, 2022, p. 9). The therapeutic reconsolidation process embodies the brain's rules for profound unlearning, and the existence of those innate rules means that each one of us is equipped to outgrow and shed the constraints of our earlier life learnings and to continue evolving our knowledge, our relationship to life, and our world of meaning.

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 145 The TRP yields transformational change, which we defined on page 22 in Chapter 2 by the same criteria or markers (Step V) that neuroscientists use in lab studies of the unlearning and nullification of emotional learnings via MR:

abrupt, lasting cessation of symptoms, • lasting absence of symptom-generating emotional reactions in the presence of cues and contexts that formerly induced their strong reactivation, and

permanence of those two changes without effort or counteractive, preventative measures.

For a lengthy list of symptoms so far observed to cease occurring promptly after completion of TRP Steps 1–2–3, see https://bit.ly/3qNPJO0. It warrants emphasizing that Steps 1–2–3 are instructions for replicating in therapy sessions the same steps that unlearned and nullified emotional learnings in laboratory studies. So, this set of steps is not a theory and is not based in theorizing. The direct result of these steps facilitated in therapy is the appearance of the same unique markers of profound unlearning that neuroscientists regard as evidence that unlearning via reconsolidation has occurred. Thus, this framework isn't a merely inferential invoking of some plausibly relevant aspect of neuroscience in support of a particular type of therapy. This is a very specific, empirically confirmed process that has unique, verifiable results that cannot occur in any other way, according to all current scientific knowledge. Because TRP Steps 1, 2, and 3—the unlearning sequence—are the only way currently known to neuroscience for bringing about those markers of transformational change behaviorally (non-pharmaceutically), we may infer that Steps 1, 2, and 3 must have occurred whenever the markers are observed in therapy, whether or not the therapist or client was cognizant of this sequence of experiences taking place. That important inference can and should be tested by retroactively scrutinizing the therapeutic process for the experiences defined by Steps 1, 2, and 3 occurring just prior to the appearance of the markers. That scrutiny requires a sufficiently detailed record of the moment-to-moment therapeutic process. The eight case examples in Part 2—sessions conducted by different clinicians using the diverse methods of eight different systems of psychotherapy—carry out that exercise. They are offered as representative examples of our extremely consistent observation for over two decades, across many hundreds of cases, that when therapy yields the markers of transformational change, the prior presence of TRP Steps 1–2–3 is detectable unambiguously. That is what is shown in each of the cases in Part 2, representing these eight systems of psychotherapy:

AEDP (Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy) in Chapter 7 • EFT (Emotion-Focused Therapy) in Chapter 8 • EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) in Chapter 9

146 The Emotional Coherence Framework

IFS (Internal Family Systems Therapy) in Chapter 10 IPNB (Interpersonal Neurobiology) in Chapter 11 ISTDP (Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy) in Chapter 12 Psychedelic-assisted therapy in Chapter 13 SE (Somatic Experiencing®) in Chapter 14

Three criteria guided our selection of the case examples listed above: the case must result unambiguously in the markers of transformational change; the case must be documented with sufficient detail to allow identification of the steps of experiential process taking place moment to moment; and for each therapy system, we used the first case that we found that met the first two criteria. Thus there was no cherry-picking involved. By surveying such demonstrations of detecting TRP Steps 1–2–3 immediately preceding the markers of transformational change appearing, the value and power of the TRP for psychotherapy unification becomes self-evident, as does its value for demystifying the process of deep, lasting change in psychotherapy (which is illustrated also by the discussion in Chapter 2 of how the unlearning sequence advances and clarifies the “corrective emotional experience” paradigm). Thus the stage is now set for transformational change to become the natural standard of effectiveness in the psychotherapy field. Numerous other systems of psychotherapy that regularly produce transformational change could have been included in the unification demonstration in Part 2 if not for book length limitations. Hakomi (Weiss et al., 2015), Sensorimotor Psychotherapy (Ogden et al., 2006), Social-Cognitive Transactional Analysis (Bianchini & de Nitto, 2019), the Ideal Parent Figure methodology (Brown & Elliott, 2016; Elliott, 2021), Presence Psychotherapy (Lepak & Carson, 2021), Deep Brain Reorienting (Corrigan & Christie-Sands, 2020), and Traumatic Incident Reduction (TIR) (Gerbode, 2006), among many others, belong in this group. For case examples of transformational change via TRP in sessions of Alexander Technique, Neurolinguistic Programming, Progressive Counting, and Tapping, see https://bit.ly/15Z00HQ.1 Therapists who knowingly practice according to the TRP guide their clients to find and transform all existing implicit learnings generating a given symptom, with no pre-assumptions as to either the domain of experience in which those learnings arose (attachment, existential, social, etc.), or the therapeutic techniques that best fit the client's material and processing style. As noted in earlier chapters, all steps of the TRP are defined abstractly as process functions and subjective experiences, without being tied to any particular techniques for implementing them or to any particular clinical school, theory, or system. Clinicians who opt to guide their work using the TRP as their primary map therefore have a full range of choices of concrete methods and personal styles for implementing the process. The authors prefer to conceptualize and use the TRP within the larger context of the Emotional Coherence Framework described in this book because of the

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 147 naturalness and seamlessness of the relationship between the two— specifically their shared, humanistic, non-pathologizing view of the coherence of the emotional brain and of implicit-learning-based symptom production (Ecker & Bastianelli, 2022). The entire TRP is a direct application of empirical findings of memory research by neuroscientists, so it is fully transtheoretical. That does not mean it is necessarily fully harmonious with the theoretical framework of every school of psychotherapy. In light of the empirical rigor undergirding the TRP, we believe it behooves each school of psychotherapy to adjust and evolve for consistency with the TRP, rather than tampering with the TRP in order to embrace it. Imagine a panel discussion between leading practitioners of the nine psychotherapy systems represented in this book, focused on describing how their diverse therapeutic approaches carry out the component steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process—which itself is not and cannot be the possession of any one therapeutic system. The panelists' use of the TRP would create a shared, empirically based frame of reference and a shared vocabulary, allowing these practitioners to discuss their methods in a manner meaningful to each other and to practitioners of yet other clinical systems. That scenario is, in concrete terms, the paradigm of psychotherapy unification we envision through the TRP. Such use of the TRP can provide the fields of psychotherapy practice and research with a universal language and unifying shared understanding through which seemingly dissimilar approaches to transformational change can be compared meaningfully, revealing their metapsychological and methodological common ground. Indeed, any authentic formulation of the brain's rules for transformational change of implicit emotional learnings must necessarily have the kinds of integrative utility that we have described here. Panel members could compare, for example, the sequence in which their methodologies usually carry out the steps of the TRP. The sequence A–B–C– 1–2–3–V might be optimal in most, but not all, therapeutic methodologies.
