It is apparent that there are some distinctive variations in the sequence of preparatory steps, A–B–C, which can be understood in relation to the particularities of methodology of those systems. The presence of the unlearning sequence—TRP Steps 1–2–3—in each type of therapy supports the central message of this book: The unlocking and transformational unlearning of problematic emotional learning occur when the target learning is reactivated in awareness and, during that reactivation, the individual also experiences fundamentally contradictory knowledge that specifically disconfirms the target learning. We predict that any system of psychotherapy (or series of therapy sessions) will be found to produce deep, lasting change only if the sequence of experiences described by TRP Steps 1–2–3 takes place successfully— independently of whether the therapist or client is aware of these steps taking place.

Is it really always MR? We realize, of course, that claiming that therapeutic transformational change is always due to memory reconsolidation, and specifically to TRP Steps 1–2–3, is a big claim, and that a big claim requires big evidence to make it credible. We think the twenty-six detailed case examples presented in this book, representing nine very different systems of psychotherapy applied to a very wide range of serious symptoms, is itself a significant step in the direction of big evidence and credibility (and many other case examples have been published; for an index of them, see https://bit.ly/2tKXdyX). In each of our case examples, what is demonstrated is a well-defined therapeutic process (TRP Steps 1–2–3) that was derived directly from extensive MR research, promptly producing a unique and very strong therapeutic effect, namely the markers of transformational change, which neuroscientists regard as the strongest possible evidence of MR in human studies of behavioral unlearning. That configuration does not leave much room for other explanations of the observed therapeutic effects. In fact, that configuration is recognized as scientifically valid evidence of the causal role of MR as an internal mechanism of change (Ecker & Vaz, 2022; Kazdin, 2007). But what about therapy cases that result happily in the markers of transformational change, yet scrutiny of the case's detailed documentation reveals no sign whatsoever of TRP Steps 1–2–3? Do such cases indicate that MR via the unlearning sequence, TRP Steps 1–2–3, is not the only process that results in transformational change? That is a very important question about the scope of the TRP. Answering it involves recognizing that each of those three core steps of the TRP is defined as an internal experience, not any particular external procedure or action. For that reason, all three steps sometimes can and do occur serendipitously as internal experiences implicitly, that is, without any visible external facilitation, verbal labeling, or even metacognitive awareness on the part of the client at all. Neuroscientists have shown in lab studies that the memory reconsolidation process

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 149 can occur outside of conscious awareness (Delorenzi et al., 2014). As noted in Chapter 2, overtly carrying out the entire therapeutic reconsolidation process— Steps A–B–C–1–2–3–V—is not defined as being necessary for producing transformational change, rather it is defined as best practice for maximum consistency and efficiency of accomplishing Steps 1–2–3 and thereby producing transformational change across all cases in one's practice. It is possible for the truly necessary Steps 1–2–3 (a repeated juxtaposition experience) to occur serendipitously and implicitly—outside of the client's awareness—without completing A–B–C first, though A–B–C are pragmatically necessary in order to fulfill 1–2–3 consistently as a deliberate methodology. Thus, for any psychotherapy system that regularly yields the markers of transformational change, we expect all six steps to be detectable in sessions that did in fact produce those markers. When the markers of transformational change have begun appearing without any visible signs of TRP Steps 1–2–3 having occurred, a suitable process of hindsight inquiry can elicit and reveal them. Pursuing that inquiry process is itself best practice in all such instances. In the authors' experience across decades of practice, all such inquiries have revealed the implicit occurrence of Steps 1–2–3, which supports our hypothesis that therapeutic transformational change is always due to MR and specifically to TRP Steps 1–2–3. A striking example of finding in hindsight that Steps 1–2–3 had actually occurred is a case consultation reported by Ecker (2015a, pp. 32–33). The female therapist's client was a woman, aged 32 and married for five years, who was in the grip of an obsessive attachment to, and compulsive pursuit of, the man who had been her major love ten years earlier. This condition had been ruling her since the two had accidentally crossed paths two years ago. No physical intimacy had occurred in these two years solely due to the man's unresponsiveness. The woman's emotional infidelity was causing her much guilt. After trying a number of different approaches for many sessions with little or no effect, the therapist now felt she was flailing and was deeply uncomfortable being stuck there. To her great surprise: Then the client came into the next session and reported that a major shift had occurred. Her preoccupation and her pursuit of this man had stopped. This breakthrough was mysterious for both client and therapist. The client could offer nothing more than to speculate, “I think what you said sunk in somehow, that when an investment goes badly, sometimes it's best to cut your losses.” This referred to an offhand, momentary comment made by the therapist in the previous session, a comment that seemed more like advice than therapy. It was counteractive in nature (an attempt to build up a cognitive understanding to override the emotionally driven symptom), was not dwelt upon, and the focus of the session had moved on. Yet the client indicated that the comment had somehow led to her liberating shift. (Ecker, 2015a, p. 32)

150 The Emotional Coherence Framework In a consultation session, the therapist soon described those developments to Ecker, who suggested a way for her to guide her client to examine and identify the process of change that had occurred internally: She could ask her client, “If it was new for you to hear that ending it with him could be OK even though you had an emotional investment in it from long ago, what were you previously believing or expecting about how it would not be OK to end it?” In that way, the disconfirming knowledge would serve as a portal for accessing the constructs or schema that had been disconfirmed, which is a reverse engineering of Coherence Therapy's usual methodology of first revealing the symptom-generating schema and then, guided by the specific content of that schema, finding contradictory knowledge and creating a juxtaposition experience with it. However, when a transformational shift emerges serendipitously, typically only the disconfirming knowledge is already apparent, while the disconfirmed schema is still implicit and unknown. Then that schema can be tracked down, starting from the disconfirming knowledge, as the therapist was guided to do in this case. She carried out that inquiry persistently and then reported back to Ecker what she had learned from her client, as follows: The offhand comment happened to reach precisely into an unconscious schema that the client now put into words by saying, “I was struggling to keep my emotional investment in that relationship from being lost because I'd really put my heart and soul into that relationship, and on some level I felt that if it ended, I'd be losing so much of myself that I would die or just be an empty shell or ghost forever. But when you said it's OK to get out of an investment even if you take a loss, all of a sudden that changed, because I saw, 'Oh—people do that all the time. It's not a disaster, it's just practical.' I saw that I could let go and lose that investment in him, and I wouldn't turn to dust.” That account points clearly to a juxtaposition experience that had formed in response to the therapist's offhand comment. The woman reported also that it was not a struggle to persist in not contacting the man, though she did feel “a quiet sadness” each time she would have contacted him but did not do so. The non-reactivation of the symptom-generating schema or ego-state and the effortlessness of remaining symptom-free are key markers of erasure and transformational change. (Ecker, 2015a, pp. 32–33) In that example, the therapist's action (prompting the client to believe that “when an investment goes badly, sometimes it's best to cut your losses”) was counteractive, because it was an attempt to build up a state of mind in which the symptom would not occur. Serendipitously, that idea happened to precipitate an implicit juxtaposition experience, resulting in transformational change. Such entirely lucky, random instances can lead a therapist who is not familiar with the

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 151 TRP into the mistaken belief that counteracting is generally capable of producing that stellar outcome. Prompting the client to find and recognize the juxtaposition experience in hindsight has great therapeutic benefit: With explicitness of juxtaposition experiences comes the client's awareness of unlearning and evolving prior knowledge and of being capable of doing so. In addition there is a sizable benefit to the therapist, namely, the process of observing and learning first-hand how juxtaposition experiences take place and how to become skilled and efficient in facilitating them.

A unifying map of the psychotherapy universe The fundamental, qualitative differences between transformational change and counteractive change were described in Chapter 2. Recall that a counteractive methodology is one that attempts to build up a desired state of mind or behavior through methods that do not fulfill TRP Steps 1–2–3, the brain's required experiences for unlearning and fundamentally nullifying symptom-generating emotional schemas. Counteractive methods install new learning in memory separate from, and competing with, the memory of the symptom-generating schema, which therefore continues to exist but is, with effort, kept in a more-or-less suppressed condition, achieving partial, varying degrees of symptom reduction, in successful outcomes of counteractive therapies. In contrast, methodologies of transformational change are those that do regularly carry out TRP Steps 1–2–3, whether explicitly or implicitly, resulting in the symptom-generating schema being unlearned, rewritten, nullified, and eliminated from memory, not merely suppressed, and in symptoms ceasing fully and remaining so effortlessly, such as in the eight systems represented in Part 2 and in Coherence Therapy represented in Parts 1 and 3. For a complete account of therapeutic action in terms of memory modification, a third mode of therapeutic memory modification, described in Chapter 2, must also be included in the picture: the use of the reconsolidation window to “integrate” (meaning conjoin or graft) the memory of a positive emotional experience with the memory of the (reactivated and destabilized) distress-laden symptom-generating memory. This results in the permanent co- reactivation of both, so that the positive memory component always “interferes” with (partially diminishes) the negative component's effects. This mode of memory interference via MR is again a counteractive strategy of change, not a transformational one, and the degree of symptom reduction achieved is not predictable beforehand. Whatever degree does result will, however, be stable and permanent, in contrast to the unstable, variable, relapse- prone symptom reduction that results from counteractive methods that are not learned during the reconsolidation window and therefore create separate, competitive memory.

152 The Emotional Coherence Framework Thus for understanding all therapeutic change in terms of memory modification, there are three qualitatively different types or modes of therapeutic action, implemented by three different experiential processes, that is, by the creation of three different patterns of subjective experience. These three modes and processes are well-defined, and each either happens or doesn't happen, in a binary manner, but analyzing real-life therapeutic action in terms of these three modes sometimes requires subtle discernment, because both therapeutic procedures and their effects are analog, being finely and infinitely variable along a smooth continuum or continua. (For more extended discussion of the important distinction between subjective experiences and external procedures, see Ecker (2018, 2021).) This unifying framework could be termed the Mnemonic Therapeutic Action Unification (MTAU) framework because it serves to identify the mnemonic (memory) nature of the therapeutic action of any given therapeutic methodology, technique, or process. It does so in atheoretical, universal terms, in effect from the brain's point of view, independently of the theoretical conceptualizations of the diverse schools of psychotherapy, and without critiquing or challenging their theoretical conceptualizations. Part 2 of this book provides eight case examples of applying this framework to detect and identify the mode of mnemonic therapeutic action. The MTAU framework positions therapists to comprehensively understand and optimally utilize the entirety of the psychotherapy field's systems and methods (Ecker, 2024). Psychotherapy systems of course differ greatly in how closely their methodology is aligned with one or more of the three modes of mnemonic therapeutic action. If it were possible to analyze the mnemonic therapeutic action implemented in all sessions conducted by all practitioners of any one system of therapy, the result could be displayed as a bar graph with three vertical bars, one for each mode, with its height indicating the percentage of all sessions in which that mode was implemented. Comparing that bar graph obtained for many different therapy systems, the relative heights of the three bars would be seen to vary considerably, presumably in every possible pattern. Our strong emphasis in this book is on equipping therapists to consistently produce transformational change, which results from only one of the three modes, namely the one that carries out TRP Steps 1–2–3, the unlearning sequence of MR. From the full set of all bar graphs for all therapies, one could extract as a subset the TRP fulfillment spectrum, a ranking of all therapies according to their actual frequency or reliability of producing transformational change. This is of course only a thought experiment, but it serves to help show how the MTAU framework creates a comprehensive, discerning perspective for both understanding and meaningfully comparing therapy systems that otherwise can be very difficult to understand and meaningfully compare.2 Methods of counteractive change certainly have an important role in any therapist's practice, because they are necessary to use in various clinical situations

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 153 where carrying out the TRP for transformational change is contraindicated, as mapped out in Chapter 2 on pages 39–40. These are situations that require immediate harm prevention, crisis intervention, skill-building, resource utilization, or stabilizing pharmacological measures.

Unification of the specific versus common factors duality Psychotherapy outcome researchers have for decades been debating the relative importance for therapeutic effectiveness of specific factors versus common factors. Specific factors are the particular therapeutic methods, processes, or theories applied by the therapist. Common factors are the qualities of the therapist, client, and client–therapist relationship that are always present, in varying degrees, across all types of psychotherapy, such as positive regard, trust, accurate empathy, the therapeutic alliance, and the therapist's confidence in the methodology, among other aspects. In our view, understanding therapeutic change in terms of memory reconsolidation breaks the long stalemate in this polarized debate. As noted in Chapters 1 and 2, mainstream outcome research has all along relied heavily on the randomized control trial (RCT) for measuring the efficacy of psychotherapy. In an RCT, the measured outcomes of large groups of individual therapy cases are calculated statistically, and the results for client groups that had different therapies are compared to each other and to a control client group. Strikingly, for all fifteen types of therapy tested in RCTs across at least forty years, very nearly the same level of efficacy was consistently measured, a rather modest reduction of symptoms by about one standard deviation in the mean score on outcome measures, which represents a 20 to 25 percent reduction in the measured strength of symptoms (Shedler, 2015; Smith & Glass, 1977; Wampold & Imel, 2015). That data has been regarded as the primary evidence for the effectiveness of psychotherapy, though it is only slightly better than the efficacy of placebo therapy. The uniformity of efficacy across therapy systems required an explanation. The prevailing, mainstream explanation that emerged, known as common factors theory, is that the differing specific factors have very little influence on efficacy—about a 15 percent effect according to the statistical analyses of RCT data—whereas the common factors are responsible for 85 percent of the 20 to 25 percent effect of therapy. That is the argument on the common factors side of the debate. Two main challenges have faced common factors theory (reviewed by Ecker, 2015b; Shean, 2014). First, the statistical nature of RCT data analysis inherently hides the existence of any potent specific factors utilized effectively in a small percentage of outlier transformational sessions within the study. That fact makes it illogical and unscientific to conclude from RCTs that specific factors are fundamentally weak. Second, numerous non-RCT studies designed to detect potent specific factors have indeed done so. For example, a meta-analysis by

154 The Emotional Coherence Framework Weinberger (1995) found that the specific factor of guiding clients to face what they had been avoiding accounted for 40 percent of variance in therapy outcomes, whereas the therapeutic alliance, which is one of the most widely emphasized common factors, accounted for only 11 percent of the variance. Similarly, other studies have shown successful therapeutic outcomes correlating strongly with facilitation of richly emotional experience previously blocked, combined with conscious reflection on the emotional meanings that have emerged through this experience (e.g., Baikie & Wilhelm, 2005; Elliott et al., 2003; Gendlin, 1966; Greenberg et al., 2008; Missirlian et al., 2005; Pennebaker, 1997). That is the argument on the specific factors side of the debate. Note that bringing awareness to previously suppressed feelings and meanings is a specific process that is not inherently facilitated by the common factors alone, but it is inherently facilitated in TRP Step B (the experiential retrieval of emotional learnings from implicit memory into explicit experience) and Step 1 (reactivation of that same retrieved emotional learning to start the unlearning sequence). Others have argued that the specific-versus-common-factor debate is a false dichotomy. Castonguay and Beutler (2006, p. 353), for example, concluded that the “controversy reflects an 'either/or' assumption that is conceptually flawed and empirically untenable.” A review by Cuijpers et al. (2019) considered several criteria that must be met by any candidate mechanism of therapeutic change and concluded that so far, “no common or specific factor meets these criteria and can be considered an empirically validated working mechanism” (p. 207). However, memory reconsolidation was not considered. The unlearning sequence identified in MR research resolves the polarized debate by being a unification of the specific-versus-common-factor duality: The unlearning sequence functions both across therapies as a common factor required for transformational change (as shown for nine systems of therapy in this book and for five other systems as noted in Chapter 1) and as a specific factor in the sense of being a well-defined process, but not a specific technique or manualizable procedure. The unlearning sequence has a very strong “specific treatment effect,” meaning a symptom-dispelling effect that is not due mainly to client–therapist relationship factors but rather to a specific experiential process (TRP Steps 1–2–3) recruiting a well-defined mechanism of change, namely memory re-encoding via MR. While it is plausible that the conventional common factors could be largely responsible for the mild, 20 to 25 percent reduction of symptoms measured in RCTs, it is not plausible that the conventional common factors alone could usually be largely responsible for 100 percent reduction of symptoms in transformational change. As indicated in Chapter 5, there is a subset of therapy clients for whom the common factors alone can induce transformational change because the client's experience of the therapist's empathy and attunement, for example, happens to specifically contradict and disconfirm a symptom-generating mental model of what is possible in human relationships. In other words, the client's

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 155 experience of the therapist serves to carry out the unlearning sequence. This is found to occur in a small subset of all therapy cases, however. It is the exception, not the rule. In the large majority of cases, the common factors alone are not sufficient to induce transformational change because they do not specifically contradict and disconfirm a symptom-generating schema of the client. As is shown in Chapter 5, not all schemas of insecure attachment are disconfirmable by the client's experience of a therapist, and other types of schemas certainly aren't. Nevertheless, even in those cases, the common factors still play an important and necessary role as catalysts that make it possible for the client to engage in the deep, vulnerable, experiential work involved in the unlearning sequence. It has been suggested by Ecker (2013) that psychotherapy RCT data might be more accurately interpreted as showing only that about 15 percent of therapists participating in RCTs have applied effective specific factors. Also noted (p. 137) is that “the client–therapist relationship remains indispensably important for good psychotherapy. This is not an either/or situation. It now seems clear that in the most effective psychotherapy, an environment of good non-specific common factors supports facilitation of the specific factors of emotional accessing and memory reconsolidation.” Demonstrating the point that the common factors are usually not sufficient, in themselves, to fulfill the unlearning sequence and thereby produce transformational change, there is an observation that occurs regularly in the course of conducting Coherence Therapy: After a client's symptom-generating emotional schema has been retrieved into direct awareness, but prior to any attempt at guiding a disconfirming juxtaposition experience, the compelling realness and grip of the schema can still continue to be felt from session to session, as it did for Richard in Chapter 3, Ted in Chapter 4, and Regina in Chapter 5. Bringing the schema from implicit memory into explicit emotional experience is found, in itself, not to diminish or dispel it, even though the therapist skillfully supplies empathy, emotional safety, a good working alliance, excellent attunement, and the other common factors for any number of sessions. Only when contradictory knowledge has finally been found and the therapist guides a juxtaposition experience successfully—and thereby carries out the unlearning sequence, TRP Steps 1–2–3—does the schema lose its subjective realness and cease controlling behavior and state of mind, often abruptly and decisively, as we have seen.

Unification of psychotherapy and brain science It is one thing to describe or map known psychotherapeutic processes in terms of neuroscientific knowledge of brain regions and their functions, as has widely been done in writings on psychotherapy since the 1990s. That is fascinating but has not driven any fundamental advance for psychotherapy. It is another thing for brain science to discover a hitherto unknown, major capability of the brain, namely memory reconsolidation, for revising the contents of memory, as well

156 The Emotional Coherence Framework as the behavioral process that actuates that neurological mechanism and is also directly applicable in psychotherapy sessions. The fundamental advance of psychotherapy instigated by this breakthrough is a sea change for the psychotherapy field and forges a remarkable zone of unification of the psychotherapy field and brain science. As noted in Chapter 3, exactly the same behavioral process was identified much earlier from purely clinical observations of transformational change by Ecker and Hulley (1996). The fact that the same process emerged independently through such different approaches—the neurological study of learning and memory in animals and the examination of psychotherapeutic process— further deepens their unification and is a significant convergence and synthesis of the neurobiological (bottom-up) and behavioral (top-down) understandings of therapeutic change. The need for just such a binocular approach was emphasized by neuroscientist Eric Kandel (2001, p. 605) toward the end of his Nobel address, when he commented regarding a range of challenging unknowns in brain science, “These systems problems of the brain will require more than the bottom-up approach of molecular biology. They will also require the top-down approaches of cognitive psychology, neurology, and psychiatry. Finally, they will require a set of syntheses that bridge the two approaches.” The convergence, synthesis, and praxis presented in this book, already adopted by psychotherapists and counselors worldwide, is a solid step in the direction of fulfilling Kandel's vision of unification. More specifically, the brain science of MR for the first time equips the psychotherapy field with knowledge of an internal mechanism of lasting change. In the journal article “Memory reconsolidation and the crisis of mechanism in psychotherapy,” Ecker and Vaz (2022, p. 1) reviewed the situation in this way: It is a protracted dilemma of the psychotherapy field that, despite extensive empirical evidence that psychotherapy produces lasting change (Lambert, 2013), research on psychotherapy process and outcomes has not identified any fundamental, internal mechanism(s) of change. That impasse has been candidly acknowledged by participating experts. Goldfried (1980, 2019), who was the first and is still the foremost voice calling attention to this situation, has recently reiterated in a blog post, “Although the field of psychotherapy has been in existence for well over a hundred years, it nonetheless still cannot be classified as a mature science—one where there exists an agreed-upon core or consensus. With its numerous competing schools of thought, psychotherapy has yet to achieve an agreed-upon consensus” (Goldfried, 2020). We believe that with recognition of the unlearning sequence of MR as the core process of transformational change shared across psychotherapy systems, and with the therapeutic reconsolidation process recognized as the optimal general

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 157 process for consistently and efficiently facilitating the unlearning sequence using any suitable experiential techniques, the field of psychotherapy graduates into being a mature science.

Unification summary This chapter has shown that the therapeutic reconsolidation process unifies the psychotherapy field in a number of significant ways, by providing:

a unified understanding of the transformational change of emotional schemas formed in all domains of learning—attachment, existential, social, and other

clarification and demystification of how the mechanism of deep, lasting • • •

change operates in a given psychotherapy system, on both the subjective and neurological levels a cross-platform template and language that therapists of diverse orientations can share in order to understand and discuss each other's methodologies and methods, without challenging any system's conceptualization of itself a meta-map that positions a therapist to have a flexible choice of methods and approaches with a given client, and guides the use of those methods for efficient, transformational work a lens for discerning therapy systems that have an inherent capacity to produce transformational change, as distinct from those that inherently produce counteractive change that reduces symptoms only partially, through a mnemonic interference effect either with or without conjoining via MR a synthesis of the duality of specific versus common factors, resolving a decades-long debate that was not settled by psychotherapy outcome research a synthesis of brain science and the field of psychotherapeutic knowledge and practice, for the first time undergirding the psychotherapy field with empirical knowledge of an internal mechanism of change and establishing it as a scientific field

Welcome to Part 2 Our handling of the cases in Part 2, representing eight systems of psychotherapy, warrants some explanation. With the exception of the IFS case in Chapter 10, all of those cases were previously published (see citation in each case), and our presentation of each case retains only the concrete, observable client– therapist interactions and descriptions of the client's subjective experience. Only the client's and therapist's quoted, spoken words are verbatim from the original publication. All additional explanation of and commentaries on the unfolding process are the writing of this book's authors. Our added commentary primarily points out where the steps of the TRP take place as the work proceeds. There is some degree of paraphrasing of original comments describing the client's

158 The Emotional Coherence Framework moment-to-moment tone and manner. We briefly describe each system's main conceptualization and therapeutic strategy, but of course this cannot really do justice to any system, so, for an adequate account, the reader should refer to the writings of each system's founder(s) or major exponents. In Chapter 10, the presentation consists of an unpublished session transcript contributed to this book by a master practitioner of IFS, along with his brief comments on the unfolding process from the IFS point of view, in endnotes. Our own commentaries, inserted into the transcript, point out the occurrences of the steps of the TRP. Our treatment of the eight cases in Part 2 is not in any way a replacement for studying each system in its own terms, but rather is a supplementary metaconceptualization meant to be respectful of each particular system of psychotherapy—as the TRP itself is. Our purpose is to reveal the fulfillment of the TRP by each system in its own unique manner, and to show the use of the TRP as a meta-framework for illuminating and discussing the operation of any system of psychotherapy in a transtheoretical, phenomenological manner. Guiding our way through Part 1 of this book has been the central understanding, derived from both clinical experience and laboratory studies of the brain and behavior, that we humans are deeply coherent, adaptive beings—so much so that our coherence extends far beyond our perpetual striving for well-knit conscious narratives, deep down into our unconscious worlds of emotional learning. This understanding is the foundation of our broad paradigm, the Emotional Coherence Framework, and it challenges us as clinicians to move beyond our field's conventional view of symptoms as maladaptive or irrational disorders and pathologies—and instead to perceive and honor the coherent knowingness and complexly adaptive responsiveness that permeate the mind, no less in its non-conscious processes than in its conscious ones. Within this expanded view of our nature, the therapeutic reconsolidation process describes how new experience can interact with the depths of our distress-laden, implicit, coherent learnings to allow us to unlearn them. Whether implemented through one set of concrete methods or another, the TRP is an invaluable key that unlocks the emotional brain and opens up a new level of effectiveness and satisfaction in the practice of psychotherapy.

Notes 1 Given the strong focus of the TRP methodology on the emotional schemas or mental models underlying symptoms, it seems relevant here to indicate briefly how the TRP approach differs from Schema Therapy, which enhanced Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy with a strong emphasis and conceptualization of schemas and by integrating experiential work. Pierre Cousineau, PhD, an experienced practitioner and international supervisor and trainer of Schema Therapy, has written that he views the TRP as a major breakthrough in defining a core process for fundamentally modifying schemas, and he has therefore been working to fully integrate the TRP into the Schema Therapy framework. He and Sophie Côté, PhD, herself an advanced practitioner and

A Framework for the Unification of Psychotherapy 159 international teacher of Coherence Therapy and the TRP, are the authors of a forthcoming (as of 2023) book on TRP-guided Schema Therapy that will equip practitioners to facilitate decisive depotentiation of discovered, symptom-generating schemas. The book will be published first in French by Dunod, then in English. 2 In this context it is instructive to consider Polyvagal Theory, formulated by behavioral neuroscientist Stephen Porges. Apart from the ongoing controversy over its scientific validity, the psychotherapeutic use of Polyvagal Theory consists of creating perceptual experiences that the human mind responds to by feeling safe, which in turn induces a psychophysiological state of openness to social interaction and connection, with feelings of heightened well-being and ease. These effects can be of significant relief to individuals normally in a state of feeling unsafe, emotionally shut down, and socially disengaged. However, the positive effects persist only if maintained by ongoing environmental reinforcement and reward, and disappear without that (as stated by Porges directly to Ecker in London on November 16, 2019). Thus, the practices directly implied by Polyvagal Theory in themselves produce counteractive change (either with or without MR-mediated conjoining), not transformational change. However, a therapist familiar with the TRP could make adjunctive use of Polyvagal Theory practices with a client in order to induce a state of receptivity to a subsequent experiential process that is transformational.

Hidden in Plain Sight One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change

Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy (AEDP) Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

Defined by its founder, psychologist Diana Fosha, as a system for bringing about transformational change in the effects of attachment trauma, Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy (AEDP) emerged within the psychodynamic paradigm and is based on a synthesis of attachment theory, neurobiological research, and mother–infant studies (Fosha, 2021; Yeung & Fosha, 2015). It emphasizes an experiential, emotionally engaged process of reparative attachment, with a particular focus on inviting the client's full attention to the present moment of experiencing the therapist's empathetic attunement and accompaniment. “Key to the therapeutic action of AEDP is the undoing of aloneness and thus, the co-creation of a therapeutic relationship experienced as both safe haven and secure base where transformational healing can occur.”1 AEDP is a nonpathologizing approach that aims to mobilize the individual's inherent capacity for well-being. In the following case example of AEDP (Lipton & Fosha, 2011), the therapist was clinical social worker Benjamin Lipton. As the account proceeds, we point out the steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process2 (TRP) occurring within the methodology of AEDP. For Lipton's and Fosha's commentary on this case in terms of AEDP concepts, we encourage readers to refer to their article. Here, all utterances of client and therapist are exact quotes. Our purpose in mapping an AEDP case onto TRP fulfillment is to expand our demonstration of the universality of the TRP as a unifying core process responsible for transformational change produced by any methods of psychotherapy. The 40-year-old client, “Daniel,” was a recently divorced father of a young son. As a boy he had been socially awkward and lonely during a “latchkey childhood of neglect and isolation,” with parents who were “emotionally shutdown, career-driven scientists.” In junior high school at age 11, Daniel had skipped two grades and was much younger than other students, and a teacher who seemed to take a paternal interest and offer a refuge from loneliness instead perpetrated sexual abuse for a year. Daniel began therapy six months after ending a 20-year drug dependency, one year after his mother died of cancer, and two years after a divorce. DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-9

164 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change Daniel stated his goals for therapy in terms of wanting now to deal honestly with his life and face a range of emotional issues he had been avoiding all along. He wanted to “come clean and be brutally honest about who I am and how I got to where I am so I can figure out how to get out of this mess.” (His reference to past self-deception regarding himself contributes to TRP Step A, symptom identification. The “mess” would be found in the course of Daniel's sessions to consist of avoidance of affect, depersonalization, depression, shame, ungrieved grief, a dark aloneness with a sense of being hunted, and panicky anxiety.) In his second session, Daniel gave a long description of his parents that was revealing but rambling, disorganized, and at an emotional remove—saying of his father, for example, “he's impossible to talk on the phone with. It makes you uncomfortable every second because he doesn't respond to anything. He's completely detached and he doesn't engage you.” (Daniel's depersonalized phrasing contributes further to the symptom picture for Step A and shows his adaptation to the disengaged, depersonalized styles of his parents.) When that long meandering ended, the therapist replied, “Daniel, what are you feeling inside right now as you share this with me? So that we, right away, in our work, Daniel, work against the sort of detached, talking head experience and really help you stay connected to your body and your emotions? Which is what I really want to help you with and think you never really got help with before?” In that response, we have italicized how the therapist spoke so as to create for Daniel a very personal, relational experience of receiving tender attunement and safe emotional candor—a key feature of AEDP that would be repeated many more times. Equally important, the therapist has transparently commented on Daniel's “detached, talking head” mode of relating by inviting him to shift into connection with his body and emotions. This benign challenging of avoidance of affect combined with an invitation to allow the flow of affect is also a characteristic feature of AEDP (one that it shares with other experientially focused therapies emerging within the psychodynamic paradigm). Both aspects of the therapist's response suddenly present Daniel with entirely unexpected, unfamiliar relational possibilities. Both aspects contradict the presuppositions and expectations in Daniel's implicit mental model of what is possible for him in interpersonal interactions and the rules of behavior that he must follow in order to be acceptable to others and safe in interpersonal interactions. Although those existing schemas that define and dictate how he participates in interpersonal interactions have not been explicitly elicited or voiced (which would be TRP Step B), they are nevertheless reactivated (TRP Step 1) by his being invited to violate them—an effect recognized by Lipton and Fosha in their comment (2011, pp. 254–255) that “Recognizing and integrating a new, positive relationship in the here and now organically evokes its historical contrast—the painful experiences of the original relational trauma.” Thus the new relational possibilities offered by the therapist are being experienced by Daniel as contradictory knowledge that is juxtaposing with his reactivated schemas (for TRP

Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy 165 Step 2). This fulfillment of TRP Steps 1 and 2 is the all-important juxtaposition experience that the brain requires in order for existing schemas to undergo profound unlearning and annulment through memory reconsolidation. An AEDP therapist assumes in advance that the client's specific symptoms, whatever they are, are generated by underlying schemas or mental models of insecure attachment that can be disconfirmed and unlearned through reparative attachment experiences in relation to the therapist (often termed corrective relational experiences in AEDP writings).3 Based on that assumption, the therapist immediately proceeds to respond in ways intended to create such reparative experiences from the beginning of the first session, before knowing the unique content of the client's specific schemas. “The work to develop secure attachment throughout the course of therapy is the therapy” explain Lipton and Fosha (2011, p. 266). Thus TRP Step C, the finding of contradictory knowledge or contradictory experiences that will disconfirm the client's symptom-generating schema(s), is moot in AEDP, because no such finding is necessary under the assumption that disconfirmation will occur through reparative attachment experiences that the therapist is trained to create proactively. In effect, Step C is done before therapy begins, and the therapist begins with Step 2, which in turn induces Step 1 as described above. What matters for fulfilling the unlearning sequence of memory reconsolidation (TRP Steps 1–2–3) is the concurrence of the mutually contradictory experiences defined by Steps 1 and 2, not the order in which they are initially vivified. In response to the therapist's comments, Daniel answered, “It's sad.” With that, at least for the moment he accepted the invitation to engage with the therapist in intimate, vulnerable emotional self-revealing, presumably a new experience that further contradicted his insecure interpersonal expectations. The therapist soon focused again on the relational moment by suggesting, “If you just imagined here with me for a minute that we just shared the feeling of sadness together…” Daniel then uttered reflective but intellectualized comments—holding back this time—and in response the therapist persisted by asking, “So what's it like to have me inviting you to be sad with me?” Daniel answered, “I suppose it's like a forbidden action that you want to do but then feel like you're not supposed to… I can be depressed or whatever it is, but not in any way that I don't feel guarded or ashamed, or, y'know, immediately want to have some sort of post-sad strengthening moment where I pretend that it's not affecting me.” This is the explicit emergence of an underlying schema of insecure attachment, evoked by being violated by “a new, positive relationship in the here-and-now”: Feeling and showing sadness is “forbidden” and shameful, and would make him unacceptable and unlovable, worsening his desolate aloneness, so it is urgent to suppress and hide his sadness under a pretense of strength. Subjectively it is his real self that is forbidden by his parents' terms of attachment. (This explicit feeling and voicing of the schema fulfills TRP Step 1, the target schema consciously reactivated concurrently with Step 2,

166 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change a contradictory experience, namely the therapist's warm, empathetic acceptance of his sadness. The therapist will continue to create experiences that contradict this schema, repeating the juxtaposition experience numerous times throughout the session, which is Step 3, completing the unlearning sequence.) When Daniel soon added, “I resort to humor or I try to make other people happy,” the therapist asked, “So could we take literally like a minute to check out what it would be like not to try to make me happy, but just to feel…?” This was a straightforward invitation to Daniel to put aside those tactics and his familiar, negative relational expectations and, instead, to open himself to experiencing secure connection by expressing his own true feelings to the therapist (which would be another disconfirming juxtaposition experience, contributing to TRP Step 3, repetitions of the juxtaposition). This time, accepting the therapist's overture, Daniel said, “I'll just fall apart” and began to cry, and then added through tears, “I spend most of my time feeling like I could burst into tears.” Daniel could no longer resist his true feelings spilling into (now safe) expression. The therapist then repeatedly found opportunities to guide Daniel into both having and mindfully recognizing that he was having an emotionally intimate relational experience (again fulfilling Step 3). Daniel soon commented, “I think there's just so much—the reservoir of sadness is just so huge and I steel up.” The therapist replied, “I was just thinking that. No wonder you steel up. There's so much to steel up against.” “And I want so much not to feel this way,” Daniel admitted, going a bit further into open vulnerability than before. “What way?” asked the therapist. Daniel, going yet further, clarified, “I don't want to feel alone.” Seeing his next opportunity for dyadic relational deepening (another Step 3 experience), the therapist asked, “Do you feel alone right now?” “Less so,” Daniel acknowledged. Perhaps sensing Daniel's increasing receptivity, the therapist now ventured to ask, “Do you feel my presence with you?” “Yeah,” Daniel confided. (Here the underlying schema being reactivated and disconfirmed is almost certainly a mental model of expecting permanent, desolate aloneness in life among human beings, with his real self forever hidden from everyone, because that is the only world he has ever known. Having that expectation for one's entire future life tends to generate pervasive depression.) Continuing to create experiences of safe, emotionally close dyadic connection, the therapist asked next, “What's that like for you? What's it like to have another man not abandoning you and also not having an ulterior motive with you?” Daniel replied, “Unique” (indicating that disconfirmation of expected relational limits is occurring); the therapist replied, “I bet”; and Daniel added, “I've had people who wanted to be there for me. It's—but, unless you—most people who want to be there for you then need you to tell them what to do, and its hard

Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy 167 then not to feel like you're putting people out or dragging them along when you can't really explain it to them.” The AEDP therapist, ever sifting the client's response for opportunities to focus the client yet more fully on his felt experience of the relational moment, now asked, “Are you sensing that from me?” “No,” said Daniel. This was another Step 3 experience, again a juxtaposition of familiar negative relational expectations with the disconfirmation of those expectations by the therapist's relational qualities. The therapist prompted, “So if you stay with me right here in this moment…” At this, Daniel began to cry deeply and powerfully, and the therapist said softly, “I'm right here, Daniel. Right here.” Daniel sobbed, and as he did the therapist added, “So much grief, so much held in for so long.” This open expression of his most intense feelings, warmly received by the therapist, was an even stronger juxtaposition experience (adding to Step 3), and it did therapeutic double duty in also allowing Daniel to feel his long-suppressed feelings of intense grief, for a new degree of integration and movement toward emotional resolution. (This deep, direct experience of his long-suppressed grief is probably reactivating and disconfirming an underlying schema that would be put into words as “The grief inside me is oceanic, far bigger than I am, so I've got to keep it suppressed or it will totally engulf me in emotional agony that will never end, destroying my mind and my life.” That schema is very common in therapy clients carrying intense ungrieved grief. Daniel is finding here that feeling his grief is finite and workable, disconfirming that schema.) Daniel wept for some time, and finally looked up shyly into the therapist's eyes and said, “Thank you. Wow!” followed by a deep sigh and visible bodily relaxation. “You are so welcome,” replied the therapist, who then asked, “What are you thanking me for?” “I think I've been needing to do that my whole life,” Daniel explained. “I knew it, but I didn't know it. Whew.” After a long, introspective pause, he added with a warm smile, “So this is what it's like, huh?” With a warm smile in return the therapist confirmed, “Yes, this is what it's like. It feels very good to share this with you, Daniel.” Daniel said, “It's like a new beginning. Hard, strange—but good. Thank you.” His last few utterances seemed to be spoken from a subjective vantage point that had shifted—a position of inhabiting interpersonal emotional security, while looking back at his former insecure positioning in his entire earlier life. The cessation of Daniel's chronic symptoms of avoidance of affect and depersonalization, along with his somatic expressions of comfort with expressing intense, vulnerable emotion, were strong initial markers of transformational change (TRP Step V). Throughout the session, the therapist has repeatedly asked Daniel about the nature or quality of the current moment's relational experience, engaging him in metacognitive processing, which is a major aspect of AEDP methodology.

168 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change Lipton and Fosha (2011) recognize that “The experience of secure attachment… in and of itself, is necessary but in fact often insufficient to cement enduring psychological change. In processes of psychological transformation, both experiential shifts and intentional reflection upon those shifts are necessary in equal measure…” (p. 263). The TRP framework further clarifies that the “reflection upon those shifts” that is critically necessary for producing transformational change consists of a sustained juxtaposition experience (TRP Steps 1–2–3), which is an affectively rich, metacognitive recognition of core beliefs and expectations alongside an experience or knowing that disconfirms them unmistakably and decisively.4 Thus, in AEDP the steps of the TRP tend to be carried out in the sequence 2–1–3–V, with Steps A and B occurring intermittently throughout. As noted previously, AEDP guides practitioners to assume that they already know the content of the client's underlying schemas (insecure attachment), so they also already know what experience will disconfirm those schemas (the therapist's warm empathetic acceptance), which obviates the need for the TRP's preparatory Steps B and C—but also raises the question of how AEDP guides practitioners to adjust the methodology when the client's underlying schemas turn out not to be of the assumed type.5 Because the unlearning sequence was well fulfilled in Daniel's second session, it is not surprising that markers of resulting transformational change began to appear during the session, tentatively verifying (Step V) that the therapeutic reconsolidation process had been carried out successfully. Daniel continued to report significant markers of change in his next session, two weeks later. He said, “It's like there's some pit and you're telling me I can walk across and I'm like, 'No, it's a pit.' And you're like, 'No, there's an invisible glass floor.' \[Laughs with mixture of anxiety and evident delight\] I'm like, 'OK, there's an invisible glass floor.' \[pause\] And I'm starting to walk across it… in my time. I'm starting to believe more and more there's an invisible glass floor… I feel like in many ways I'm coming out of a nightmare, but I'm not all the way there. Um—it's almost like I have this smidgeon of hope or something, or light \[gestures upward\], like ceilings are cracking… \[long pause\] It's like I'm evolving…” A few minutes later, in a step that is an important characteristic of AEDP, the therapist guided Daniel to focus on the emerging sense of well-being that he had just described by saying, “And I'm just wondering, when you kind of tune in to that idea that you are evolving and that you're being more compassionate with yourself, what does that feel like, what's it like to just take a moment to connect with that? To not think about it, but to feel it—to drop down below the neck and breathe?” Daniel's successful dissolution of his symptom-generating target learnings naturally had restored him to aspects of native well-being that he was beginning to experience directly. By guiding him to focus more fully on and verbalize these new, positive experiences, the therapist was seeking to optimize their emergence as well as their integration into Daniel's everyday state

Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy 169 of mind and identity. In terms of the TRP, this is seen as additional (and here, largely tacit) juxtaposition experiences that dissolve existing negative constructs of identity and life story. What matters in the TRP picture is that the establishment of the client's new positive states, new identity, and new narratives also disconfirms and dissolves the old, negative ones, rather than being installed as separate learnings that compete with them. It is through the juxtaposition of the new and old schemas that the old ones are unlearned and nullified via memory reconsolidation, and the more explicit the juxtaposition, the more reliably is transformational change induced. With a big sigh, Daniel answered, “It's a relief.” He laughed with delight and added, “It's like the monster that's been stalking the neighborhood is caught.” “Wow!” exclaimed the therapist, surprised by the magnitude of the change suddenly verified by Daniel. “Will you just stay with that for a second? That's a powerful statement. I just want you to tune in to what that's like to be saying.” “It's freeing,” Daniel explained. “It's, um, it doesn't have to be that bad, y'know.” Maintaining the emotional and somatic focus, the therapist asked, “Where do you feel it?” “It's like a deep breath,” said Daniel with a big inhalation and a gesture to his lungs. “It's in the lungs. It's—it's—” and he took another deep breath. This new somatic openness of the breath was another marker of transformational change. “It's like a deep breath,” repeated the therapist. Daniel continued his thought: “—and, I guess, it's what it's like to not feel so anxious all the time; I guess whatever physical state that is that you're not being hunted, y'know,” and Daniel chuckled in recognition and relief. Daniel was identifying additional major symptoms (TRP Step A) of feeling anxious and hunted, which had now become apparent to him due to their disappearance, which he was reporting (more of Step V). Soon the therapist returned to one of those important markers and guided a deepening experience there by asking, “So, can we come back to—we're near the end of our time today, but I want to just come back to just this moment, just one more moment of that \[therapist takes a deep breath\] feeling. \[Daniel too takes a deep breath.\] I just wonder what it's like to be not only feeling that feeling that the monster that's stalking the neighborhood has been caught, but also what's it like to be sharing the experience here with me? To have that experience with me?” Previously that question had served to guide Daniel to open up to the very new and tentative experience of a secure dyadic connection (creating juxtaposition experiences in fulfillment of TRP Steps 2 and 3), but now, because evidently Daniel had successfully reorganized significantly around secure emotional openness, it served a different function, that of verifying the shifts that had taken place (Step V), for Daniel answered in a clear, declarative manner, “Comfortable. Easy.” This alone would have been a significant indication of

170 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change transformational change because, as Lipton and Fosha comment (2011, p. 275), “He is allowing himself to have an experience that—based on his procedural attachment history—we (and he) would have never thought possible.” Then several other such indicators of change emerged (Step V) as Daniel continued to described his recent experiences: “I think I've suppressed so much that a lot of emotion that was leaking out of me—or stored up pain—is just going away in many ways. Y'know, I think there are still wounds, but the sort of, like, thick, black blood from the infection that's been collecting is gone. Y'know it's hard. I still have lonely feelings, but it's less urgent. There's less panic. That's it, there's less panic.” With a smile he added, “I'm having a much better time enjoying. And I got better anti-inflammatories finally for my shoulder, too.” Daniel had a long history of neglecting self-care for health issues, so this too was a marker of change. “So, you're taking better care of yourself,” the therapist acknowledged. “I am,” Daniel confirmed, “and it feels good. I'm not destroying myself. And I don't want to destroy myself. I've done that—and it didn't help—and it hurt a lot. God knows what the long-term ramifications are going to be from all that.” Bringing the session to an end, the therapist said, “That really touches me, Daniel. You've really accomplished something amazing here. You are speaking your truth in such a deep, honest way. This touches my heart.” With a beaming smile, Daniel agreed, “I know. Me too. Me too.” His new capacity for well-being and his freedom from his previous, unrelenting distress were strikingly apparent in his manner and utterances, adding to his many emerging markers of transformational change. The account by Lipton and Fosha (2011) gives no indication of any long-term confirmation that Daniel's changes persisted effortlessly, which is a crucial marker of transformational change in the TRP framework. However, it seems plausible that they would have persisted, for the most part, so we may take this case as a good exemplar of how AEDP produces transformational change.
