Fully understanding this and other chapters in Part 2 of this book requires first reading Chapters 1, 2, and 3, which explain transformational therapeutic change and how it occurs through a particular recruitment of the brain's mechanism of memory reconsolidation, accomplished by the therapeutic reconsolidation process or TRP. Familiarity with the TRP is assumed. Chapter 2 defines and explains the TRP at length, including the extensive empirical research on which it is directly based. Chapter 3 demonstrates the focused facilitation of the TRP in psychotherapy sessions. 3 This assumption answers “yes” to the question, “Is it always about attachment?”, so AEDP lies at one end of the spectrum of positions in the “great attachment debate” considered in Chapter 5, which also discusses the possibility that the underlying,

Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy 171 symptom-generating schema or mental model of some clients has nothing to do with attachment and therefore cannot be transformed by relational experiences with a therapist. 4 Those are also the requisite ingredients of an actual “corrective emotional experience” according to the TRP framework, as explained in Chapter 2. 5 For discussion of symptom-generating schemas that do not consist of insecure attachment, and therefore are not disconfirmable through reparative attachment experiences with a therapist, see Chapter 5.

Emotion-Focused Therapy (EFT) Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

Based in the humanistic paradigm of psychotherapy and often utilizing experiential techniques drawn from Gestalt Therapy and Person-Centered Therapy, but also influenced by systemic concepts and attachment theory, Emotion- Focused Therapy (EFT) has been developed since the mid-1980s for both couples and individuals. Its primary creators were psychologists Robert Elliott, Leslie Greenberg, Susan Johnson, Laura Rice, and Jeanne Watson. A core principle of EFT is that human emotions express human needs and therefore can be adaptive if, with skillful therapeutic facilitation, the underlying needs are recognized self-compassionately, which in turn enables people to change problematic emotional states and the problematic patterns they create in interpersonal relationships. EFT practitioners guide clients to experience their emotions and authentic hidden feelings and needs in the safe setting of therapy so that, rather than avoiding or controlling their feelings, those emotions serve to create awareness of what is important or needed in their lives (e.g., Greenberg, 2011; Greenberg et al., 1993; Johnson, 2004). EFT for individuals is also known as Process- Experiential Psychotherapy. Greenberg explained in an online interview (Van Nuys, 2010b) that “the emphasis in EFT is… on how to work with people's actual feelings in the session and then how to work with changing emotions in the session, so that the real emphasis is on trying to understand emotional processes and how emotions change.” He has often formulated the essence of EFT's mechanism of change as “changing emotion with emotion” (Greenberg, 2010, p. 36). He also recognizes that “Changing the emotion schematic memory structures in therapy most likely occurs through the recently investigated process of memory reconsolidation” (2010, p. 33) and “introducing new present experience into currently activated memories of past events has been shown to lead to memory reconsolidation by the assimilation of new material into past memories… The memories are reconsolidated in a new way by incorporating these new elements” (2010, pp. 37–38). Clarifying whether his model of “changing emotion with emotion” is compatible with the memory reconsolidation framework is important, in our view, toward equipping the psychotherapy field with an understanding of therapeutic DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-10

Emotion-Focused Therapy 173 change that is rigorously accurate and universally applicable and effective, so we address this question later in this chapter. The EFT case example here is from Greenberg (2010, pp. 39–41). Our added commentary points out the fulfillment of the therapeutic reconsolidation process1 (TRP) within the unfolding EFT methodology. For Greenberg's own commentary on this particular case, see the original publication. Our purpose in mapping an EFT case onto TRP fulfillment is to expand our demonstration of the universality of the TRP as a unifying core process responsible for transformational change produced by any methods of psychotherapy. In an initial assessment interview, the client, a 39-year-old woman whom we are calling “Trish,” tearfully described herself as feeling depressed, as she had felt for most of her life but significantly more so in the past year, causing her to stop working and rarely leave her house or answer the phone or doorbell. Her relationships with members of her family of origin had become particularly difficult and painful. (Identifying symptoms of depression and associated isolation began TRP Step A.) The therapist also learned that Trish and her three sisters no longer had contact with their alcoholic mother and that her father, a wartime concentration camp survivor, had always been emotionally removed from the family and perceived as often being critical and judgmental. Physical punishment had been the norm throughout her childhood. Greenberg does not describe Trish's condition as complex attachment trauma or complex PTSD, but that case conceptualization would certainly apply. The therapist observed that although Trish was able to focus on her internal experience when receiving empathic responses that helped her to focus inwardly, she tended to avoid painful and difficult emotions, sinking into states of helplessness and hopelessness whenever she began to feel sadness or anger or her need for closeness and acceptance. Trish also mentioned having feelings of resentment and sadness toward her father but also a self-blaming, shameful view of herself as a “failure.” At times she minimized her father's physical abusiveness with the view that “being slapped was just normal.” (Feelings of helplessness, hopelessness, self-blame, and shame contributed further to Step A, the symptom picture.) Based on Trish's presentation of symptoms, the therapist was now inferring that in childhood and into adult life Trish had often felt unsafe, abandoned, alone, and shamed by verbal and physical blows (indicating complex trauma and contributing toward TRP Step B, retrieval of underlying emotional learnings). In the third session, with the support of the therapist's empathic attunement, Trish talked about not receiving approval from her father and added, “I believe I'm a bad person, but deep down inside I don't think I'm a bad person… yeah, I'm grieving for what I probably didn't have and know I never will have.” (Her explicit voicing of “I believe I'm a bad person” is TRP Step B, the accessing of underlying, symptom-generating emotional learnings. Her comments also yielded important information for TRP Step C regarding contradictory

174 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change knowledge in three areas: She has indicated a “deep down inside” awareness of the contradictory knowledge that she is not a bad person; that her emotional distress is due to actual emotional hardships that she has suffered—absence of caring attention and loving acceptance and connection from parents—rather than due to any real defects in herself; and that the true meaning of her emotional distress is her valid grieving. TRP practitioners find that a large fraction of therapy clients already hold such knowings that contradict their problematic emotional learnings, but the juxtaposition experience required for actual disconfirmation and unlearning has never occurred.) The therapist then guided Trish into an empty-chair dialogue with her father. Picturing him in the chair across from her own, she began to voice the specific meanings of her painful emotions directly to him: “You destroyed my feelings. You destroyed my life. Not you completely, but you did nothing to nurture me and help me in life. You did nothing at all. You fed me and you clothed me to a certain point. That's about it.” (Her contradictory knowledge for Step C is further developed by this unprecedented, explicit recognizing and voicing that the cause of her distress is her father's harmfulness and his failure to meet her natural emotional needs for connection and nurturance.) The therapist, drawing on some of Trish's previous comments, guided her by saying, “Tell him what it was like to be called a 'devil' and have to go to church every—” She said to her visualized father, “It was horrible. You made me feel that I was always bad, I guess when I was a child. I don't believe that now, but when I was a child I felt that I was going to die and I was going to go to hell because I was a bad person.” (The client has been guided efficiently into the experiences of TRP Steps 1 and 2: visceral reactivation of the emotional learning, “I'm bad,” and, simultaneously, the experience of the contradictory, disconfirming knowledge, “I wasn't bad, I was only believing your religious demonizing of me.” That is the juxtaposition experience required by the brain for profound unlearning to occur.) As Trish continued, she began to depart from her usual self-protective adaptation of avoiding her own unmet needs, by telling her father, “It hurts me that you don't love me—yeah—I guess, you know, but… I'm angry at you and I needed love and you weren't there to give me any love.” Her father's culpability for his emotional injuriousness to her is becoming more apparent to her as a result of her new freedom to feel and express her unmet needs to him. She could now tolerate the emotional pain of attending to her unmet, core needs—a primary focus of EFT—because the therapist invited her to express them and his empathetic accompaniment kept her from feeling alone as she did so. Aloneness strongly amplifies distress, as a rule, often to an unbearable level of intensity, making emotional dissociation or numbness necessary for coping. Here, Trish's recognition of the validity of her need for love is another knowing that contradicted the target learnings, so it fulfilled TRP Step C and also Step 3 by creating a tacit but effective juxtaposition with her original mental model, “Dad is

Emotion-Focused Therapy 175 unloving toward me because I am bad and unworthy of love.” That schema is now being unlearned and replaced by knowing that “Dad's unloving, denigrating behavior means he failed to be a loving father to me.” This repeated the essence of her previous juxtaposition experience, so it is Step 3. A learned identity-construct or mental model of oneself as bad, unworthy, and unlovable is the very source of the feeling of shame, so the annulment of that model of self through the TRP brings cessation of shame. This illustrates how, in the TRP framework, an unwanted emotion is ended when the underlying schema that was generating it is unlearned and replaced by a contradictory knowing that has viscerally disconfirmed the schema. That is a process of changing mental model with mental model, as distinct from changing emotion with emotion. Later, with more encouragement from the therapist, she told the image of her father about her fear: “I was lonely. I didn't know my father. My father, all I knew you as, was somebody that yelled at me all the time and hit me. That's all—I don't remember you telling me you loved me or that you cared for me or that you thought that I did well in school or anything. All I know you as \[sic\] somebody that I feared.” Trish was continuing to tolerate retrieving her emotional knowledge of the specific forms of suffering that she had endured, inflicted on her by her father. This again furthered Step C and Step 3 as described previously, because this inventory of ordeals was now serving as her knowledge of his mistreatment of her, which continued to disconfirm her self-blaming, selfshaming ways of understanding his behavior, creating the same tacit juxtaposition as before. Her next statements to him did more of the same. “Tell him how you were afraid of being hit,” prompted the therapist. “Yes, and you humiliated me,” Trish continued. “I was very angry with you because you were always hitting me; you were so mean and I heard Hitler was mean, so I called you Hitler.” At one point she added, “I guess I keep thinking that yeah, you will never be a parent, that you would pick up the phone and just ask me how I'm doing. It hurts me that you don't love me.” (This is yet more of Step C and Step 3, more and more fully disconfirming her original emotional learning that his behavior was a normal parental response to her badness.) Later in the session she confronted him particularly forcefully: “I'm angry at you because you think you were a good father, you have said that you never hit us and that's the biggest lie on earth, you beat the hell out of us constantly, you never showed any love, you never showed any affection, you never ever acknowledged we were ever there except for us to clean and do things around the house.” She ended the session by saying, “I needed to be hugged once in a while as a child or told that I was OK. I think that's normal.” Those last four words affirming the validity of her unmet needs may have been an initial, overt marker of transformational change, TRP Step V, because they indicate that her lifelong model of herself as bad and unworthy was not defining her subjective experience at this point.

176 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change In the next (fourth) session, the therapist used two-chair work, in which the client sits and speaks alternately in each chair, creating an outer conversation between two different inner parts or subpersonalities. The aim here was to guide Trish to access, feel, and express her inner critic in one chair (a further retrieval of target learnings, for Step B and Step 1) and, in the other chair, to respond from the part(s) of herself that can offer very different knowings (for Step 2). (This brings the emotional schema(s) of the critic into juxtaposition with disconfirming knowings held by Trish apart from the critic's knowings, for Steps 1 and 2.) In this process, the voice of the critic softened (suggesting successful disconfirmation of the critic's mental models) and Trish, no longer suppressed by self-invalidation, began to feel a sense of her inherent worth and to express her grief over not being loved. This included a revisiting of the knowings that had become prominent in the previous session: Trish said, “Even though Mom and Dad didn't love me or didn't show me any love, it wasn't because I was unlovable; it was just because they were incapable of those emotions. They don't know how to—they still don't know how to love.” At this point, nowhere in evidence was the collapse into helplessness and hopelessness that had been predominant whenever she felt sadness or unmet needs in her first session. That non-occurrence of the symptom of emotional collapse adds to Step V as a marker of transformational change. Furthermore, that symptom's non-occurrence is in turn a marker of non-reactivation of the developmentally young identity schemas of unworthiness that previously ruled her state of mind, now transformed and replaced by a differentiated adult identity schema of inherent self-worth. That schema non-reactivation likewise adds to Step V. Here the original account moves to Session 7, in which the work focused on Trish blocking her feeling of wanting to be loved by her parents to protect herself from the pain of that need not being met. The part of herself that protected her with this blocking tactic became named the “interrupter.” This work continued through Session 9 where, in two-chair work, her interrupter in one chair criticized Trish visualized in the other chair, saying, “You're wasting your time feeling bad 'cause you want them; they are not there. So it's best for you to shut your feelings off and not need them. That's what I do in my life. When people hurt me enough I get to that point where I actually can imagine, I literally cut them out of my life like I did with my mother.” (This was Step B, retrieval from implicit to explicit knowledge of her learnings and tactics for protecting herself from the pain and desolation of extreme emotional neglect by her parents.) In the other chair, Trish inhabited and expressed the self that needs and wants to experience being loved and accepted. Understood in terms of the structure of symptom-generating schemas delineated in Chapter 3, that explicit two-chair interaction revealed two different, conflicting solutions to the problem of the painful unmet need for being loved. The solution of the interrupter part (previously outside of awareness) was to block the experience of feelings, stop trying for that need to be met, and numbly soldier on without being loved by parents

Emotion-Focused Therapy 177 or anyone. The solution of conscious Trish was to keep hoping and waiting for their love even though that entailed feeling the hurt, sadness, and anger. These two different solutions were different preferences, and they were certainly at odds with each other, but they were not mutually incompatible models of reality, so experiencing them simultaneously was not a juxtaposition experience in which one would be disconfirmed by the other. The therapist observed in Session 9 that “The hopelessness that was so dominant in the early sessions now is virtually nonexistent. The voice that wants love and acceptance becomes stronger, and the critic \[interrupter\] softens to express acceptance of this part of her. At the same time she is feeling much better and activation of her negative feelings decreases.” Those several markers verifying change contributed significantly more to Step V. In another round of empty chair work with her father in Session 10, for the first time Trish felt and gave voice to a compassionate understanding of him, which Greenberg notes is an empirically observed marker of change, hence an important further contribution to Step V. Trish stated to her visualized father, “I understand that you've gone through a lot of pain in your life and probably because of this pain, because of the things you've seen \[in the concentration camp\], you've withdrawn. You're afraid to maybe give love the way it should be given and to get too close to anybody because it means you might lose them. You know—and I can understand that now, whereas growing up I couldn't understand.” She was continuing to hold him accountable for the ways that he had failed her and hurt her, while also allowing her compassion to be central in a new, more complete understanding of how their lives together had unfolded. No longer in the grip of previous emotional reactions generated from a young-child state, she was able to access adult knowings about her father, which (understood from the TRP perspective) were juxtaposing with and disconfirming yet more of her previous way of making sense of his behaviors in terms of herself being bad and unlovable, so this was a new round of TRP Steps 1, 2, and 3. Commenting on that dialogue at the end of the session, Trish said, “I feel relief that I don't have this anger sitting on my chest anymore.” This was a particularly decisive, somatic marker of change contributing to Step V. Finally Greenberg states that at the end of this 14-session therapy, Trish was free of the lifelong, shame-generating core belief “I am not worth loving” and free of the depression-generating hopelessness that was triggered previously by needing to be loved. Those are transformational changes. He also comments, “she is now more able to communicate her needs, to protect herself from feeling inadequate, and to be closer to her sisters.” Those changes are significant ones for Trish, but, as described, seem not yet fully transformational. We may assume that Trish felt sufficiently satisfied with her changes after 14 sessions to end therapy at that point. As this case example shows, EFT typically carries out the steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process in the sequence A–B–C–1–2–3–V. It is instructive

178 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change to consider why EFT methodology defined as “changing emotion with emotion” would fulfill the TRP, given that, as shown earlier in this case, close scrutiny of clients' phenomenology reveals that a particular pattern of emotion changes when the mental model generating that emotion is unlearned and nullified (ending its subjective realness) by being contradicted and disconfirmed by a different mental model. The emotion of shame chronically felt by Trish was arising from her identity-model of “I'm bad and not worth loving,” which was originally formed as the meaning that she construed for her father's extreme harshness

toward her. (In ordinary terms, she believed her father's negative messages about her.) Her shame disappeared as soon as that module of emotional learning was disconfirmed and unlearned by being juxtaposed with her own inner recognition of a fundamentally different meaning for his behavior, namely his failure to be loving even though she was and is good and lovable. That phenomenology is misrepresented by an overall characterization of “changing emotion with emotion.” Greenberg himself recognizes (2010, p. 33) that “Therapists therefore need to work with both emotion and meaning, making and facilitating change in both emotional experience and the narratives in which they are embedded.” Also, as noted in Chapter 2, a controlled human study by Speer et al. (2021) examined the effects of internally discovering positive personal meaning in a past negative experience that had previously been regarded as entirely negative. These researchers concluded that (p. 7) “Across four experiments, we found converging evidence that positive meaning finding led to enhanced positive emotion and positive content at future retrieval… Rather than providing external intervening information for updating, individuals internally generated this on their own…” Here again it is shown that emotion is changed by changing its underlying mental model. Facilitating annulments of problematic schemas with maximum efficiency is the purpose of the TRP, and Greenberg's case example shows how well EFT can fulfill the TRP and produce transformational unlearning of symptomgenerating mental models. As noted earlier, he also affirms the crucial role of memory reconsolidation as the mechanism of that lasting change.

Although his EFT motto “changing emotion with emotion” does not adequately

identify the critical phenomenology, it nevertheless does guide EFT practitioners to facilitate the critical phenomenology because, as Ecker (2018, p. 80) has pointed out, “By combining emotional reactivation of the target learning with a very different emotional experience of the original situation, a disconfirmation of model occurs implicitly, even though the attention of therapist and client may be focused on derivative emotion.” It is a well-recognized conundrum in the psychotherapy field that how clinicians conceptualize the process of change that they carry out does not necessarily identify all parts of the phenomenology that actually occurs in their sessions and is crucial in the process of change.

Emotion-Focused Therapy 179 Greenberg's recognition of the core process of transformational change is nevertheless apparent when, for example, he explains (2010, p. 38) that “an experience in which a client faces shame in a therapeutic context and experiences acceptance, rather than the expected disgust or denigration, has the power to change the feeling of shame.” Thus he acknowledges that it is the learned expectation of receiving responses of disgust or denigration—which is a mental model, not an emotion—that generates the emotion and is the target of change.

Note 1 For a concise list of the component steps of the TRP, see Table 2.1 on p. 34 or p. 144 in Chapter 6. Fully understanding this and other chapters in Part 2 of this book requires first reading Chapters 1, 2, and 3, which explain transformational therapeutic change and how it occurs through a particular recruitment of the brain's mechanism of memory reconsolidation, accomplished by the therapeutic reconsolidation process or TRP. Familiarity with the TRP is assumed. Chapter 2 defines and explains the TRP at length, including the empirical research on which it is directly based. Chapter 3 demonstrates the focused facilitation of the TRP in psychotherapy sessions.

Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

EMDR was first developed in the late 1980s by psychologist Francine Shapiro for the treatment of post-traumatic stress symptoms, and is now used to address a wide range of presenting symptoms (Maxfield, 2019; Shapiro, 2018). The target of change in EMDR is memory material of various types underlying and generating the presenting symptoms, which makes EMDR deeply kindred with the therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP). To accomplish the accessing and transformational change of those memory contents, EMDR methodology utilizes dual focus, in which the client focuses attention on two different experiential areas at once: an internally experienced component or expression of the problematic memory material (a specific image, expectation, meaning, emotion, body sensation, thought, etc.) and, concurrently, an external sensory stimulus, which in EMDR consists of a bilateral oscillation of perceptual attention (whether through eye movements, audio tones, or physical touch-taps). Dual focus is present also in some other therapeutic systems of transformational change, such as Neurolinguistic Programming (NLP), Progressive Counting, and acupoint tapping, but reliance on bilateral stimulation is EMDR's distinctive form of dual focus. EMDR's conceptual model, known as Adaptive Information Processing, describes the brain's memory systems as always striving for survival and adaptive mental health, but susceptible to becoming stuck on unprocessed memory contents formed in negative experiences. EMDR is understood as functioning to access, re-process, and update this distress-laden, symptom-generating material in the client's memory networks, bringing about a fundamental, in-depth resolution of negative emotional experiences rather than a relatively superficial, counteractive managing of symptoms. EMDR methodology consists of a protocol with eight phases of preparation and processing, described comprehensively by Shapiro (2018). Our EMDR case example comprises a series of five sessions conducted by licensed professional counselor Beverly Schoninger and reported by Shapiro and Forrest (1998, pp. 74–88). The therapist, who kindly assisted with this chapter by answering our questions (Schoninger, personal communication, July 25, 2011), carried out DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-11

Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing 181 the entire EMDR protocol, including SUDS (Subjective Units of Distress Scale) ratings. Our account includes only the dual focus, bilateral stimulation work and the client's immediate responses to it. The commentary on the unfolding EMDR process is ours, with the aim of making apparent the embedded steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process.1 Our purpose in mapping an EMDR case onto TRP fulfillment is to expand our demonstration of the universality of the TRP as a unifying core process responsible for transformational change produced by any methods of psychotherapy. The client, “Susan,” in her early forties, was in her second marriage, with two adult sons from her first marriage. Susan sought EMDR for relief from over four years of panic attacks stemming from a traumatic experience 10 years earlier, while living with her first husband, “Keith,” and their younger son, “Ernie,” in a small dairy-farming village with a population of several hundred in the USA's Midwest. In her first session, as she began to tell the therapist about that trauma, her face flushed and she began hyperventilating, on the verge of a panic attack, but she managed to continue. She explained that at bedtime on June 7, 1984, the wind was blowing violently. She had grown up in the Midwest, was keenly alert to the danger of tornadoes, and had herded her family into their basement for safety on many occasions—though she once wished their house would blow away so they would receive the insurance money and be able to start new lives. Keith had come to the Midwest with Susan only a few years previously and had a patronizing attitude toward her vigilance for storms, regarding her as alarmist. On this night, Susan convinced Keith that they should abandon their upstairs, air-conditioned bedroom for the night and sleep in the guest room on the ground floor, where the constant howling of the wind would be muffled. At 12:50 am, a loud clap of thunder and flash of lightning awoke Susan. She could hear pouring rain and a persistent low whistling, like wind blowing in the eaves or a car horn driven by a weak battery. Then Ernie ran into the room because the sounds had awakened him, too. At first Susan thought the whistling might be the tornado alarm from the next town. Looking out the window, she saw total darkness. There were no lights on in town, not even at the fire station next door. She realized that the whistling was not a tornado alarm; it was the tornado itself. Susan shouted, “Keith, come on! We're going to the basement!” and started running, followed by Ernie. Keith was awake but in no hurry. Susan saw him reaching for his pants as she hurried toward the kitchen, flung open the door to the stairs descending to the basement, and raced down to safety. Right away she heard a loud cracking as the siding on the house started to break up, and then she was unconscious. When awareness returned, Susan was in complete darkness, soaking wet and buried in three feet of rubble in her basement. Rain was still pouring down, drenching her in her thin nightgown. The air was acrid with the smell of heating

182 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change oil oozing from a break in the basement oil tank. The stairs were no longer there. The rows of shelves up to the ceiling, once stacked high with belongings, were gone also. The ceiling was gone. There was no house above her. Ernie was beside her, but Keith was not. When the rain finally subsided, Ernie crawled out from under the rubble, climbed up out of the cavity that had been their basement, and ran for help. A team of paramedics eventually arrived and, in the near-total darkness, brought Susan up to ground level and to shelter for the night, while Ernie joined rescue workers. That there was no sign of Keith was troubling but Susan assured herself he was all right. In the morning Susan returned to the scene. The devastation caused by the tornado's 300-mile-per-hour winds was beyond comprehension. Eleven of the 12 houses in their immediate neighborhood were flattened, and so was the town itself. As Time magazine later chronicled, in only 20 seconds the town had been “wiped right off the map.” Visiting the recovery command center, Susan and Ernie were taken to see their local policeman. He looked haggard and sad and said, “Susan, Keith's dead.” So were eight others, seven of them Susan's immediate neighbors, including her best friend, Jill, Jill's husband, and their eight-year-old daughter. Many more in the town had been injured. This first session included initial training in safe place imagery, which is used in EMDR for self-soothing and for ensuring the client's emotional stability in the event that an unworkable level of distress becomes reactivated during the work or between sessions. (Safe place imagery is used for emotional deactivation if and when necessary. Its content is not necessarily matched to that of the client's traumatic memory and is not intended as part of the EMDR process for therapeutic change of memory contents.) On the following day, the second session consisted of another rehearsal of using safe place imagery and of taking a thorough inventory of Susan's specific experiences during a panic attack: the feeling of anxiety; a lump in the throat; light-headedness; dizziness; spacey disorientation; pain in chest, neck, and shoulders; and tingling in hands and feet. In answering the question, “When are you most likely to lose control of your body?” Susan replied, “When something happens in my body I don't understand, pain that is not explained, or in crowded stores or at the office.” (This detailed identification of both the what and the when of Susan's symptoms was TRP Step A.) Two weeks later, the third session began with EMDR's step of selecting a “target” to serve as the initial subjective focus for the first set of bilateral eye movements. The therapist asked Susan to select, from her memory of the event, the moment or image that she felt to be the most distressing part of it all. Susan identified the image of her husband putting on his pants as she hurried toward the steps to the basement. The therapist then guided Susan to identify the “negative cognition” associated with that image and, for that purpose, soon asked her gently, “Susan, do you have any feelings of guilt about what happened to Keith?”

Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing 183 “No. No, I don't feel guilty,” Susan said without hesitation. The therapist persevered and explained, “Well, some people might feel guilty about this. You know, when people die, very often their loved ones feel it was their fault in some way, even if it wasn't. Even if it couldn't have been. Check deep inside. Let your gut answer, not your mind. Do you think you might have any feeling that it was your fault?” “Oh!” Susan exclaimed, wide-eyed, and after a long pause she acknowledged, “My gut does feel like that, like it was my fault, like I was the cause of Keith's death.” Tears were now running down her cheeks. Susan identified the accompanying negative feelings as sadness and, asked where in her body she felt this, she indicated her chest and throat. (This was TRP Step B, retrieval of the implicit meaning, “It was my fault,” which was a mental model that

Susan had formed for making sense of her husband's death, with no awareness of forming it until now.) The therapist asked, “What would you like to believe instead?” This was the next step of the EMDR procedure, the client's identification of a preferred “positive cognition” that defines what the client wants to experience as true instead of experiencing the negative cognition as true. Susan said she would like to believe and feel, “I did the best I could.” The client's articulation of a positive cognition in EMDR often proves to have accomplished TRP Step C—the identification of the knowing that will contradict and dissolve the existing symptom-maintaining knowings. The challenge is to bring this mere idea of a positive cognition into vivid emotional realness so that it can serve as an actual experience of contradictory knowing (in TRP Step 2). The EMDR process arrives at that vivification in sometimes surprising ways, as will become apparent. The first set of bilateral eye movements began with Susan focusing on the target image and its accompanying elements—the conviction, “It was my fault,” and the feeling of sadness and its sensations in her chest and throat. Immediately Susan began crying, and as set after set unfolded she roller-coastered through a wide range of emotions and meanings. Each set began with Susan focusing on what had emerged from the previous one. “I didn't want him to die,” she moaned, gasping for breath through her tears. Then, “I caused his death,” which brought with it feelings of guilt and chest pain. After the next few sets she felt lighter, but then went on to ask, “Why didn't I die too?” and felt frustrated and angry with herself for being unable to protect Keith, since she was the one who knew about tornadoes. Later, she felt a fresh wave of guilt welling up in her throat because the tornado had broken every bone in Keith's body, yet she had walked away without a scratch. After the session's final set of eye movements, Susan said, “There's a piece inside about my being a no-good person. It doesn't make sense to me. I don't know where I got this stuff that I was bad.” It was her panic attacks that had led Susan to seek EMDR therapy, but the underlying material that had now come into awareness (TRP Step B) during this

184 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change initial session of dual focus processing, bilateral stimulation work focusing on memories of the tornado experience consisted of constructs of angry selfblame and self-condemnation (I could have protected Keith but failed to do so; I caused his death; I'm a no-good person) and guilt for surviving unharmed. How these specific meanings and feelings might be related to the panic attacks was not yet apparent. Two days later, at the start of her next session, Susan commented that she'd had “no idea that feeling was in me,” referring to the self-blame that had surfaced and that continued to feel true, for she added, “I should have been able to make Keith understand the seriousness of the situation.” After a long pause, in a sad voice she said, “Someday he would have learned to listen to me,” and tears came. The therapist then asked her to focus on those words—“I should have been able to make Keith understand”—for this session's first set of eye movements. After the set, Susan said her feeling of grief was even stronger. After another set the emotion of grief reached a peak of intensity, and Susan said she was feeling sadness and frustration in her chest and throat. Crying, she asked, “Why did he leave me alone?” The therapist could not yet know it, but in those moments Susan retrieved her suppressed emotional distress in its full depth (TRP Step B: experiential retrieval of symptom-generating emotional meanings). Over the next few sets of eye movements, she reported feeling calmer. Then came the moment, following another set, when Susan calmly said, “It was a choice he made. It had nothing to do with me. Our soul chooses.” Having allowed the full intensity of her blocked grief to flow through her body and mind, suddenly Susan was now accessing, experiencing, and voicing a very different, calmly clear knowing that sharply contradicted the constructs of selfblame that had been distressing her deeply until just minutes earlier (fulfilling TRP Step 2: initial experience of contradictory knowing in juxtaposition with the target learnings). The quality of the experiential knowing expressed in Susan's last utterances will be recognizable to readers who are experienced EMDR practitioners, but to readers unfamiliar with this approach, those words may read as mere affirmations or positive thinking. However, it is characteristic of EMDR that a new knowing contradicting the target construct can suddenly and unpredictably emerge during a set as an experiential, whole-body experience of a lucid truth, not just an idea. In some cases, the client recognizes the contradictory knowing as something known all along, but only in its own separate context. In other cases, the contradictory knowing feels completely new and unprecedented to the client, in which case it does not really seem to be a compartmentalized piece of prior learning. Rather, it is as though the individual's inner being possesses a hidden store of intuitive knowledge that has been precisely tapped for a needed unit of illumination. Whatever its actual source, the newly emergent contradictory knowing has the specificity and compelling realness required for

Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing 185 successfully disconfirming and dissolving the target construct. This is EMDR's distinctive way of fulfilling TRP Step C and Step 2. The therapist immediately recognized the transformational value of what had just emerged and said to Susan, “Stay with that,” and then conducted another set of eye movements. After this set Susan said, “I can take care of myself” and again cried, and then said, “But it was his choice to live or die, and he was ready to go.” (This was TRP Step 3, a first repetition of the same juxtaposition experience that achieved Step 2.) Transformational change was occurring in these moments. Susan's constructs of self-blame no longer felt emotionally real to her. She had construed and learned them in the aftermath of the tragedy and now she had disconfirmed and unlearned them through a juxtaposition experience created by her new knowings. The juxtaposition consisted of the side-by-side experience of “I was responsible for Keith's actions and should have been able to make him listen to me and get to safety; so it is my fault he died in the tornado, and I am a very bad person” and “He made his own choice, beyond my range of influence, about how to respond when I summoned him to safety; I did the best I could, I cannot control everything in life, and it is not my fault that he made the choice he did and died as a result.” After another set she said, “I'm feeling sorry for myself.” The next set focused on that feeling and led to her saying, “I'm feeling abandoned by my family. They've pretty much dismissed what happened to me.” Susan explained that in the initial period after the tornado, her parents and extended family members gave her a great deal of caring attention, but their expressions of sympathetic concern had tapered off much too soon. With a few more sets, these thoughts and feelings receded and were replaced by yet a different area of distress when she said, “I feel guilty about the money. I benefited: We had homeowners' insurance.” The next set began with a focus on those words, and led to Susan again saying, “I do feel he did the best he could. He was a dreamer, you know, 'Don't think about it and it will just go away.' I was the practical one.” She had returned to and was further articulating her

lucid recognition of Keith's autonomy, again disconfirming her self-blame (which was another repetition of the juxtaposition experienced earlier in the session, adding to Step 3; the TRP's unlearning sequence, Steps 1–2–3, was now well fulfilled). After a set then focused on her last utterances about Keith's independence of choice, she said, “What is there about me that I can still trust?” The therapist asked what she meant, and she explained, “I'm not the person I thought I was. I'm not the totally competent person who handles things and gets things done. That was the basic me. Now who am I, anyway?” Susan was now grappling with the implications or ripple effects of recognizing and respecting Keith's autonomy in choosing how he acted that night. Perceiving his choicefulness was now leading her to accept the (existential) limitations of her own power to influence

186 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change what happens—and this new knowing directly challenged and disconfirmed her longstanding identity (her mental model of herself) as having essentially unlimited ability to make things happen as she sees best (which is TRP Steps B, 1, and 2 in relation to her learned model of personal identity). Susan's comments, “I'm not the person I thought I was… Now who am I?” were a marker of emerging transformational shift in her identity constructs (Step V) and signaled that she was undergoing new growth in her sense of self. The session's final set began with a focus on her question, “Now who am I?” Following that set, Susan rated her distress to be zero and, when also asked by the therapist to rate the felt truth of her originally articulated, desired positive cognition, “I did the best I could,” she gave it the highest possible score of “completely true” (a quite strong Step V marker of transformational change). Susan came for her fifth and last session, a half-hour follow-up, three days later. She said she was feeling great and her symptoms were almost completely gone. She explained, “The things that were happening in my body don't happen anymore. Even at work, where I'm now doing the job of two people, I can let things roll off my back.” Her workplace had been one of her triggers of panic attacks. The absence of her previous emotional and somatic reactions in the presence of their formerly strong triggers was a clear marker verifying transformational change (TRP Step V). She said she had felt one minor panic attack since the last session, but that this experience itself fed directly into the change process because it happened “in a store, of course,” and it led Susan to realize that the department store, and also some parts of her workplace, presented her with strong reminders of the tornado trauma: high shelves overhead stocked with items (as those along her basement walls had been), the general din of shoppers and PA-system announcements (like the surrounding roar of the tornado's winds ripping the house apart), and the visual turmoil of many things happening all around her. Susan's realization that these features were only present reminders of a past ordeal was a vivid, felt knowing in itself, not just a cognitive insight. Understood in terms of the TRP, this new knowing had functioned as contradictory knowledge that juxtaposed with and disconfirmed the meaning that her emotional memory system had been giving those features: “A tornado is here!” The latter meaning had been generating her panic attacks in stores and her office. Those reminder cues had now lost their power to drive Susan into a state of panic (another marker of transformational changing adding to Step V). The well-defined coherence of the panic attacks might also apply to the panic attack Susan almost had in her first therapy session: At least one of those same cues could have been present, such as high book-filled shelves. As Susan's sessions illustrate, the EMDR process is often nonlinear. There is no predicting what material will emerge next at any given point, and seemingly discontinuous shifts into unexpected or even seemingly unrelated material can be about as frequent as recognizable continuity. Susan's constructs of self-blame

Eye-Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing 187 emerged first. After self-blame came her knowledge that her extended family had withdrawn sympathetic attention much too soon for her, so she felt abandoned by them. Then her guilt over benefiting from the insurance money came into awareness, and finally she was feeling the shift in identity wrought by realizing that her husband had chosen his own fate, beyond her range of influence. Facilitated by dual focus processing work, Susan's mind and brain brought into awareness from implicit memory a series of five distinct areas of distress-laden meaning and feeling for conscious processing: self-blame, grief, abandonment, guilt, and identity. It is noteworthy that during her EMDR sessions, none of the therapeutic process directly addressed Susan's panic attacks per se, and in her short final follow-up session she reported having a mild panic attack since the final eyemovement session three days earlier, which meant that the eye-movement work had not yet completely dispelled her panic symptoms. Yet, from that panic attack Susan recognized for the first time—after more than four years of panic attacks—the specific environmental features that were triggering her panic. She then recognized also that these triggering features were merely reminders of an ordeal that was in her past, not in her present, and this recognition created a juxtaposition of meanings that disconfirmed and nullified the imminent-threat meaning of these current cues. It also illustrates how the unlearning sequence of memory reconsolidation can occur in daily life outside of therapy sessions. The case also demonstrates the important point that traumatic experiences generate distress-laden memory consisting of not only episodic memory of the experience of the event, but also mental models that generate various ongoing symptoms of their own—such as Susan's neocortical construal that she was responsible for her husband's death (generating guilt and self-condemnation) and her subcortical construal that tall shelves full of items means a tornado is upon her (generating panic attacks). To generalize about EMDR in relation to the therapeutic reconsolidation process, we note that the TRP's steps are typically carried out by EMDR in the sequence A–(C)–B–1–2–3–V, where (C) represents the identification of the client's desired positive cognition, which may or may not prove to represent the contradictory material that finally emerges experientially in Step 2. After the underlying memory contents have come into awareness, how and why do continued experiences of dual focus then facilitate the accessing of contradictory knowledge? This has been explained by Ecker (2015c) in terms of the phenomenology of attention and memory, briefly summarized as follows: In the normal course of daily life, when the client's distress-saturated memory material becomes reactivated, it does so outside of awareness, so there is no mindful awareness of that material, and the client's state of mind is taken over by it. In contrast, dual focus anchors the client's subjective viewpoint in the present safe environment, outside of the distress-saturated memory material, while directing attention to that material mindfully. This anchored viewpoint allows

188 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change metacognitive consideration of the material without succumbing to its “spell.” This “unmerged attending” to the symptom-generating memory material—

consciously recognizing its unquestioned expectations and beliefs—

allows the brain's built-in mismatch detector to evaluate each of those recognized elements, which cannot happen when non-mindfully under the spell of the reactivated

material in the usual way. The spontaneous conscious emergence of contradictory knowledge, as Susan described, is the result of the automatic mismatch detection process finding a mismatch with the memory material and bringing that mismatching knowledge into awareness.2 A research review by Maxfield (2019) covers 72 formal studies of EMDR. It is well known that the results of these studies have produced both support for the efficacy of EMDR as well as negative findings accompanied by some sharp challenges to EMDR's efficacy and scientific credibility. In our view, the actual therapeutic potency of EMDR becomes apparent not in the standard outcome research designs that have been applied, but rather in close scrutiny of individual cases that have produced transformational change unambiguously, such as is presented in this chapter and also in many EMDR writings and video demonstrations. As noted in Chapter 1, the outcome research field has relied heavily on research formats that are incapable of detecting the very existence of transformational change. Researchers of course are free to keep requiring RCT (randomized controlled trial) credentials that have little relevance to actual therapeutic effectiveness, but when therapy clients report full, lasting disappearance of major symptoms in no uncertain terms, therapists have all the evidence they need for meaningful, satisfying work of real service to humanity. Furthermore, in conjunction with our atheoretical, empirical knowledge of the memory reconsolidation process of unlearning, study of single cases shows the effectiveness of EMDR methodology in fulfilling that potent therapeutic process, as demonstrated in this chapter.3 That unambiguous demonstration of TRP fulfillment by the actual practice of EMDR puts its scientific validity on firm ground, and confirms the recognition first expressed by founder Shapiro (Solomon & Shapiro, 2008) that EMDR utilizes memory reconsolidation.

10 Internal Family Systems Therapy (IFS) Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

One of the enduring meta-frameworks of psychotherapy consists of recognizing the multiplicity of the mind—that is, the normal existence of numerous different subpersonalities within an individual's mind—and defining methodologies for actively interacting with these subpersonalities for therapeutic effects. The initial forms of that tradition were developed in the early 1900s by Jung and by Assagioli (Psychosynthesis), later followed by Berne (Transactional Analysis), Watkins and Johnson (Ego State Therapy), Perls (Gestalt Therapy), and Satir (the “parts party”), among others. Whether such systems refer to a “subpersonality,” “subself,” “ego state,” “complex” or “part,” they view each such subunit of the mind as having its own personality with distinct views, feelings, needs, agenda, and responses, and a significant degree of autonomy. In addition, the Jungian and psychosynthesis frameworks centrally involve the Self, described by Ferrucci (2004, p. 64) as follows: It is possible to experience the self as pure consciousness, apart from any content: “I am.” From this psychological place, the self has a panoramic view of all the personality contents instead of being identified with just one of them at a time. In the psychosynthetic conception, the self is neither the passive spectator extraneous to the show nor the actor completely involved in it. It is the producer, who stages the whole show with expertise, good timing, and tactful handling of the actors. When clearly experienced, the self can decide to identify fully and easily with any personality content, from romantic love to furious anger to physical appetite. But it is also able to dis-identify from the content. The experience of self allows choice at all times. Thus the whole personality is available to the self. Internal Family Systems Therapy (IFS), developed by psychologist Richard Schwartz, PhD, since the 1980s, operationalizes the multiplicity paradigm, including the Self, into a versatile methodology by using systemic concepts to navigate and facilitate the inner ecology of the “parts” involved in symptom production (Schwartz, 2021; Schwartz & Sweezy, 2020). Parts that carry the living emotional DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-12

Internal Family Systems Therapy 191 memory, or burden, of original, unresolved, overwhelmingly intense sufferings, and that therefore have been kept as far away from conscious awareness as possible, are called exiles. Parts that operate to prevent any direct experience of those distress-laden exiles are called protectors, of which there are two types, managers, which proactively deploy tactics designed to prevent any direct experience of an exile (such as perfectionism, workaholism, or people-pleasing), and fire-fighters, which deploy emergency tactics to re-suppress an exile's distress that was coming into conscious experience (such as substance abuse, sexual arousal, or raging). In many cases, a client's presenting symptoms are discovered to be the tactical behaviors or states of mind self-protectively generated by protectors. Other symptoms are revealed to be the distress of one or more exiles infusing the conscious personality. The Self, however, is not a part, rather it is a person's undamaged, unconditioned essence. The therapist guides the client to access the viewpoint of the Self and to attend to, interact with, and intervene upon the usual functioning of the ecology of the parts, with the aim of making it workable for the exiles to emerge into direct awareness so that they unburden by openly feeling and expressing their long-held distress and needs to the Self. Unburdening is regarded as being therapeutic by de-suppressing distress, by ending the aloneness and disconnection that the exile was enduring, and by the exile receiving the Self's distinctive, inherent qualities, such as empathy, compassionate understanding, loving acceptance, loving interest, and unending presence and connection. IFS embodies the principles of humanistic psychology in that it is non-pathologizing, it views the therapeutic process as a facilitation of the client's own native capabilities and processes of change and growth, and the therapist shows full reliance on and respect for the client's authority of inner self-knowledge. The client–therapist relationship is a crucial catalyst for facilitating the therapeutic process, but the primary driver of therapeutic change is the interactions between the Self and the parts. For a map of how that methodology is systematically implemented, see the two books cited in the previous paragraph or the concise account by Kredler (2023), which, similar to this chapter, presents an IFS case example mapped in terms of how the therapeutic reconsolidation process is fulfilled. The case example below, a single session of IFS that produced transformational change, was contributed for this chapter by certified IFS therapist Derek Scott, RSW, founder of the Internal Family System Counseling Association in Ontario, Canada, an IFS author (e.g., Scott, 2016), and IFS trainer strongly endorsed by Richard Schwartz. The session was conducted remotely via online video, so it serves also to show the suitability of that medium for doing deep, experiential work that accesses non-conscious areas of core emotional distress. In fact, it is pre-verbal emotional distress in infancy that emerges as the focus of the session, and the work richly exemplifies inner child work as well as IFS. Here we provide the full transcript of the session with Scott's comments on the unfolding IFS process in endnotes. Our own commentaries, embedded in

In the TRP framework, a distress-laden emotional learning or schema has two main sections, one consisting of knowledge of the problem (vulnerability to a particular suffering) and one consisting of knowledge of the solution (tactics urgently necessary for avoiding or ending that suffering). The ego state focused on the experience of the suffering is the part that IFS terms the exile, and the ego state focused on the protective strategy or tactic is the part that IFS terms the protector, manager, or firefighter. As the therapist indicated just previously, the two are very tightly linked together, so much so that they are regarded as aspects of one schema in the TRP framework. Understanding a client's response by discerning it as either expressing a problem or a solution (an exile or a protector) is a critically important skill for consistent success with both the TRP and IFS. That initial juxtaposition, if sustained as the session continues (TRP Step 3), subjects the schema to rapid, profound unlearning, completing the TRP. This would nullify the mental

11 Interpersonal Neurobiology (IPNB) Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

A primary aim of psychotherapy guided by Interpersonal Neurobiology (IPNB), developed by psychotherapist and child psychiatrist Daniel Siegel in the 1990s, is liberation from the grip of emotional implicit schemas formed in response to patterns of distressing interaction suffered in infancy and childhood. Prominent in IPNB is the recognition that specific mental models formed by the individual are a major part of symptom-generating implicit memory, and that early and ongoing insecure attachment relationships can dissociate important cognitive, emotional, and memory functionalities of the brain, causing a wide range of interpersonal and intrapsychic deficits and corresponding problems of behavior and states of mind. The therapeutic implication, according to IPNB, is that the positive use of the same influence—dyadic relational experience, now in the client–therapist relationship—can create reparative attachment experiences that can establish integrated brain functioning, undoing the dissociative effects caused by the original, harmful attachment patterns. Integration is important because it is the cooperative interaction of brain systems handling very different aspects of our functioning on all levels. Key features of the therapeutic process in IPNB include the client's felt experience of the therapist's empathetic emotional attunement and accompaniment; guidance from the therapist for attending to and verbalizing neglected right-brain and subcortical activity comprising implicit emotional knowledge and responses; guidance for identifying how current triggers resemble past experiences; and cultivation of integrated awareness of what was suffered in the past, ending projection of the past onto the present situation. Siegel's emphasis on the retrieval of the contents of implicit memory into explicit awareness and direct, emotional experience has made a substantial contribution to the psychotherapy field (e.g., Siegel, 2006, 2020). He has described the effects of that implicit-to-explicit reorganization in terms of emotional and neurological integration, and has mapped out distinct functional areas of integration so that therapists can actively facilitate them and thereby induce therapeutic change. Siegel also teaches a style of informing therapy clients about brain functioning that de-pathologizes symptoms, largely eliminating the stigma DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-13

208 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change and shame that many clients feel regarding their symptoms and fostering the client's hopefulness and motivation in therapy. In choosing an IPNB case example for mapping its methodology onto fulfillment of the therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP), as always we searched for a published case having a sufficiently detailed account of the client–therapist interaction to allow for unambiguous TRP mapping. Without that specificity of what actually happened moment by moment, our TRP mapping can appear to be merely our biased interpretation rather than an objective, phenomenological account whose accuracy is self-evident. However, we found that published accounts of IPNB cases consistently describe the unfolding therapeutic process in qualitative, somewhat abstract terms without providing a concrete, specific account of the client–therapist interaction, whether via transcript or fine-grained narrative description.1 Our commenting on this is not intended as a criticism; presumably that style of case presentation is fully adequate for the pedagogical purposes of IPNB authors. However, for our particular purposes it is insufficient, for the reason just indicated. We believe that the importance of including IPNB in Part 2 of this book warrants making an exception to our rule of demonstrating TRP mapping only for cases with sufficiently detailed documentation. We ask the reader to bear in mind that the TRP mapping that follows is at times somewhat inferential, rather than always self-evident, only due to the narrative soft focus of the case material. IPNB methodology is illustrated below in a case vignette by IPNB author and teacher, marriage and family therapist Bonnie Badenoch (2011, pp. 73–74). Our inserted comments indicate our inferences of how the steps of the TRP2 are being fulfilled, given the style of case presentation noted above. For

Badenoch's or Siegel's own accounts of the concepts and methods of IPNB, we encourage readers to refer directly to their writings cited above, as well as Badenoch (2008). Our purpose in mapping an IPNB case onto TRP fulfillment is to expand our demonstration of the universality of the TRP as a unifying core process responsible for transformational change produced by any methods of psychotherapy. Cerise came to me because all of her close relationships ended in her pulling away when emotional intimacy became intense. \[Symptom identification, TRP Step A\] We worked our way through a number of childhood memories in which she had felt overwhelmed by her mother, but this work did not produce much change in her relational apprehensions. We began to ask her deeper mind to guide us toward the source of her unchanging fear. Almost immediately, she felt the behavioral impulse of backing away while she saw an image of her parents in their ballet of mutual avoidance. \[Accessing the symptom's underlying emotional learning has begun, for TRP Step B. Cerise's self-protective distancing from her parents' troubled relationship, considered along with the very similar presenting symptom

Interpersonal Neurobiology 209 of distancing from her own potential couple relationships, indicates a learned, generalized expectation that being in any couple relationship will be an entrapment in a miserable experience similar to what her parents have suffered.\] We began to focus our attention on these two internalized dancers. Much as we did in working with her child states of mind, we asked both inner parents, in turn, what was hurting or scaring them. \[For the discovery work, the therapist is making use of how Cerise's inner images of her parents are serving as portals for accessing her implicit knowledge pertaining to them and bringing that implicit knowledge into explicit awareness. The readiness of implicit memory systems to respond cooperatively with such querying is nicely demonstrated by the therapist's style of facilitating this process. In what follows, it is important to understand that each inner parent figure is one of Cerise's own ego states that is vicariously merged with her implicit knowledge of each parent. So, interacting with each internal parent figure is an integrative process, creating connection and shared knowledge between previously dissociated emotional learnings and mental models, and opening up the possibility of juxtapositions and disconfirmations that produce transformational change.\] Requesting inner guidance again, she got the sense that we could begin most easily with her father. Waiting in receptivity after her question about what was happening inside him, Cerise began to sense in her body the same behavioral impulse to pull away that she felt when a lover wanted increasing connection. \[This seems to imply that Cerise learned the self-protective response of emotional distancing from her father's example of using that tactic, adding to Step B.\] Staying with this movement and letting her father know that we would remain with him, she began to have an intuitive sense of his frightening loss of connection with his depressed mother, experiencing it not in a cognitive but in a visceral way. \[So, Cerise's implicit knowledge of her father includes knowing that, from his experience of his mother's emotional disconnection, he learned to use emotional disconnection proactively to protect himself from abandonment: leaving before being left. In life with her parents, Cerise learned implicitly that the danger of emotional abandonment is the problem and leaving before being left is the necessary solution. That is her underlying schema driving her behavior in couple relationships. TRP Step B is well accomplished at this point. The therapist now knows that the expectation of emotional abandonment is what has to be disconfirmed and unlearned, and immediately aims to do that:\] We offered understanding, comfort, and continuous connection—key elements of what had been missing for him throughout his childhood, and thus a disconfirming experience. \[The father ego state is now experiencing its reactivated expectation of abandonment, which is TRP Step 1, concurrently with the contradictory

210 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change experience of secure attachment with the adult ego state in the present interaction, which is TRP Step 2. It seems very likely from the therapist's manner of working that this crucial juxtaposition experience would have been a sustained, extended experience, fulfilling TRP Step 3 and completing the unlearning sequence of memory reconsolidation.\] In her body, she could feel his emotional tension release as the brain circuitry holding this locked-away pain opened to the new relational experience we were offering. \[This disappearance of the somatic feeling of the schema-generated distress is an initial marker of transformational change for TRP Step V.\] We then moved on to do the same work with her mother. However, Cerise experienced these wounds as so much more complex and variegated that many inner experiences were required before her inner mother began feeling a relaxation similar to what she had experienced with her father. \[This presumably means that the inner mother's state of distress consisted of several different emotional schemas, each of which had to be discovered, accessed, and brought through the unlearning sequence, TRP Steps 1–2–3.\] We can trust this inner process to unfold in its best way, even when it takes a long time. Sometimes the tangled implicit memories that hold a particular inner state in place require us to simply be present over and over again as we make our way through the layers. In the presence of safety and care, through the kind and gentle holding that creates a cradle in which painful experience can emerge, the healing will happen as quickly as it can, even when that is slowly. As we worked with Cerise's mother, we noticed that her inner father watched the process between us and his wife. Instead of backing away, he seemed curious and open to understanding the nature of the wounds underlying her behavior. \[The fact that the inner father's previous response of fearful withdrawal is no longer occurring is another Step V marker of a transformational change indicating that the unlearning sequence has been carried out successfully for that schema.\] As soon as her mother came to peace, she and her husband were able to form a more connected relationship internally. Their implicit dance of avoidance was over…

After completing this round of resolving experiences, Cerise's encounters with her parents in other memories that had originally contained this same emotional valence of avoidance now showed them softened and more available to one another. \[This similarly indicates additional markers of transformational change in her implicit learnings of life within a couple relationship.\] It was as though working with them around their pains and fears had soothed similar pangs throughout the system. The resolution of her inner parents' avoidance turned out to be the key to change in Cerise's outer life. Once the two inner parents gained empathy for and connection with one another, her fear of closeness became a distant memory that she experienced as a brief behavioral impulse to back away that she no longer

Interpersonal Neurobiology 211 needed to follow. \[This is the most important marker of transformational change and fulfillment of Step V: The client's lasting behavioral and emotional freedom from the presenting symptoms in actual situations that previously would have evoked them.\] As this case example shows, IPNB typically carries out the steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process in the sequence A–B–C–1–2–3–V.
