12 Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

Developed by psychiatrist Habib Davanloo (1990, 2000) since the 1970s within the psychodynamic paradigm, Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) is a conceptual and methodological framework for working actively to bring into direct awareness and experience the unresolved emotional disturbances that have been generating symptoms from outside of awareness.

“Although based strictly on psychoanalytic theory and psychodynamic principles, the therapeutic approach has radically departed from standard practice in many ways” (Coughlin & Katzman, 2013, p. 486). The emergence into direct, visceral experiencing of previously non-conscious emotional themes, impulses, and memories is termed unlocking the unconscious. Once in awareness and faced and felt, as well as being well understood cognitively, these core emotional disturbances prove to be fully resolvable. The goal of ISTDP is “total resolution of intrapsychic conflicts, leading to emotional freedom and fulfillment of full human potential” (Coughlin Della Selva, 2006, p. 544). Such total elimination of specific symptoms and the distress-laden states that ISTDP terms “intrapsychic conflicts” corresponds to transformational change in this book's memory reconsolidation framework. We show in the following case example of ISTDP that when such total resolution occurs, the memory reconsolidation process of unlearning is detectable immediately preceding the breakthrough. To avoid possible confusion, we note that our memory reconsolidation framework does not share the psychodynamic framework's conceptualization of internal “conflicts” as a general description of the core phenomenology driving symptom production, because the existence of emotional learnings, or schemas, that compel production of symptoms adaptively (to prevent worse sufferings, for example) does not in itself involve any conflict, even if collateral conflicts exist between such schemas and other regions of memory and personality. Another difference in terminology is ISTDP's use of “patient” to refer to the person engaged in psychotherapy, whereas we use “client” throughout this book to avoid giving implicit or explicit support to the medical model of psychotherapy.

DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-14

Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy 213 However, for this case example of ISTDP, “patient” is used in order to accurately represent both ISTDP and the particular case examined here. A central conceptualization of ISTDP is that therapy patients keep their unresolved emotional disturbances thoroughly outside of awareness using particular tactics—called “defenses” in ISTDP and throughout the psychodynamic tradition—and feel anxiety when this material comes too near to awareness. In fact, “presenting problems are viewed as the inevitable result of the patient's excessive reliance on defenses against anxiety-provoking feelings, wishes, and impulses” (Coughlin & Katzman, 2013, p. 487). ISTDP terms “resistance” the very existence of these awareness avoidance tactics, or defenses, at the start of therapy. From the first session, ISTDP guides the therapist to detect and directly comment on the patient's anxiety and avoidances, first inviting recognition of them and then inviting the patient to allow limited, tolerable experiences of the normally avoided feelings, emotions, impulses, and memories. ISTDP methodology includes a careful, systematic assessment of each patient's tolerance level for this process, and the methodology has three different modes of implementation for patients at widely different levels of ego strength (Abbass & Town, 2013). The therapist's repeating challenge of avoidance finally tends to evoke anger at the therapist, who invites open, unrestrained expression of this anger. The ensuing, deepening emotional process brings the emotional surfacing and open expression of core underlying emotional distress persisting from earlier life experiences, usually childhood sufferings of mistreatment by parents. This is the unlocking of the unconscious sought in ISTDP. It is at this point in the process that the true core of the enduring emotional distress is recognized, faced, consciously processed for the first time, and brought to resolution. ISTDP is centered on a particular model of the emotional processes operating in that core of enduring distress. A major part of that model has been spelled out succinctly by Coughlin and Katzman (2013, p. 487): “When the desire to love and be loved is thwarted or neglected, deep pain and grief are experienced. Rage toward the loved one who is causing that pain is also activated. The experience of such intense and often murderous rage toward a loved and needed parent gives rise to anxiety and guilt that is often overwhelming and is rendered unconscious.” Similarly, Abbass and Town (2021, p. 400) state, “Intense early attachment trauma cause high levels of unresolved grief, rage and guilt about rage… that manifests as a firm belief that they are not deserving of positive experiences and should accept negative treatment from others.” Certainly that particular configuration of core emotional disturbance, with intense but suppressed rage accompanied by guilt and self-punishing, is present in some subset of therapy seekers. Whether that subset is large or small, whether ISTDP practitioners are trained to consider and recognize the genuine absence of suppressed rage, and how ISTDP is carried out for other configurations of core distress are interesting and important questions.

214 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change Our ISTDP case example is from Coughlin Della Selva (2006), who was the therapist and who titles this case “The Good Girl” in an article titled, “Emotional processing in the treatment of psychosomatic disorders.” Clinical psychologist Patricia Coughlin trained with Davanloo and is an internationally eminent ISTDP practitioner, teacher, and author (e.g., Coughlin, 2017). We encourage the reader to refer to the original article for the author's account of ISTDP's concepts and methods and how they were implemented in this case. Here we reproduce only the article's account of what happened in the room in various therapy sessions, plus our own commentaries indicating fulfillment of the steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP).1 Our purpose in mapping an ISTDP session onto the TRP is to expand our demonstration of the universality of the TRP as being a unifying core process responsible for transformational change produced by any methods of psychotherapy. All sessions were recorded. In her first session, a 34-year-old single professional woman defined her main focus as her chronic difficulties in developing a full, lasting relationship with a man, and added that she had gone into depression each time a relationship had ended. Her father died when she was 14, and her first depression occurred one year later. She also began to suffer episodes of ulcerative colitis following the ending of a couple relationship. Hospitalization was necessary on several occasions, and she was now on high levels of steroids, but even with this medication, she was experiencing both urgency and frequency, with seven to eight bloody stools each day, and was now routinely wearing “adult diapers.” Her physician had recently told her that surgical removal of her colon might be the only possible solution. In the hope of avoiding such a fate, she decided to pursue psychotherapy, against the doctor's strong objections. TRP Step A, symptom identification, was well fulfilled by these descriptions of short-lived couple relationships accompanied by depression and ulcerative colitis. Coughlin notes that “the patient had received two previous psychodynamic therapies (4 years each), which were helpful at the time, but resulted in no lasting change in symptoms or character.” The first session included the following interaction after the initial description of the repeated loss of couple relationships (T = therapist, P = patient): T: You made an interesting comment—that today you're in a good mood but that you frequently get sad. I noticed, and wondered if you were aware of it, that as you talked about the dissatisfaction with your life, you had a smile on your face. P: That kind of incongruity—yes. T: So, what's the smile then? P: The smile is probably just my discomfort with really facing up to the true anguish and true pain it causes me, and I know I tend to put the best face on everything, including, quite literally, my face.

Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy 215 T: So you have some awareness that you tend to cover up these deep, painful feelings. P: That's right; I think that's right. That chronic pattern of avoiding the experience of emotions of distress is an important addition to the symptom picture, Step A, and is the symptom that the therapist is particularly watching for and responding to as an ISTDP practitioner. The therapist was now considering the strong possibility that pervasive, longterm suppression of emotional distress was a major contributing cause of the other symptoms. She subsequently responded to every opportunity to address any affect avoidance when it appeared, such as this instance in one of the early sessions: P: I feel drained. I feel sobered. I'm also aware of how I feel about you and our interactive style. It's a complicated double feeling. On the one hand, I'm finding it useful; on the other hand, I'm feeling irritated. (She then goes on at some length justifying her irritation.) T: So there's some irritation toward me. How do you experience this irritation inside? P: Why can't I say what I feel towards you? You're not telling me about your life. It doesn't matter that rationally I know you're not here to tell me about you and, frankly, I don't care, but I have this resentment that it's my pain that's being unearthed and it's me and my complexity—me that's being commented on—feeling like an object in some way. You're drawing attention to certain things I do that I might not be conscious of—I recognize that rationally. I'm just telling you, viscerally— T: But you don't like it. P: I don't like it. Then I ask myself why. T: Well, let's not go to why yet, because you have a tendency to go to your thoughts. I asked you how you experienced your irritation and you tell me about your thoughts—not the feeling. P: Why is that not the feeling? T: Those are thoughts. P: How would I experience the feeling? Maybe I don't experience the feeling! To me, that thought is the feeling! As noted, a major feature of ISTDP methodology is the therapist's focus on calling attention to the patient's “defenses”—the tactics that avoid the direct experience or expression of core feelings and emotions—and then prompting experiments in not resorting to those tactics but rather actually having the avoided experience and expression of feelings and emotion. As viewed from the perspective of the TRP, avoidance (suppression) of core feelings and emotion is a primary identified symptom (Step A). ISTDP methodology does not then

216 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change aim directly for TRP Step B, discovering the specific underlying schema (emotional learning, mental model, implicit knowledge) requiring that suppression of

affect. Rather, the therapist guides the (initially very limited and therefore tolerable) suspension of the affect-avoiding tactics, and, in doing so, communicates in many ways that the patient's feelings and emotions are valid and that experiencing and expressing them here in the session is welcome and healthy. That is a fulfillment of TRP Step C, the patient's accessing of an experience that will serve to contradict and disconfirm what is known and expected according to the target emotional learning. The specific content of the patient's underlying schema that self-protectively requires affect suppression is still unknown, but it certainly includes an expectation that actually feeling and expressing her true feelings and emotions will bring intense suffering of some kind, which is why suppressing them is urgently necessary. That expectation is reactivated during this interaction, and yet what the patient is perceiving is the therapist's accepting, nonjudgmental attitude toward her feelings and emotions, which stands in contradiction of the schema. The patient is not only encountering the idea that her feelings and emotions are valid and acceptable, but also, more importantly, is having actual interpersonal experiences of that validation and welcoming of her feelings and emotions, and is having those repeated experiences while the opposite expectation is reactivated. That is the all-important juxtaposition experience that is created by TRP Steps 1 and 2, and the repetition of which is Step 3. Thus already the therapeutic process is fulfilling TRP Steps 1, 2, and 3, the transformation sequence necessary for the unlearning and nullification of an emotional schema. However, what is lacking at this early point is specificity of disconfirmation of an affect-disallowing schema, due to not yet accessing such a schema and making it explicit (TRP Step B). In TRP Step 1, the target schema needs to be not only reactivated, but also, based on Step B, reactivated with metacognitive recognition of the schema's specific mental model and expectation. For example, suppose there exists a schema which, put into words, is “If I feel and express negative feelings of any kind, I will be utterly disgusting and unlovable to Mom and Dad, and that's terrifying, so I've got to keep my feelings blocked and buried.” The truth and the emotional realness of that frightening expectation are not disconfirmed, and the schema is not depotentiated, by experiencing a therapist's genuine validation and welcoming of her negative feelings and emotions. And even with explicit awareness of that schema while it is reactivated, something more than a therapist's acceptance of all affect is likely to be needed in order for that schema to lose its power to keep affect suppressed, and that something more can reliably be found only on the basis of knowing the schema's specific content. As this ISTDP case develops, we will see how its methodology does finally result in emergence of the schema's specific content, allowing specificity of disconfirmation and the fulfillment of TRP Steps 1, 2, and 3, as the brain requires for schema nullification to occur.

Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy 217 The therapist continued to use events during and between sessions to prompt awareness of suppressing emotional responses and of the directly resulting flareups of depression and intestinal symptoms. This process involved a gradual increase in the intensity of emotion that was unsuppressed and directly felt. It also kept repeating the juxtaposition experience, described above, in the therapeutic relationship. That work is well illustrated by this transcript from the tenth session: P: Several months ago I dealt with someone at work on the phone with whom I had gotten very upset. As the result of his questioning of me, I also felt a lot of self-doubt. Yesterday I had an experience with an agent on the phone in which I knew I was completely right, but he started attacking me and I was so overwhelmed by it that I short-circuited. I get so—I get depressed. I was depressed all day. I feel blocked. Now I understand the problem, but I am blocked. T: It sounds like you haven't let yourself—even after you got off the phone with him—experience the anger with him. You internalize it and become depressed. P: I also felt it in my stomach—well, maybe not my stomach but my intestines get clenched and then I notice I have to go to the bathroom more often when something like that happens. T: So do you want to focus on the anger toward him? P: Yeah, well, I was talking to a friend, who said just imagine what you want to do to him. Like she suggested I imagine hitting him with a baseball bat, so I imagined like really pounding this guy—not just pounding him but visualizing him up against the wall. T: Where? P: Hitting him in his stomach! That's interesting. With a baseball bat—

pushing it into him. But it coexists with a fear of my own weakness; I mean—could I really kill him? Am I strong enough? T: But the impulse is—? P: The impulse is to kill him, but I think part of the reason— T: If you don't go to why. P: Yeah. Now tears are coming and this is what happened all day yesterday. T: That's the way you avoid the experience of the anger. P: That's what I tell myself. T: This man means nothing to you. P: You're right. No, he really doesn't, other than in this one interaction… I do feel like pounding him on his shoulders. Then I would feel like punching him in the face—and you're right—I do feel like being rid of him completely because then I won't have to deal with him anymore. T: How do you get rid of him? P: And then, if he's not dead, I shoot him. I want to get rid of him but if I'm not done with him, then I shoot him.

218 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change T: P: T: P: T: P: T: P: T: P:

So he's down? Yes—he's on the floor and then I want to squash his face. (smiling) Even this you do nicely. But it's a vicious attack. You mean this is vicious? What do you mean I'm doing it in a nice way? When you went to the kicking you were smiling. It's that I really felt better. I'm smiling, not because I'm being gracious about it, but because it feels good. I feel better. I'm not being gracious, but I smile because I realize I feel better. Enjoyment, actually. Seeing him on the floor and you stamping his face. He's dead. Can you describe what he looks like? Actually, his head is tilted to one side and his eyes are closed. He's just gone. But, you know, this must have something to do with my family because, you're right, I don't care about this guy, but I start to think about a member of my family, like my brother, being gone. It reminds me— Your brother comes to mind.

In a session months later, she focused on her rage toward a boyfriend who broke up with her years ago. That breakup plunged her into feeling seriously depressed and suicidal and into having her first acute attack of ulcerative colitis, which required hospitalization and resulted in a rapid 20-pound weight loss. P: Hollow and depressed, yes. You know, I almost had a flash of being able to hurt him. I feel like kicking him in the balls—that wouldn't kill him, but I really want to hurt him. Just picturing that. I mean, I don't know if this is still avoiding killing him but—it would just hurt him and then leave, you know. T: So you want to do what? P: I kick him and I feel that I would kill him. Then I think of his neck; I could have hurt him. I feel like hitting his face. I would pound on his face and actually his face was weak to begin with because he was in a car accident and they had to put it back together, so I really could have hurt him. I would have killed him. I would pound on his head. I'm trying to picture it and then, the phrase that comes to mind is “shit out of him.” I could have destroyed him but instead— T: You keep going like this with your hand, so you have an image? P: No. I avoid it. I hark back to when I thought of suicide and imagined slashing my neck. T: So you wanted to do that. P: When I was 25 and thinking about dying (after the breakup), I wanted to die and I wanted to take a knife to my neck. But I don't explicitly— T: But you didn't face that's what you wanted to do to him! P: Yeah. I have a vivid picture of him. I imagine putting it right down to his solar plexus—right where I feel such tremendous hollowness when I left

Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy 219 the hotel. When I think of leaving that hotel and driving off alone, I can actually imagine going straight down into his center. T: Then what? P: He's dead—real dead—I'm not smiling to avoid it but I feel happy. At the first moment, I feel glad, before I face his dad, who I love. I don't go right away to feeling horrible and guilty. I feel happy. It's one big—actually, with him, I could have done it. Even though I have terrible upper body strength, in that moment, I was so furious! In that session, the patient's greatly increased capacity for feeling rather than suppressing negative affect allowed her to feel and imaginally enact her murderous rage toward the man who rejected her. Her original response to his

rejection—helpless victimhood with emotional and physiological collapse— has changed into a state of aggressive empowerment energized by her rage. Certainly that is a significant therapeutic advance for her. And yet, the therapeutic process still has not revealed and disconfirmed any specific underlying schema requiring affect suppression, so the dandelion root could remain intact at this point, even though this particular visible dandelion flower has been plucked. In a subsequent session, however, the root material emerged powerfully. The session began with the patient saying she'd had a fantasy on the way to the office that she would arrive having had an accident with diarrhea (a frequent concern in managing her ulcerative colitis). She had imagined that the therapist would be disgusted with her, fly into a rage, and push her out of the office. The therapist then utilized this transference process by inviting expression of affect directly toward the therapist. T: P: T: P: T: P: T: P:

Again, let's deal with it as it's occurring here with me. Uncontrollable rage. That I would be in an uncontrollable rage? I tell you to get out of here. That I deserve to die. As you speak, though, I don't feel like crying. I feel angry and I feel like striking back. I'm more in touch with it. I would fight you back. This is progress. I don't feel like crying. I would fight back. How? If you were pushing me, I would push you back. And I don't think it's at all clear, if you were in a rage and I'm in a rage, who would win. How do you see it, because you're saying this will be hand-to-hand combat? I'm not going to back down. We're going to get into it. We're going to get into it and have a fight. I don't think it's by any means clear who would win if you're in a rage and I'm in a rage. I push you and you push me back. When I look at you now I know reason would prevail, and I see sympathy in your eyes, but in my mind, in this fantasy—it's my mother. She's fierce. I just feel like hitting her back.

220 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change The previous expectations of the therapist's rejecting responses had arisen from non-conscious emotional memory of mother's rejecting responses, but then, when the therapist's actual demeanor happened to differ too greatly from mother's (“I see sympathy in your eyes”), the projection became nonviable and mother's image appeared, revealing the true target of the patient's rage and fighting spirit. This emergence into awareness, via the patient's open expression of her transference reaction, of her core material of emotional distress is the moment of the unlocking of the unconscious in ISTDP terminology. In her ensuing responses to her mother, the learned emotional necessity of affect suppression— the underlying schema adaptively requiring affect suppression—finally comes into awareness, fulfilling TRP Step B: T: Where do you see this happening? P: It's funny, you know, I go back to the potty scene (clearly relevant to her bowel disease, but not described in the original article), where for some reason the kitchen is shadowy. It's in that long, narrow kitchen. I don't picture myself a 3-year-old, cowering. I picture myself as an adult, pushing her away. How would she react? I think she'd hit me back. She'd hit me back. My mother is tough. T: This would be hand-to-hand combat. P: It is hand-to-hand combat. It's not a gun or the knife. I want to strangle my mother. I want to kill my mother. I still want to say, they don't really know about ulcerative colitis, but, all this “Control yourself!”—I can't stand it! With her last few words, “all this 'Control yourself!'—I can't stand it!”, the patient has experientially accessed and explicitly recognized and revealed part of a potent emotional schema that requires her to suppress her feelings and emotions. It is a schema consisting of her childhood knowledge of her mother's terms of attachment (meaning, as discussed at length in Chapter 5, parents' requirements and rules that the child must meet in order to be acceptable and avoid rejection, abandonment, shaming, and/or abuse). The patient's deep, urgent emotional learning that she must obey mother's demand, “Control yourself!”, as a core condition for being acceptable to mother, is at the root of her suppression of

affect and probably other forms of self-containment as well. As a result of consistently receiving the therapist's permission and encouragement to feel and express her anger in response to mistreatment, the patient has finally arrived here at feeling her anger at her mother for prohibiting her natural self-expression. In these moments she is experiencing conscious awareness of (a) mother's perpetual demand, “Control yourself!”, (b) the intense, lifelong suffering this demand has caused her, (c) her own response of obedience to that demand, and (d) the full force of her angry protest against mother for imposing this on her, which brings with it (e) recognition that she is now free to stop trying to comply with mother's requirements. A conscious juxtaposition experience is

Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy 221 occurring, consisting of TRP Steps 1 and 2: The dependent child's schema of urgency of compliant self-suppression is being experienced concurrently with a disconfirmation of that schema, namely, an empowered adult readiness for autonomy and freedom of self-expression. The immediate result is the unlearning and depotentiation of the childhood attachment schema, a transformational change. In declaring “I can't stand it!”, she has arrived at the end of feeling she has to comply with mother's requirements. Avoiding the long-dreaded consequences of not controlling herself to appease mother is no longer worth the suffering that this self-suppression causes her. T: Do you want to let her know this before you kill her, what this is all about? P: No, with you I wanted to explain but now, I don't want to talk. I feel angry and I don't feel like explaining myself. I'm sick and tired of her being the only one who's entitled to feelings, which is how it was. I want her out! I actually want her out. Her total disinterest in justifying herself to mother is a strong confirmation that this is a shift into authentic adult autonomy and differentiation, not mere rebellion. Process markers such as this contribute to TRP Step V, verification of schema nullification. Also, “her being the only one who's entitled to feelings” is important further specificity and recognition of both mother's terms of attachment and the patient's schema compelling self-suppression all her life until this session. T: She's on the floor and you're kicking her, but then you also said to go for her neck? P: Take my hands and I just squeeze the life right out of her. I feel so strong lately. I had to shovel snow and I felt strong. I am squeezing her neck. I'm in a blind rage and I want her out—just squeezing the life right out of her. T: So you imagine choking her or you break her neck? P: I choke the life out of her until—I feel that same insensible feeling I felt with that boyfriend. I feel very coldblooded. I focus on her eyes and I don't know how I'd know, but I would know. I would go for her neck, but I must be repressing, because I feel it in my neck. I'm still holding something back. I still feel as though I'm choking. T: What does it feel like? P: I'm still holding my anger back. Ugh! I would scream. It would be—ugh!— it would be murderous, it would be animalistic—everything she hates. Everything she hates, it would be. I feel so much better now. It's that same animalistic pleasure I had with my boyfriend. You're right; I'm not just sweetness and light. After it's done, I don't start crying right away. That's actually the most painful revelation of this process—is not that I go to tears, but that this is what I want. Mission accomplished! I feel proud of myself.

222 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change T: You feel strong and capable and now you've gotten rid of this pain in the neck and you wiped her out. P: I still feel angry and I don't know why. It's like killing her isn't enough. I still feel angry. I still feel in a murderous rage. Maybe killing her isn't enough. Maybe it's the rest of my family. I don't know. T: To kill her isn't enough. P: It's to exorcize these rules. I mean, they are just impossible. This again is her conscious, experiential recognition that it is her own acceptance of and compliance with mother's “rules” (terms of attachment) that are keeping her in an emotional straightjacket. “Everything she hates” is yet further specificity and conscious recognition of the learned emotional necessity (the coherence) requiring self-suppression: She would be hated by her own mother for having her own emotions, which only mother is allowed to have, so it has been urgent to keep her own emotions suppressed and hidden. That is the young-ego-state schema in which her compliance with mother's “rules” is held to be absolutely necessary. She has now brought that coherent schema into the explicit awareness of an adult ego-state that has learned, through the therapeutic process, that her emotions are valid and acceptable to feel and express. She again is experiencing, even more fully than before, concurrent awareness of both her emotion-disallowing schema and its disconfirmation by her adult authority to stop complying and free herself. That repeats the juxtaposition experience, which is TRP Step 3. The therapist now supports both the emerging specificity and the emerging autonomy: T: So what are these rules you want to break? Like with your boyfriend, it's not enough to kill him, but then you had a sexual impulse—“Oh, sex with his dead body”—all those rules you want to break. What would make it more horrible? P: To decapitate her. I don't know if it's these tabloids, but it's real. If I'm in a blind rage, I'd slice her neck. I want her out. I think I'd actually incinerate her. Actually get her out. What do they do to chop things up—I want her ground up. I want her gone. Even when I picture her gone, I feel this rage. Ugh! It's still not enough. Something is still buried because I still feel like screaming and I don't know why. Maybe it's that I want to tell her—I don't know what this is—but I still long for my mother. I want my mother. I don't know, because I also love my mother. I don't know if it's tears or anger—maybe what it is, but I don't want to have to kill my mother in order to live! (crying heavily now) That's not what I want. I want my mother to love me. T: Tell her. P: I want you to love me. I don't want to have to kill you, but I'm sick of all these hoops—always—always!! T: So much got in the way. You want rid of that part of her and to gain access to her—to be loved by her and to feel close. There's a lot of emotion.

Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy 223 P: I feel like, I have so much fun with you. You're great. It's also, “Why do you feel so bad about yourself?” T: You want her to put aside all the self-loathing? P: That's what got in the way. My mother, I mean, Patricia, my mother is extra-

ordinary. And, when I think of the shit that she went through. (weeping) My mother, I wish, I wish you could have been happy. I wish you weren't treated so badly. (weeping) When you tell me those stories—I just feel so bad you had to go through all that. It is clear in the emotional process that unfolded that the full releasing of her suppressed rage was necessary for arriving at the true core of the patient's distress, her grief for herself and for her mother. This spontaneous emergence of both her process of grieving over not receiving loving mothering and her heartfelt compassion for her mother would be very unlikely to happen if the terms-ofattachment schema still had significant emotional power, so these clear, strong, tender feelings are further indications that depotentiation of that schema has occurred, for a fundamental resolution of her autonomy struggle and her insecure attachment, producing a liberating shift into individuated adulthood. Of course, the most decisive markers of transformational change, fulfilling TRP Step V, would be the patient's subsequent, explicit, ongoing reports that she remains completely free of that schema's symptomatic manifestations, namely affect avoidance, depression (her collapse into disempowerment and victimization, which has indeed kept her self-expression very well controlled), and ulcerative colitis due to somatization driven by suppression of intense rage. Her main presenting problem, short-lived couple relationships, also very possibly had been caused to a significant degree by that schema's generalized expectation that “Control yourself!” is a rule she must obey for acceptance in any primary-bond relationship, causing emotional blockage (limiting her emotional and sexual responsiveness in her couple relationships) plus various other forms of self-inhibition. Therefore the persistence or disappearance of her couple relationship problem is also relevant to verification of schema nullification. That full array of markers of transformational change was confirmed by the therapist's follow-up after a course of therapy that consisted of 60 sessions: At her 3-, 8-, and 14-year follow-up visits, all therapeutic gains were maintained. Her disease was in complete remission. Results of colonoscopies confirmed that there was no active disease present in her intestine. Of great significance she weathered three major losses without any recurrence of depression or bowel disease. Her stepfather, father-in-law, and younger sister all died during the follow-up period. The death of her younger sister was sudden and traumatic. She reported some guilt and suffering after this death. She had one session at that time and she allowed herself to acknowledge and experience her competitive feelings with her

224 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change sister, her death wishes toward her, and her guilt about them. Transcript of that session provides evidence of her healthy mourning. (Coughlin Della Selva, 2006, p. 549) P: That's no more. That's not a problem anymore. In fact, I have a real sense of peace about it. No matter how it comes up, I always end up with a feeling of peace. T: So, not only are you no longer punishing yourself, but you end up with a feeling of peace about your sister. P: I also realize, in a deep way, that even though she is dead, my relationship with her goes on for the rest of my time on Earth. I can have all kinds of feelings come up now about her—I can love her, hate her—and, if she had lived, it would have been a very rich relationship. The patient had married, and she described this relationship: P: I feel very safe with him. There's a lot to be said for being loved and having an optimistic temperament, which he does. Every day I am grateful. The way I really feel is, I've had enough loss and I celebrate what I have. T: The important thing is that you have the closeness now. P: Oh yes, every single day, because, you know, people say to me, “Oh, you're newlyweds,” but still, every day, I feel so happy. If I wake in the middle of the night, it just feels so beautiful and I come into the office saying, “I'm so happy.” I treasure him and I feel treasured, so I feel that, in spite of the problems I told you about, I am so happy (sitting forward) that I feel my life has been changed. I love him and I feel loved. Her ability to deal appropriately with conflict and anger became apparent in another part of the session: P: Yes, I did. I got very angry at him. T: How did you deal with that? P: At first I was so angry I left the house. When I calmed down, I came back and spoke to him about it. I said, “This is a betrayal. I love you but I won't have this in my life. You must decide. If you want to be with me, you've got to quit drinking. I will support you in every way possible, but I won't do it for you.” She reported also about her physical health: P: I must tell you, symptomatically, I feel fabulous. Ah, I don't, it just doesn't go to my stomach anymore, I mean— T: So there's a feeling of vitality. You don't feel sick anymore.

Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy 225 P: Oh, I feel great. T: Really well. Energetic? P: I'm energetic. I don't know where that anxiety goes anymore—well, it doesn't go somatically, I guess I just get it out now, directly. Now, most of the time I just feel relaxed and I savor, just savor feeling so good—it's like an animal pleasure. Just to feel. T: Just feeling alive. In this representative case of ISTDP, the steps of the therapeutic reconsolidation process were fulfilled in the order A–C–1–2–3–B–C–1–2–3–V. In other words, the methodology carried out the unlearning sequence first without bringing any underlying target learning into explicit awareness (A–C–1–2–3) and then, after explicit awareness had been achieved, again the unlearning sequence was carried out (B–C–1–2–3), producing transformational change.

Note 1 For a concise list of the component steps of the TRP, see Table 2.1 on p. 34 or p. 144 in Chapter 6. Fully understanding this and other chapters in Part 2 of this book requires first reading Chapters 1, 2, and 3, which explain transformational therapeutic change and how it occurs through a particular recruitment of the brain's mechanism of memory reconsolidation, accomplished by the therapeutic reconsolidation process or TRP. Familiarity with the TRP is assumed. Chapter 2 defines and explains the TRP at length, including the extensive empirical research on which it is directly based. Chapter 3 demonstrates the focused facilitation of the TRP in psychotherapy sessions.

13 Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy: Ayahuasca Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic, and Laurel Hulley

Psychedelic experiences can result in potent therapeutic change when induced within a program of psychotherapy that skillfully provides preparation of mindset, an environment of accompaniment, safety, and supportiveness during the experience(s), and a subsequent process of review, reflection, and integration (as reviewed by, for example, Carhart-Harris & Goodwin, 2017; Hartogsohn, 2018; Healy et al., 2021). The question we begin to address here is whether psychedelic experiences that produce transformational change—the complete and lasting elimination of a problematic state of mind and/or behavior—do so by creating experiences that fulfill the therapeutic reconsolidation process (TRP).1 We examine a well-documented case of therapeutically facilitated ayahuasca experiences that ended a 29-year-old woman's intensely distressed condition of complicated bereavement and depression stemming from her mother's suicide (González et al., 2022). It is apparent in the client's account of her ayahuasca experiences that the critical, specific steps of the TRP occurred repeatedly. The recipe for ayahuasca, an Amazonian brew, always entails boiling stems of the vine Banisteriopsis caapi (containing tetrahydroharmine, harmaline, and harmine). A plant that provides N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) is usually added, in this case leaves of the shrub Psychotria viridis. Those are the main ingredients. Ayahuasca has long been used as potent holistic medicine in more than seventy different indigenous communities. Its use by the psychotherapy field has been demonstrated for depression (Osório et al., 2015; Palhano-Fontes et al., 2019), addiction (Thomas et al., 2013), and grief following the death of a loved one (González et al., 2020, 2022). Maia et al. (2023) provide a comprehensive review of studies of ayahuasca's therapeutic effects, and González et al. (2020) provide a brief review of research of its neurological and psychological effects. The case study presented by González et al. (2022) and largely reproduced below was part of a larger study in which the principal investigator was Barcelona psychologist Débora González. She and co-author Marc Aixalà were co-therapists in this case. The ayahuasca-assisted therapy program consisted of 14 weekly individual psychotherapy sessions and three ayahuasca experiences DOI: 10.4324/9781003231431-15

Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy: Ayahuasca 227 conducted in a private clinic in Barcelona, Spain. The ayahuasca sessions were carried out in groups of seven participants who ingested ayahuasca, supported by four facilitators who interacted only in response to communications from the participants. All seven participants had problems of grief that they wanted the ayahuasca experiences to help resolve. For details of procedure in the hours before and after each 4-hour ayahuasca experience, see González et al. (2022). During the hour before drinking the brew, participants engaged in various techniques that fostered communication among them and anchored their mindsets in a focus on grieving. Participants had their own mattresses on which to sit or lie down, and each was blindfolded to reduce external distraction and maximize an internal focus of attention. Three to five days after each ayahuasca experience, each participant met with a therapist individually for a 90-minute process of narrative reconstruction of the ayahuasca experience using the Restorative Retelling technique (González et al., 2022; Neimeyer & Rynearson, 2022). In this session, the therapist sensitively facilitated not only the client's integration of all significant aspects of the experience, but also, and especially, a reflective process of meaning-making intended to therapeutically evolve the client's beliefs and schemas. This facilitation is apparent in the transcript below. The client here, whom we call “Alba,” had lived her whole life believing the story her family told her about how her mother died in an accident when she was 4 years old and her little brother was 2. Then, shortly before Alba arranged for ayahuasca-assisted therapy, her aunt confessed to her what had actually happened: Her mother was home with Alba and her brother when she took her own life by jumping from a balcony. The two children were not present in the room when their mother jumped and as adults have hardly any memory of her. In response to learning the truth of how her mother died, Alba felt she had been profoundly cheated throughout her life, especially by her father, and felt overwhelming feelings of grief as well as rejection of her family. She also said she was now having trouble moving her life forward because of feeling intense longing for her mother and a family she could trust. She scored 51 on the Inventory of Complicated Grief (ICG), where a score over 30 indicates a problem of complicated grief, with a maximum possible score of 76 (Prigerson et al., 1995). On a separate measure, she also had a high score for depression. The effects of Alba's first two ayahuasca sessions are described by González et al. (2022, p. 4) as follows: “The psychological content that emerged during the first ayahuasca session in this case study was not directly related to the grief process. Immediately following the second ayahuasca session, \[Alba\] unexpectedly relived the traumatic event of her mother's suicide, visualizing details of the scene she never witnessed.” It was her third ayahuasca session and its Restorative Retelling session that resulted in lasting, liberating change. In the latter session, Alba “was invited to close her eyes and remember what happened during the ayahuasca ceremony.

228 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change She was asked to identify the most emotionally charged fragments of her experience and to organize them into a coherent narrative. When she felt ready, she began to retell the experience in detail…” (González et al., 2022, p. 5). Reproduced below is the entirety of Alba's account as reported by González et al. (2022, pp. 5–7). Italic comments in brackets are also from the article, with minor paraphrasing. Each inserted TRP COMMENTARY has been added by this book's authors for the purpose of pointing out experiences directly contributing to TRP fulfillment. Our commentaries are situated within the subjective realness of Alba's perceptions and experiences. Alba first explains that she went “to another place, suddenly with a jolt” and began to have “loads of visions: of animals, shapes, colors, junk,” with feelings of a “panic I'd never felt before, like in a dream.” She was afraid of “losing control” and “being alone.” She felt that in this other place “nobody could help me.” Cl: They were like a figure, one on top of the other… they turned into a totem pole, the totem was a mask, with like, aggressive faces… like sneering demons sticking out their tongues, long tongues. They were in front of me, they came for me and grabbed at me… it was like… fuck! Where the hell has this come from? It's so real!… This actually exists in some place, and I'm in that place… Th: Do these figures mean anything to you? Cl: The figures? (She shakes her head.) … No… well, yeah, they do kinda, but I would not know how to describe it. Th: What do these figures suggest to you? Cl: I do not know if I've been conditioned from seeing Mexican art… but now that I think about it, it was like they were guardians, entities, and spirits. Th: Why do you think they appeared at that moment? What role could they be playing? Cl: …They were there to make me understand… or to make me aware of other states. They appeared in order to show themselves. So that I could “see.” \[The therapist's questions prompted Alba to engage in metacognitive reflection, and she recognized significant positive meaning in experiences that were panic-inducing and did not previously make sense. Alba's account then continues with an important transition.\] In all that mad situation, since I saw that no one on earth could help me, I asked for my mother. \[Next, she describes how, as she was lying on her mattress during the session, she felt her mother sitting on the edge of the mattress beside her, and she began to feel she was in a\] more defined place, with an aura that was, like… heavenly! Like, transparent, as if I was surrounded by a kind of fabric, like a sheen… and this gave me a lot of calm. And I remember that there was also a guide, like an entity or something… that gave me the feeling of this… “Everything,” you know? Th: This “Everything”?

Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy: Ayahuasca 229 Cl: Well, I got the feeling that it's what people call God, you know? A god… like God is Everything. It was an energy that was like, unearthly. And it… this energy brought me to my mom. It had a really strong bond with my mother. Th: How do you feel when you are with your mom and this energy that's “like God”? Cl: Well, the way I feel it, it's how love is unconditional, but love like… (she hunches over and thinks) like love is the be-all and end-all. It's the meaning of life. TRP COMMENTARY: We have to take into account here that Alba is finding words to indicate an ineffable experience, so her words are only a hint of her experience. Even so, it is clear that in response to asking for her mother, Alba not only experienced being visited by her, she also was shown her mother as being closely accompanied by an all-loving God through “a really strong bond.” Alba and her mother are together in the Allness of this loving God. This view of her mother constituted powerful contradictory knowledge (TRP Step C) in relation to any of Alba's prior mental models of her mother as unloving, bad, uncaring, abandoning, and unreachable. Implicit juxtaposition experiences2 (TRP Steps 1–2–3) are occurring between this extraordinary contradictory knowledge and all such constructs representing her mother, disconfirming and nullifying those constructs. Our point here is that lasting therapeutic change occurs not merely by having strongly “positive” experiences, but by having experiences that specifically disconfirm and nullify the mental models maintaining symptoms. Cl: \[Alba then describes how her mother went in and out of the scenes, showing different situations to her. In the next scene, mother and daughter are watching a family meal from outside. During this scene, the mother communicates a need to Alba\] to have a kind of alliance with me, admitting that things had been tough \[family dynamics after the suicide\], that she understood that my relationship with my father was difficult… with my uncles… but that I had to understand it all from their point of view. Th: She wanted you to understand your family? Cl: Yeah, that she'd left behind a really difficult situation for everyone… and that they all had their own crosses to bear, their own stuff to deal with and they could not have dealt with things any differently, same as I could not have… She wanted me to see beyond the surface of things. Th: So that dialog with your mother allowed you to understand your relatives from another point of view? Cl: Yeah. Th: And what did you feel, being able to understand them differently? Cl: I felt, like, unconditional love. And at the same time I felt so sorry, like, a deep sense of pity… because they had lost a sister, and the way they

230 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change lost her… and my father was her partner. Perhaps my father is a waste of space, who's maybe never done anything right, never helped me to get better, but that's not the whole picture. TRP COMMENTARY: One of the necessary ingredients for true repair after causing intense suffering is for the offender to express sincere, sympathetic, regretful understanding of the suffering that was caused. That provides the harmed person with both accountability and a knowledge that there exists heartfelt caring at the core of the relationship. Alba has indicated receiving expressions of that from her mother, and at her mother's initiative. Once again, that experience functions as disconfirmation of mental models of mother as being entirely uncaring, indifferent, selfish, and disengaged. Evidently Alba's need for such repair from her mother was met sufficiently—at least for the moment—because then Alba was receptive to a very different message that came next from her mother, guiding Alba to reconsider her experience of the family by stepping out of herself to look closely at each family member's own subjective experience after the suicide. Alba's ability to engage deeply in this process certainly was facilitated by the experience of immersion in all-pervading divine love. With each compassionate recognition of a family member's own subjective state and viewpoint, Alba recognized their behavior as having a new and different meaning from the entirely negative meanings that she had previously been attributing in terms of her own unmet needs. Here again we see the accessing of contradictory knowings (TRP Step C) that then disconfirmed her negative mental models of family members through implicit juxtapositions with those negative models. That this liberating, transformational process was being actively guided by her mother is itself undoubtedly something precious for Alba—a profound experience of receiving wise, caring mentoring from her mother, which again serves as a disconfirmation of her mental model of her mother as utterly failing to be closely engaged and truly helpful. Cl: \[In the next scene revisited by Alba, she and her mother are meeting in private:\] She just broke down… she begged me for forgiveness, and she accepted responsibility for the way things had turned out. It was as if she had not been able to cure herself in life, she was never able to see what I was seeing… \[After the therapist digs a little into the meaning of this conversation, Alba explains:\] I've always had this need to have a talk with my mother that I could never have, and nobody could take her place. TRP COMMENTARY: Alba has now experienced receiving from her mother more of what creates deep repair: unrestrained feelings of anguish, remorse, and contrition, heartfelt requests for forgiveness, and total acceptance of responsibility for the sufferings caused. In fact, in Alba's account we see those crucial elements of repair in an ideal form and degree that is rare. An important aspect

Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy: Ayahuasca 231 of the repair achieved is the thorough disconfirmation and annulment of Alba's negative meanings and models of her mother (through additional implicit juxtaposition experiences, as described previously). Yet another potent schema that Alba has indicated she was harboring is her expectation that for the rest of her life she would be living in the painful distress of her greatest need being impossible to satisfy—her need for reparative reconnection with her mother. That kind of hopeless model of one's entire future is a potent generator of not only depression, but also collapsed motivation of the “why bother?” type, because no achievement could possibly make any difference at all toward fulfilling that greatest need. It is this dismal expectational schema that was generating Alba's symptoms of “having trouble moving her life forward because of feeling intense longing for her mother and a family she could trust”; and it is the profound disconfirmation and unlearning of this schema that ended those symptoms. Cl: Then I'm in another situation where I'm there, as if I'm her, in the hospital bed, and I'm not completely dead yet… I think she must've felt so bad in that moment. I do not know if it's just my projection because it's something I've thought about so many times… Th: …what exactly did you experience in that moment? Cl: I was lying on the bed like this (she lies down), and suddenly, I do not know how, I lifted my hands (she crosses her hands across her chest) … and in that moment… bam!… I experienced being in a coma. Then I got hit by this huge wave of sadness, that was the same sorrow that she was going through in that state, my mom. And then I became aware of, like, fuck, I've gone and thrown myself off the balcony, I've left my two children in the house, this has really happened, I'm here… and so much sorrow, so, so much sorrow (she buries her face in her hands). TRP COMMENTARY: This subjective inhabiting of her mother's private state of mind gives Alba an even more direct and convincing knowledge of her mother's intense caring and consideration toward her children—a profound contradiction and disconfirmation of any models of her mother as disengaged, uncaring, and indifferent to their suffering. Next, continuing her revisiting process, Alba describes becoming a participant in a new funeral for her mother, which is particularly meaningful to her because she was kept from attending the actual funeral. So, this again is a disconfirmation of what had seemed to be a hopelessly permanent deprivation. Cl: …and the funeral, well it's happy. I mean, like, not super happy… it's emotional. As if everything I was experiencing with all this energy (the “Everything” or “God”) was being projected onto all of us, and the family was soaking it all up, you know?… Th: What emotions were there?

232 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change Cl: A feeling of community… of being at peace with the process of death. Like, understanding that death has some kind of meaning. Th: What meaning does death have, for you? Cl: …That everything's not what it seems… that there are laws that move things that have a deeper consequence that we cannot see right now, and maybe we'll never see in this life. If we could see it in levels, like… this happens here, but also there (she gestures with raised hands) what's happening is something else. So then you say… ah, right! (death) is just another collateral damage, nothing more. But you see only someone who's sad, who's suffering, who leaves her kids in a flat, taking her own life… It's wild. TRP COMMENTARY: Alba's words only hint at the ineffable quality of her experience in the funeral scene, regarding her recognition that visible happenings have far more meaning and significance than is apparent. It is clear that what she experienced was a potent disconfirmation of her prior, all-negative meanings that she had been attributing to her mother's suicide. Those all-negative meanings, which, like her expectation of never getting reparative reconnection with her mother, had been generating a mood of depression and an absence of motivation, were unlearned and annulled through implicit juxtaposition experiences created by these lucid disconfirmations. Th: Okay…, thank you for sharing your experience. If you wish, you can open your eyes when you are ready. \[Allowing time for her to sit up and open her eyes.\] … How do you feel? Cl: (smiling) Good. The therapist now began the final phase of the Restorative Retelling process, in which the focus is on guiding metacognitive reflections on how the ayahuascainduced experiences impact “the schemas that the participant previously held regarding her mother, her relatives, the world, and herself.” The therapist was aware that that process of schema revision had already naturally begun during the retelling already completed. The aim now was to further facilitate the therapeutic revision of schemas to the maximum possible degree. Th: Now, let me ask you a few questions about your experience. Do you think that this experience has changed the impression you had about your mother in any way? Is there any kind of knowledge or information you have now, that you did not have before? Cl: Yes, the only thing is… the reality of everyday life makes you… (she sighs) I dunno. But it's definitely left its mark; something has changed. There's a bit of it that will not be the same as before, but I do not know if

Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy: Ayahuasca 233 it's specifically about how I see my mother… After the experience, I get the feeling that I even see her differently in the photos. Th: Differently? Can you tell me about those changes in the photos? Cl: It's still her, but her attitude has changed… she seems more calm, more serene… She had this dark, heavy energy before… but now it's like I look at the photo and I remember that second part (of the experience), that

language… then, I look at the photo in a different way, I explain it to myself differently, and I see her in a different way. TRP COMMENTARY: Alba's comments are confirming a fundamental revision of her mental model of her mother, from a person with “this dark, heavy energy” to someone “more calm, more serene.” We also know that she now perceives her mother as deeply caring and understanding toward her. These indications of the elimination of negative, distress-laden schemas begin to establish TRP Step V, the verification of markers of transformational change. Th: And has all this promoted any change in how you relate with her? Cl: Yes, because I think that now she's… closer, more… accessible!… it used to be so disturbing because she's someone who disappeared and just… she was gone, there was nothing. Nothing! And now I have my little place (clasping her hands across her chest) where, if I want, I can find her. There's a space here where we can find each other. Not in the human and material way that I want, but now she's closer and more within reach. I have more tools and resources, because I've seen it and experienced it, so I know that if I want, and if I make the effort—because I see it as an effort—I can access her. I can ask her to be there, and she'll be there. TRP COMMENTARY: In addition to the transformation of her mental model of her mother, a transformation has occurred in her mental model of their connection. Previously, her mother was “someone who disappeared and just… she was gone, there was nothing. Nothing!” Now, the “alliance” that her mother told her she was seeking with her is established, and Alba feels and knows that an inner togetherness is always available whenever she wants to enjoy it. These are more markers of transformational change, adding to TRP Step V.

Additional markers of change As noted, on the Inventory of Complicated Grief (ICG), Alba had scored 51 before beginning this therapeutic program. One week prior to her third ayahuasca session, her ICG score was down to 34, but still above 30, the threshold level indicating complicated grief. One week after that third session and the narrative reconstruction session that followed it, her ICG score was 7, and after another

234 One Core Process in Therapies of Transformational Change three weeks her score was 13, indicating effective resolution of her complicated grief condition. On another standard instrument, Alba's score for depression was high before, but was well below the threshold after, this therapeutic process. Verification of transformational change through memory reconsolidation (TRP Step V) requires, however, a longer-term confirmation that specific symptoms no longer occur and specific symptom-generating schemas no longer feel true and no longer reactivate. To make that verification, the first author of this book contacted co-therapist and principal investigator Débora González, resulting in the designing of a follow-up consisting of interviews to which Alba was invited six years after her ayahuasca-assisted therapy. We are grateful

Zeigarnik Effect

Reviewed by Gary Drevitch on November 10, 2025

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/docs/editorial-process

The Zeigarnik Effect is the power of unfinished business or interrupted or uncompleted activity to hold a privileged place in

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/memory

. Unfinished tasks create a cognitive burden, weigh more heavily on the mind, and are more easily recalled than completed tasks.

The Zeigarnik Effect explains why people are haunted by unfulfilled

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/motivation

and may be more apt to recall what they haven't achieved than what they have. Some have speculated that the cognitive burden of unfinished work causes some to see themselves negatively and contributes to such problems as

impostor syndrome

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/imposter-syndrome

Understanding the Zeigarnik Effect

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/zeigarnik-effect#understanding-the-zeigarnik-effect

Harnessing the Zeigarnik Effect

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/zeigarnik-effect#harnessing-the-zeigarnik-effect

Understanding the Zeigarnik Effect

Research has also established that unfulfilled goals can create intrusive thoughts when doing unrelated tasks and lead to poor performance of those tasks. However, creating specific plans for the unfulfilled goals eliminates the interference. Drafting and committing to a completion plan, researchers say, releases the cognitive burden and frees cognitive resources for other pursuits. Score 1 for to-do lists.

Does the Zeigarnik Effect operate in interpersonal relationships?

Created with Sketch.

The Zeigarnik Effects may explain the power of unprocessed negative events to undermine intimate relationships. Such events may be preferentially remembered and mentally replayed until they undermine trust and put partners on a downward cascading path of suspicion and hostility.

How was the Zeigarnik Effect discovered?

Created with Sketch.

The effect was first described by Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik in 1927. She was inspired to study the phenomenon after her professor, prominent psychologist Kurt Lewin, noticed that a waiter could remember in detail restaurant orders that had not yet been paid but could not remember the details of the orders once everyone had paid.

After designing experiments to observe the effect and explore the mental components, Zeigarnik found that an uncompleted task creates tension that makes its elements cognitively accessible until the task is discharged. Her experiments involved the assigning of tasks to study participants and, under controlled conditions, interrupting them at the halfway point or allowing them to complete the tasks undisturbed, then, an hour later, asking the participants to recall the details of their tasks.

article continues after advertisement

Harnessing the Zeigarnik Effect

The Zeigarnik Effect can be

harnessed to boost recall

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/natural-order/202209/how-the-little-known-zeigarnik-effect-impacts-everyone-daily

. If you are trying to learn or memorize a body of facts, take time out in the middle of the task to focus on some other activity. Then, return to the learning task. Taking short breaks—of a few minutes to one hour—during a series of study sessions improves learning.

Can the Zeigarnik Effect be used to combat

procrastination

https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/procrastination

Created with Sketch.

Yes. Taking the first step on a project, no matter how small, can create enough tension when the task is interrupted to motivate the resumption of the task.

What does the Zeigarnik Effect teach us about multitasking?

Created with Sketch.

The Zeigarnik Effect makes a powerful case against multitasking. Focusing on one task at a time will avert intrusive thoughts of unfinished work that will only create delays in finishing all the tasks. Completion of each task approached sequentially instead of simultaneously will clear mental space for the next task.

Psychology & Behavior

The Core Idea

In 1927, Bluma Zeigarnik was sitting in a Viennese café with her doctoral adviser, Kurt Lewin, when Lewin noticed something about the waiter. The waiter could remember every detail of an open order — who ordered what, which table, which modifications — with perfect accuracy. The moment the bill was paid and the table cleared, the information vanished. Ask the waiter five minutes later what the table had ordered, and he couldn't recall. The open order occupied his mind. The closed order released it. Lewin turned to Zeigarnik and said: there's a dissertation in that.

Zeigarnik designed the experiments. She gave subjects a series of simple tasks and interrupted half of them before completion. She then tested recall. The result: subjects remembered the interrupted, incomplete tasks 90% better than the completed ones. The incomplete task stayed active in memory. The completed task was filed away. The mind doesn't treat finished and unfinished business equally. Unfinished business occupies a privileged position — it persists, it intrudes, and it demands resolution.

The mechanism is cognitive tension until closure. The incomplete task generates a state of unresolved processing that the brain is driven to resolve. The tension is not a metaphor. It is a measurable increase in cognitive activation. The brain allocates working memory to the open loop, keeping it accessible and intrusive, until the task is completed or the loop is closed through some other resolution — writing it down, delegating it, explicitly deciding to abandon it.

LinkedIn's "Complete your profile" bar exploits this mechanism. The bar shows "Your profile is 85% complete" — and the 15% gap creates an open loop that nags. Not loudly. Persistently. Duolingo's streaks operate through the same mechanism: an unbroken streak is a completed pattern, and breaking it creates an open loop that generates tension disproportionate to the actual consequences. Netflix's "Continue watching" and cliffhanger autoplay are the Zeigarnik Effect in narrative form: the episode ends mid-scene, mid-crisis — creating an open loop so intense that the viewer's brain demands resolution. Progress bars at 90% are more motivating than progress bars at 12% because the proximity to completion intensifies the cognitive tension.

David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD) system is the most sophisticated application of the Zeigarnik Effect in productivity. Allen's core insight: your brain is a terrible storage system for open loops. Every unprocessed commitment occupies working memory as an open loop. Each loop generates cognitive tension. The cumulative effect of dozens of open loops is the feeling of being overwhelmed — not because the tasks are difficult, but because the aggregate cognitive tension saturates working memory. Allen's prescription: capture every open loop externally and process each one to its "next action." The act of capturing closes the loop cognitively. The waiter doesn't need to remember the order because the pad remembers it.

The strategic implication: open loops are the most powerful engagement mechanism that doesn't require a reward. Variable reinforcement works through dopamine and anticipated reward. The Zeigarnik Effect works through cognitive tension and the drive for closure. You don't need to promise something good at the end of the loop. You just need to leave the loop open. The human brain will do the rest.

Strategic use falls into two categories: create productive incompleteness (onboarding steps that pull users toward completion) or reduce unproductive incompleteness (clear your inbox, capture commitments so your brain can release them). Related to attention residue — unfinished tasks consume mental bandwidth even when you've switched to something else. The waiter's mind was not choosing to remember the open orders. His brain was involuntarily maintaining them because they were unresolved.
